Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

Count the joints, chart the fever · Six weeks of arthritis, then joints and fever set the subtype

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Arthritis for 6 weeks or more, before age 16, with no other cause is JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis). The diagnosis is clinical.

Set the subtype by the first 6 months:

  • Systemic: any joints, plus daily fever spikes for 2 weeks or more, with an evanescent salmon rash, nodes, big liver or spleen, or serositis
  • Polyarticular: 5 or more joints, symmetric; no fever or rash
  • Oligoarticular: 4 or fewer, usually a knee or ankle

Treat with an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) first, such as naproxen; weekly methotrexate when arthritis persists. Systemic: NSAID and steroids, then a biologic.

Slit lamp every 3 months if oligoarticular or RF (rheumatoid factor) negative polyarticular, ANA (antinuclear antibody) positive, onset before 7 and within 4 years of onset; otherwise every 6 to 12 months.

Low counts in two or more cell lines in a child labelled systemic JIA: bone marrow before any steroid.

Diagnosis
JIA subtypes All – true swelling, morning stiffness that eases, 6 weeks, no other cause · Systemic – fever 2 weeks or more plus rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or serositis; boys and girls equally · Polyarticular – 5 or more joints; peaks at 2 to 5 and 10 to 14; girls more · Oligoarticular – 4 or fewer joints; ages 2 to 4; girls more
Mimics: what the stem shows instead
MimicThe tellTreat
Gonococcal arthritissexually active; one joint or a few, asymmetric; tenosynovitis; vesiculopustulesCeftriaxone
Lyme arthritisone large joint, usually the knee, after erythema migrans in an endemic areaDoxycycline
Hypothyroidismaches and fatigue, no true swelling; height velocity fallsLevothyroxine
Vitamin D deficiencydiffuse bone pain, same all day; no swellingVitamin D and calcium
Leukemiacytopenias, bone painBone marrow first
Dengue, malariaacute fever after travel; dengue lowers the counts and bruises; malaria has no rashInfection workup, not JIA therapy
Management and treatment
Management ladder: JIA
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineNSAID such as naproxen; steroid injection into a few jointsArthritis persists on the NSAID
PersistentWeekly methotrexateMethotrexate fails
RheumatologyA biologicTop rung
By situation Systemic – NSAIDs and steroids, then a biologic · MAS – ferritin in the thousands, high triglycerides, falling ESR and fibrinogen, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation): high-dose steroids, after a marrow if two lines are low · Uveitis – oligoarticular highest, polyarticular too, systemic lowest; enthesitis-related (older boys, HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen type B-27)) gives a red, painful eye · One hot joint – in a child on methotrexate it is septic until the fluid says otherwise
Practice
  1. 5-year-old girl with 6 weeks of swollen knees and wrists 3 weeks of fever to 39.5 °C each evening, normal by morning salmon-pink rash with each spike that fades hepatosplenomegaly WBC 21,000/mm³ · platelets 610,000/mm³ · ANA low-titer positive · RF negative → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis → quotidian fever with an evanescent rash and 6 weeks of arthritis, with high counts: systemic JIA; a low-titer ANA does not exclude it, lupus lowers counts, and rheumatic fever's fever is persistent with a rash whose margin expands
  2. 5-year-old girl with 2 weeks of daily fever and 3 weeks of a swollen right knee parents' log: spikes to 39.8 °C each evening rash with each spike Seen in the afternoon, well appearing T 37.0 °C · ESR 64 mm/h → Continue the evaluation for systemic JIA → quotidian fever returns to normal between spikes, so a normal clinic temperature excludes nothing; no focus and well between spikes is not a bacterial infection
  3. 6-year-old boy diagnosed with systemic JIA a year ago, now persistently febrile oozing at venipuncture sites hepatosplenomegaly WBC 6,000/mm³ · platelets 92,000/mm³ · ferritin 18,000 ng/mL · fibrinogen 110 mg/dL · ESR 6 mm/h (70 last month) · AST 220 U/L · triglycerides 380 mg/dL → Macrophage activation syndrome → in systemic JIA, persistent fever with ESR and fibrinogen falling as ferritin, triglycerides and AST climb, and oozing from consumed clotting factors: macrophage activation syndrome; with only platelets low, high-dose steroids
  4. 4-year-old girl diagnosed 1 month ago with arthritis of the left knee and right ankle ANA positive no eye pain, redness or blurred vision Knee swelling improving on naproxen Afebrile · visual acuity 20/30 both eyes → Slit-lamp exam for asymptomatic uveitis → young, ANA positive and few joints carries the highest uveitis risk, and it is silent: slit-lamp exams every 3 months
  5. 4-year-old boy with 6 weeks of evening fever spikes since a trip to Costa Rica pink rash with each spike, gone by morning right knee swollen 6 weeks; spleen tip palpable Well between spikes hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL · platelets 640,000/mm³ → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis → weeks of quotidian fever with an evanescent rash, mild anemia and high platelets: systemic JIA; dengue and malaria are acute and usually lower platelets, and malaria has no rash
  6. 7-year-old boy with 4 weeks of daily evening fevers to 39.6 °C normal temperature each morning salmon rash during fevers; both knees and the left wrist swollen for 7 weeks pericardial rub Afebrile in clinic → High WBC and platelets, high ferritin; ANA and RF negative → systemic JIA is inflammation without autoantibodies: high WBC, platelets, ESR and ferritin; ANA and RF usually negative
  7. 3-year-old girl with 8 weeks of a swollen, warm left knee limps after waking, better by afternoon right ankle also swollen No fever or rash; lives in a nonendemic area; no tick bites Afebrile · ANA positive → Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis → 4 or fewer joints for 8 weeks with morning stiffness: oligoarticular JIA; nonendemic with no tick bite argues against Lyme; ANA positive and young: slit-lamp exams
  8. 13-year-old girl with 2 months of aching legs, hips and back pain the same all day; no morning stiffness no joint swelling; tibias tender to pressure Strict vegan diet without fortified foods Afebrile · height and weight steady → Vitamin D deficiency → diffuse bone pain that never eases and no swollen joints, on an unfortified vegan diet: vitamin D and calcium
  9. 14-year-old girl, ankles aching 3 months since starting daily walks this month knees, elbows, wrists; all swollen bilaterally stiff mornings that ease Tired despite 9 hours' sleep; new plant-based diet Afebrile · weight 95th to 90th percentile · height steady · chest normal → Naproxen → 5 or more joints within months, symmetric, stiff in the morning and easing: polyarticular JIA; naproxen first, methotrexate if it persists; deficiency pain never eases or swells joints, and falling weight with steady height is not hypothyroidism
  10. 4-year-old girl labeled systemic JIA 6 weeks ago, joints improving on naproxen now pale, with petechiae on her trunk and legs lymph nodes enlarged in the neck and groin T 39.4 °C · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · WBC 2,100/mm³ · platelets 38,000/mm³ → Bone marrow aspiration → low counts in two or more cell lines in a child labeled systemic JIA: bone marrow first; leukemia mimics JIA, and a steroid can mask it and change the marrow
  11. 9-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a swollen right knee stiff after waking, better by noon no preceding diarrhea, urethritis or rash; nonendemic area No injury; walks with a slight limp Afebrile · WBC normal · ESR 32 mm/h → Naproxen and reassess at 6 weeks → JIA needs 6 weeks of arthritis with no other cause: treat the pain and reassess before labeling it or starting methotrexate
Pairs with Acute Leukemia in a Child: the marrow comes before the steroid. Septic Arthritis in a Child: one hot joint on methotrexate. The Limping Child: sick or well, then age and time.
Transferable rule

Before naming JIA, time the arthritis, chart the fever and look at every cell line.

Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth

trisomies, cri-du-chat and Turner · the newborn with multiple anomalies · the floppy newborn · the trisomy 18 murmurWhich finding belongs to only one syndrome: the hands, the tone, the nose or the eye?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Name the syndrome by its rarest finding, never its commonest: a heart defect, cleft palate and cryptorchidism sit on several lists.

  • Trisomy 18 (Edwards): overlapping fingers, hypertonia, micrognathia.
  • Trisomy 21 (Down): hypotonia, transverse palmar crease.
  • Cri-du-chat (5p deletion): the cat-like cry.
  • Turner (45,X): the webbed neck.
  • CHARGE (coloboma, heart defect, atresia choanae, retarded growth and development, genitourinary and ear anomalies): among these, the only one with choanal atresia; coloboma is CHARGE or trisomy 13.
  • Trisomy 13 (Patau): midline defects; a small head separates it from CHARGE.
  • VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb): no eye or nasal component.

Maternal age acts through meiotic nondisjunction: sporadic, not inherited.

Diagnosis
The feature map: one signature finding each
SyndromeSignatureAlso
Trisomy 18Clenched fists, overlapping fingers; hypertoniaGrowth restriction, microcephaly with prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set pointed ears, absent palmar creases, limited hip abduction, rocker-bottom feet; ventricular septal defect (VSD); Meckel diverticulum, malrotation and omphalocele in over three quarters; about 95% die in the first year
Trisomy 13Cutis aplasia, microphthalmiaMicrocephaly, holoprosencephaly, omphalocele, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, coloboma, cryptorchidism; highly lethal
Trisomy 21Transverse palmar crease; hypotoniaUp-slanting fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots, protruding tongue; under 2.5 kg; heart defects, intestinal atresia; young mothers too
Cri-du-chatCat-like cryMicrocephaly with protruding metopic suture, hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, hypotonia
TurnerWebbed neckLow hairline, widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, short stature; coarctation
CHARGEChoanal atresia; colobomaCleft lip or palate, hypotonia, anosmia: common, not identifying
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge)Hypocalcemic seizure, absent thymic shadowConotruncal defect such as truncus arteriosus, cleft palate
VACTERLImperforate anus or radial ray defectHemivertebrae, tracheoesophageal fistula, renal anomaly
Fanconi anemiaAbnormal thumbs with abnormal pigmentationCafé-au-lait macules, short stature, renal and ear anomalies; marrow failure later
CHARGE, letter by letter C: coloboma – a gap in an eye structure · H: heart defect – tetralogy of Fallot or VSD, commonly · A: atresia choanae – a 5-French catheter will not pass either naris · R: retarded growth and development – postnatal, not visible at an hour of life · G: genitourinary – cryptorchidism · E: ear – short, wide, lobeless; hearing loss
The floppy newborn Vertical suspension – held under the arms, the hypotonic infant slips through, limbs extended · Down syndrome – floppy from birth, low birth weight, up-slanting fissures · Prader-Willi syndrome – almond-shaped eyes, small genitalia, undescended testes; paternal chromosome 15 genes lost; hyperphagia later · Infant botulism – well for weeks to months, then constipation and descending weakness; soil, dust or honey; no dysmorphism · Fragile X syndrome – X-linked; may be floppy in infancy; normal birth weight, no newborn dysmorphism; long face, large ears, macroorchidism later · Congenital hypothyroidism – normal at birth; weeks later lethargy, constipation, prolonged jaundice; newborn screen
The trisomy 18 murmur, and the blue newborn VSD – the commonest; holosystolic, left lower sternal border, louder as pulmonary resistance falls · Atrial septal defect – fixed split second heart sound (S2), left upper sternal border · Patent ductus arteriosus – continuous, left infraclavicular · Transposition, truncus arteriosus – central cyanosis, single S2; not trisomy 18 lesions · Acrocyanosis – blue hands and feet, pink lips and tongue: normal
Management
What to do Bilateral choanal atresia – an airway emergency in an obligate nasal breather: oral airway until surgical repair · Trisomy 18 – multidisciplinary supportive and palliative care · Infant botulism – botulism immune globulin · Acrocyanosis – reassurance
Practice
  1. Newborn girl has fetal growth restriction and microcephaly hypertonia, with clenched fists second digit overlapping the third Prenatal ultrasound showed a ventricular septal defect Afebrile · HR 150/min · lips and tongue pink → Trisomy 18 → overlapping fingers with hypertonia is the trisomy 18 hand; trisomy 21 is hypotonic and trisomy 13 is the midline trisomy
  2. Newborn girl delivered for fetal growth restriction hypertonia; clenched fists second finger over third, fifth over fourth prenatal ultrasound: ventricular septal defect Mother 40 years old; further testing declined HR 148/min · weight and head circumference below 5th percentile → Micrognathia → micrognathia travels with a prominent occiput, low-set pointed ears and rocker-bottom feet; cutis aplasia is trisomy 13, a transverse crease trisomy 21
  3. 1-day-old boy, 36 weeks, feeds poorly small jaw, prominent occiput, overlapping fingers no palmar creases, convex soles, limited hip abduction Fetal movement decreased; prenatal testing declined HR 150/min · pink mouth, bluish hands and feet · left lower sternal border murmur → Ventricular septal defect → the trisomy 18 profile; its commonest lesion is a ventricular septal defect, louder as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; blue hands with a pink mouth are acrocyanosis; truncus arteriosus gives central cyanosis and a single S2 and belongs to 22q11 deletion
  4. 2-month-old girl with a 47,+18 karyotype feeds slowly soft systolic ejection murmur, left upper sternal border second heart sound widely split, fixed with breathing Lips and tongue pink HR 150/min · respiratory rate 44/min → Atrial septal defect → a fixed split from increased right-sided flow, heard at the left upper border, not the left lower
  5. 40-year-old woman delivers a girl with clenched, overlapping fingers hypertonia, micrognathia, prominent occiput rocker-bottom feet Infant karyotype: 47,+18 in every cell; no family history of chromosomal disease infant HR 150/min · afebrile → Meiotic nondisjunction in oogenesis → homologous chromosomes fail to separate in the egg, giving a disomic gamete; sporadic, not inherited
  6. 1-day-old girl has clenched fists with overlapping fingers growth restriction and marked microcephaly micrognathia, low-set pointed ears, rocker-bottom feet Rapid testing shows three chromosome 18 signals HR 155/min · holosystolic murmur → Full karyotype → rapid fluorescence in situ hybridization is fast but misses mosaicism; a full karyotype across multiple cells confirms and also finds translocations; the karyotype, not a microarray alone, is the confirming test
  7. 3-day-old boy has a large ventricular septal defect karyotype: 47,+18 in multiple cells abdominal ultrasound shows an omphalocele and malrotation Parents ask what care should follow HR 160/min · oxygen saturation 95% → Supportive and palliative care → about half die within 2 weeks and 95% within the first year; a multidisciplinary team plans supportive and palliative care
  8. 38-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has first-trimester screening low pregnancy-associated plasma protein A low human chorionic gonadotropin Ultrasound shows an enlarged nuchal translucency BP 118/72 mm Hg · HR 80/min → Chorionic villus sampling → a positive screen is never a diagnosis: a karyotype on chorionic villi or amniotic fluid confirms
  9. Newborn boy has a head circumference below the 3rd percentile cleft lip and palate, coloboma, microphthalmia punched-out scalp defects (cutis aplasia), postaxial polydactyly Omphalocele; cryptorchidism; holoprosencephaly on imaging HR 150/min · catheters pass both nares → Trisomy 13 → the midline trisomy: scalp, eye, forebrain and abdominal wall, with a small head and nares that are patent
  10. 2-day-old girl, born at term, has a high-pitched cry like a cat's microcephaly with a protruding metopic suture hypertelorism and a flat nasal bridge Low muscle tone; feeds slowly Afebrile · HR 140/min → Cri-du-chat syndrome → the cry names the 5p deletion; intellectual disability and short stature follow
  11. Newborn girl born at term is examined before going home webbed neck, low posterior hairline broad chest with widely spaced nipples Cubitus valgus at both elbows T 36.9 °C · HR 150/min · lips and tongue pink → Turner syndrome → 45,X: coarctation and gonadal dysgenesis go with it, so check the femoral pulses
  12. Newborn boy is floppy from birth up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds Brushfield spots; a single transverse palmar crease Feeds with a weak suck Afebrile · HR 145/min · open hands, no overlapping fingers → Trisomy 21 → hypotonia with a transverse palmar crease is trisomy 21, not the hypertonia of trisomy 18
  13. 1-hour-old boy, 37 weeks, turns blue when calm pinks up with crying: saturation 97% crying, 80% at rest a catheter will not pass either naris Coloboma, cleft palate, short lobeless ears holosystolic murmur · testes not palpable · normal head size → CHARGE syndrome → choanal atresia and coloboma together belong to CHARGE alone; a normal head excludes trisomy 13
  14. 1-hour-old boy turns blue whenever he stops crying pinks up again with each cry a catheter will not pass either naris Bilateral choanal atresia confirmed at the bedside oxygen saturation 80% at rest · HR 150/min → Place an oral airway → an oral airway does what crying was doing until surgical repair; bilateral choanal atresia in an obligate nasal breather is an airway emergency
  15. Newborn girl turns blue in the delivery room unless crying a catheter will not pass either naris desaturates with every feed oxygen saturation 78% while feeding · 97% while crying · HR 150/min → Bilateral obstruction leaves no route but the mouth → feeding is when it fails; the obligate nasal breather opens the mouth only by crying; unilateral atresia often waits for a first upper respiratory infection
  16. 2-day-old boy has coloboma and bilateral choanal atresia short, lobeless ears; cleft palate undescended testes Oral airway in place; feeding by orogastric tube HR 150/min · oxygen saturation 97% · no murmur heard yet → Echocardiogram and renal ultrasonography → the heart and kidneys are letters the examination cannot see; audiology too
  17. 3-day-old girl has coloboma of the right eye bilateral choanal atresia, oral airway placed echocardiogram: ventricular septal defect Short, lobeless ears; normal head circumference and thumbs; genitalia normal HR 152/min · afebrile → CHD7 gene testing → genetic confirmation of a diagnosis usually made clinically; the gene and the syndrome share their first two letters
  18. Newborn girl has hypoplastic thumbs on both hands several café-au-lait macules length below the 3rd percentile Ultrasound shows a horseshoe kidney; nares patent, eyes normal HR 150/min · echocardiogram: ventricular septal defect → Fanconi anemia → abnormal thumbs with abnormal pigmentation; marrow failure comes later
  19. Newborn boy cannot be fed: a catheter coils in the upper esophagus imperforate anus absent radius on the left Radiograph shows hemivertebrae HR 155/min · holosystolic murmur; echocardiogram: ventricular septal defect → VACTERL association → vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb: no eye or nasal component in this one; Fanconi anemia does not explain the esophageal atresia, imperforate anus or hemivertebrae, and its tell is abnormal thumbs with abnormal pigmentation
  20. 2-day-old boy born at term has a generalized seizure echocardiogram shows an interrupted aortic arch chest radiograph: no thymic shadow Cleft palate; dysmorphic ears ionized calcium low · HR 160/min · T 36.8 °C → 22q11.2 deletion syndrome → parathyroid and thymic failure together with a conotruncal defect
  21. 18-hour-old boy, home-born at term, floppy since birth weak suck, soon asleep held under arms, slips through; legs extended Mother 19, no prenatal care Up-slanting fissures, protruding tongue, narrow intact palate Afebrile · 2.3 kg · normal heart, lungs, abdomen → Down syndrome → hypotonia and a weak suck from birth, low birth weight and up-slanting fissures; a karyotype shows the extra chromosome 21
  22. 2-day-old boy born at term is profoundly floppy since birth suck too weak to feed without a nasogastric tube almond-shaped eyes Small penis; both testes undescended 3.2 kg · HR 140/min · normal palmar creases and palpebral fissures → Prader-Willi syndrome → loss of paternal chromosome 15 genes; hyperphagia and obesity follow in childhood
  23. 10-week-old girl, well until 4 days ago, is constipated weak cry, poor suck, drooping eyelids weakness descends face to arms, trunk Normal newborn screen; family lives beside a construction site Afebrile · sluggish pupils · normal birth weight · no dysmorphic features → Infant botulism → spores from soil and dust in a previously well infant; constipation, then descending weakness; botulism immune globulin
  24. 1-day-old girl born at term has bluish hands and feet lips and tongue pink feeding well No murmur; pulses normal in all limbs oxygen saturation 98% in right hand and foot · HR 140/min → Normal peripheral vasoconstriction → acrocyanosis, normal in a healthy newborn; cyanotic heart disease turns the lips, tongue and trunk blue; reassure
Traps Wrong trisomy: right family, another trisomy's signature finding. Tone ignored: hypertonia rules out trisomy 21. Ready slot: VACTERL fits anomalies in several systems, but needs its own components. Head not read: trisomy 13 shares coloboma, cleft palate, cryptorchidism and a heart defect with CHARGE; microcephaly and choanal atresia separate them. Loud murmur: the most striking finding and the least useful; every option carries a heart defect. Blue hands, pink mouth: acrocyanosis, not a cyanotic lesion. Truncus arteriosus: real, but a 22q11 lesion with a single S2. Atrial septal defect: also seen in trisomy 18, but heard at the left upper border.
Pearls Mosaic trisomy arises after fertilization, so the parents carry no recurrence risk. Isolated choanal atresia still sends you looking for the other CHARGE features. VACTERL and CHARGE overlap only in cardiac and renal anomalies. The gene CHD7 and the syndrome share their first two letters.
Pairs with Teratogenic Exposures: acquired dysmorphology; what are the hands doing, and is tone up or down? Congenital Hypothyroidism: hypotonic from the first hour, or later? Cyanosis in the Newborn: the catheter test and the crying maneuver; are the lips and tongue pink? Hypotonia in an Infant: the full workup and the Down syndrome health supervision grid; weak, or only floppy? Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi: which parent's copy is missing? 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome: that syndrome in depth. Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia: the VACTERL workup.
Transferable rule

Do not count the anomalies. Find the one finding that sits on the fewest syndrome lists and that you are certain belongs to this infant; shared findings show that a syndrome exists, never which one.

Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant

Correct the age, then read the chart · a percentile is a position, not a pathology

Source vignette Pt — 18 mo F, former 26-week preterm infant, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles; height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile · Q — the most likely assessment; options spanned normal growth and development for corrected age, global developmental delay and failure to thrive
The decision point

Calculate the corrected age first. Born at 26 weeks, she was 14 weeks early. At 18 months chronological age, her corrected age is about 14 and a half months. Judge every milestone against that age. She has just started walking, which is on time. Her vocabulary of 10 words is ahead of the three to five words expected at 15 months. Following a call, imitating and scribbling are age-appropriate.

All three parameters sit together at the 15th percentile. They are proportionate, symmetric and well within normal. Faltering growth requires a parameter below about the 2nd percentile or a downward crossing of two major lines, and she has neither.

Defining criteria Corrected age — chronological age minus the weeks born before 40 weeks · How long to correct — through 24 months for growth and development; newer data support 36 months in extremely and very preterm children · What is never corrected — immunizations, given at chronological age regardless of gestational age or birth weight; the one weight rule is the birth hepatitis B dose at 2 kg or more, and it is a weight threshold rather than an age correction · Normal percentile range — the 15th percentile is normal; faltering growth needs under about the 2nd percentile or a crossing of two major lines
Assessing the former preterm infant — the differential
AssessmentIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Normal for corrected agePreterm child meeting milestones and tracking a normal percentile once correctedCorrected-age milestones met, parameters proportionate above the 2nd percentile
Global developmental delaySignificant delay in two or more domains at corrected ageNot walking or no words at 18 months corrected, often with a falling head circumference
Isolated growth falteringWeight crosses percentiles downward with intact developmentWeight disproportionately low with length and head preserved
Failure to thriveInadequate calories, malabsorption or increased demandParameter below the 2nd percentile or crossing two major lines
Constitutional smallnessSmall but healthy child on a low-normal curveNormal growth velocity along their own percentile
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Growth plotted at corrected ageFirstAll three parameters together, above the 2nd percentileNormal growth; weight alone low points to inadequate calories
Developmental screen at corrected ageNextMilestones met for corrected ageNormal; delay in two or more domains needs early intervention referral
Retinopathy of prematurity exam and hearing screenScreenRetinopathy or failed hearing screenRequired by gestational age and birth weight, however well the infant looks
Cranial ultrasound, all born under 32 weeksConfirmsGerminal matrix or intraventricular bloodIVH; screen at 1 to 2 weeks, repeat to follow progression
CBC with reticulocyte countBy branchNormocytic anemia with no reticulocytosis for its degreeAnemia of prematurity; microcytosis or brisk reticulocytes point elsewhere
Failure-to-thrive laboratory workupSkipThe 15th percentile is normalProportionate, steady growth needs routine surveillance only
Scenario bank
  1. 18 mo F, former 26-week preemie, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles, with height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile corrected → Normal growth and development for corrected age → corrected age about 14 and a half months
  2. Former 26-week premature infant now 12 months chronological, how to plot her growth → Plot at corrected age until 24 months → chronological plotting overstates the deficit
  3. 6 mo old former 28-week premature infant due for routine immunizations → Immunize at chronological age on the standard schedule → prematurity is never corrected for vaccines
  4. 18 mo F, former 26-week preemie, not sitting, no words, head circumference below the 2nd percentile → Refer for developmental evaluation and early intervention → delay across multiple domains at corrected age
  5. Former 26-week premature infant at neonatal intensive care unit discharge, required screening → Retinopathy of prematurity screening — plus a hearing screen → screening driven by gestational age and birth weight
  6. 18 mo former premature infant with all growth parameters at the 15th percentile and tracking steadily → Continue routine surveillance → the 15th percentile is normal
  7. 15 mo M, former 30-week preemie, weight at the 2nd percentile with length at the 25th and head circumference at the 30th, corrected → Inadequate caloric intake → not explained by prematurity
  8. Why growth and development in a preterm child are assessed at corrected rather than chronological age → She has had fewer weeks of growth and brain development → uncorrected assessment falsely labels delay
  9. 24 mo former 26-week premature infant with normal growth and development → Stop correcting for prematurity → plot chronologically from here
  10. 6 wk old former 31-week infant, medically stable and gaining weight, parents asking about the 2-month vaccines → Give them at 2 months of chronologic age on the standard schedule → prematurity is never corrected for vaccines
  11. Why medically stable preterm infants are vaccinated on time rather than deferred → They are at high risk from vaccine-preventable disease and mount an adequate antibody response → immature is not immunocompromised
  12. Preterm infant weighing 1.8 kg at 12 h of life, mother hepatitis B surface antigen negative, due for the birth dose → Delay until the weight reaches 2 kg → the only weight-gated vaccine
  13. 1 wk old girl born at 29 weeks, birth weight 1.51 kg, tolerating feeds, normal vital signs, nondysmorphic, soft anterior fontanelle, moving all four limbs → Screening head ultrasound → all preterm infants under 32 weeks, at age 1 to 2 weeks
  14. Why prematurity under 32 weeks is the threshold for intraventricular hemorrhage screening → The germinal matrix involutes by 32 weeks → before then its thin-walled vessels rupture with swings in cerebral perfusion
  15. 3-day-old born at 28 weeks, 1.04 kg, Apgar scores 8 and 9, afebrile, no maternal fever, membranes ruptured 3 hours before birth; an hour of lethargy and hypotonia, apnea with bradycardia, a tense fontanelle, head circumference up 3 cm since yesterday, then a generalized seizure → Intraventricular hemorrhage → germinal matrix bleed; confirm with cranial ultrasound
  16. Neonate born at 29 weeks who on day 2 develops apnea, lethargy and a bulging anterior fontanelle → Cranial ultrasound → sees blood in the germinal matrix and ventricles through the open fontanelle
  17. 7 wk old born at 32 weeks, feeding and gaining well on fortified formula and ferrous sulfate, pulse 150 with a soft systolic flow murmur; hemoglobin 8, reticulocytes 1.4%, normal platelets and white count, normocytic normochromic smear → Impaired erythropoietin production → anemia of prematurity; the marrow is not asked to respond
  18. 10 wk old term infant, thriving and asymptomatic, hemoglobin 10 with a normocytic smear and normal platelets and white count → Physiologic anemia of infancy → the normal erythropoietin nadir at 2 to 3 months
  19. 6 wk old former 28-week infant with new apnea spells and flat weight gain; hemoglobin 6.5, low reticulocytes, no hemolysis → Red cell transfusion → symptomatic anemia of prematurity
Reading the neonatal history Former 26-week premature sets the age correction; it is not the problem. Mild bronchopulmonary dysplasia with normal head ultrasounds looks like a list of morbidities but is reassuring. Normal cranial imaging excludes the intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia that drive adverse neurodevelopmental outcome at this gestational age.
Intraventricular hemorrhage Mechanism — fragile germinal matrix vessels rupture with swings in cerebral perfusion (hypotension, hypoxia, hypo- or hyperventilation), and the blood can extend into the lateral ventricles · Who — under 32 weeks gestation or under 1500 g · When — the first few days of life, and often asymptomatic · Symptomatic signs — lethargy, hypotonia, seizures, apnea, bradycardia, a bulging fontanelle, a rapidly rising head circumference, acute anemia · Diagnosis — cranial ultrasound, repeated to follow progression; routine screening under 32 weeks · Versus hypoglycemia or hypocalcemia — lethargy, hypotonia and seizures, but never a growing head · Versus hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy — needs perinatal asphyxia and acidosis, not a day-3 onset after Apgar scores of 8 and 9 · Versus meningitis — needs fever or risk factors such as maternal fever or prolonged rupture of membranes
Anemia of prematurity Mechanism — oxygenation at birth (breathing, ductus closure) switches off erythropoietin; a preterm infant has also missed the third-trimester shift of erythropoietin production from liver to kidney · Why worse than term — lower hematocrit at birth, shorter red cell life span, frequent NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) blood draws, iron depletion · Timing — term physiologic anemia bottoms out at 9 to 11 g/dL at 2 to 3 months; the preterm nadir is deeper (about 7 g/dL) and earlier (1 to 2 months) · Presentation — often asymptomatic; tachycardia, a flow murmur, apnea, poor weight gain · Labs — normocytic, normochromic, normal platelets and white count; the absolute reticulocyte count may be normal for age, but there is no reticulocytosis for the degree of anemia · Management — iron supplementation and fewer blood draws; red cell transfusion if severe or symptomatic · Versus thalassemia — microcytic and hypochromic with target cells · Versus hemolysis — erythropoietin rises and the reticulocytes climb · Versus iron deficiency — microcytic, and unlikely on fortified formula with ferrous sulfate · Versus anemia of chronic disease — iron trapped in macrophages by chronic inflammation, infection or malignancy, in older children and adults
Pearls Head circumference is the parameter that predicts neurodevelopment, so preserved head growth in a former preemie is the most reassuring single measurement · A percentile by itself is not a pathology; the concerning patterns are crossing lines downward and disproportion between parameters · Retinopathy of prematurity and hearing screening are required by gestational age, however well the infant looks · A preterm infant is more vulnerable to vaccine-preventable disease, so the vaccine schedule is never delayed
Pairs with Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers the contrasting case. Ask: are the three parameters together or apart? Parameters that are together and steady are normal. Parameters that are apart, with weight lowest, indicate inadequate calories. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers the imaging diagnosis when the delay does not resolve with corrected age. Part I Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers apnea of prematurity, the diagnosis for the spells once intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia are excluded. Ask: did the spells start on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between episodes?
Transferable rule When a gestational age is given, do the arithmetic before interpreting anything. An option claiming that assessment is impossible is almost always wrong.
Uniform-answer doubtDeclining to assess is not caution; correction exists to make the assessment possible.
Treat-the-numberThe 15th percentile sounds low only against an unexamined assumption that normal means the 50th.
Class-vs-memberGlobal delay is a valid framework, but here it is judged against chronological rather than corrected age.

Acute Rheumatic Fever

The post-streptococcal sequence outweighs a vivid setting detail

The decision point

A sore throat 2 weeks ago was followed by migratory large-joint arthritis and a new holosystolic apical murmur with fever. That is 2 major Jones criteria on a strep foundation. A travel or camping detail is a setting, not a mechanism. There is no tick bite and no rash, and the 2–4 week latency belongs to the pharyngitis.

Jones criteria — 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus evidence of strep
  • Major (JONES): Joints (migratory polyarthritis) · O carditis · Nodules (subcutaneous) · Erythema marginatum · Sydenham chorea
  • Minor: fever, arthralgia, ↑ESR/CRP, prolonged PR
Pearls Type II hypersensitivity via molecular mimicry against M protein · Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells on pathology · the acute attack affects the mitral valve as regurgitation; decades later the valve disease presents as mitral stenosis · treatment is penicillin plus aspirin, then monthly benzathine penicillin for years · treating the pharyngitis prevents ARF (acute rheumatic fever) but not PSGN (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Throat culture or rapid strep testFirstOften negative by the time ARF appearsA negative swab does not exclude it; serology next
ASO and anti-DNase B titersNextElevated or rising titerEvidence of recent group A strep, required by the Jones criteria
ESR and CRPSupportsElevatedMinor criterion
ECGSupportsProlonged PR intervalMinor criterion
EchocardiographyStagingMitral regurgitationCarditis, a major criterion, even when no murmur is heard
None: Jones criteriaConfirms2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, with strep evidenceAcute rheumatic fever; no single test confirms it
Lyme serology after a camping tripSkipNo erythema migrans or tick biteLyme gives late monoarthritis and AV block, not a new valve murmur
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis → Acute rheumatic fever → penicillin plus anti-inflammatories
  2. 9 yo M with suspected acute rheumatic fever → Anti-streptolysin O titer
  3. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever; which valve is most often involved → Mitral
  4. 9 yo M with arthritis 10 days after a diarrheal illness, with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis
  5. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever and new choreiform movements → Sydenham chorea — a major criterion
  6. 9 yo M recovering from acute rheumatic fever → Long-term penicillin prophylaxis
  7. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis; history mentions a recent camping trip → Acute rheumatic fever → the trip is a setting, not a mechanism; no tick bite, no rash, and the latency belongs to the pharyngitis
Mimics Lyme needs erythema migrans. Its arthritis is late (months) and monoarticular, and its cardiac finding is AV block (atrioventricular block), not a valvular murmur. RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) needs headache and a rash involving palms and soles; it is a vasculitis, not an arthritis. JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) needs ≥6 weeks by definition.
How NBME framed it No sore throat was mentioned, only a recent refugee camp, which also invited the travel-fever decoys; Kawasaki disease appeared as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, and the mitral murmur was described, not named.
Salient decoy

edits.html:
Heart Failure in a Child

the viral prodrome that is not bronchiolitis · a gallop reassigns the failing organ

Source vignette Pt — 2 yo M, 4 days of rhinorrhea, congestion and low-grade fever, now tired with decreased urine output and labored breathing · Exam — T 38.2, HR 155, RR 48, BP 60/40, SpO2 91% on room air; scattered mobile subcentimetre anterior cervical nodes; gallop rhythm with a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex; brachial and femoral pulses 1+; nasal flaring, subcostal retractions and basal rales · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned acute rheumatic fever, bronchiolitis, glomerulonephritis, Kawasaki disease and myocarditis
The decision point

The respiratory findings are real, but every one of them is a consequence of the heart. Three cardiac findings decide the diagnosis: a gallop, a new holosystolic murmur at the apex, and 1+ pulses with a blood pressure of 60/40. A gallop is an S3, from a ventricle taking volume it cannot handle. In this setting, an apical holosystolic murmur is mitral regurgitation from ventricular dilation, not a primary valve lesion. Weak pulses with hypotension in a 2-year-old are shock. With basal rales and oliguria, this is acute left heart failure with pulmonary edema. That is why the lungs sound wet and the saturation is 91%. The viral prodrome is the cause, not a coincidence. The usual agents are coxsackievirus B and adenovirus. Myocyte injury is part direct and part immune-mediated.

Defining criteria Myocarditis — a viral prodrome, upper respiratory or gastrointestinal, then heart failure: respiratory distress, gallop, hepatomegaly, with or without arrhythmia, which is how it causes sudden death · Acute rheumatic fever gate — Jones criteria 2 to 4 weeks after untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis; a concurrent viral URI is the wrong illness at the wrong interval · Kawasaki gate — fever of 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 criteria, with a cervical node over 1.5 cm; four days of fever with no criteria does not open it · Workup — troponin, ECG showing sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST change, chest film showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema, and echocardiography showing diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction
Pertinent positives & negatives Gallop rhythm — an S3, the most specific finding in the stem for ventricular failure · Holosystolic murmur at the apex — functional mitral regurgitation from a dilated ventricle, new in a failing child · BP 60/40 with 1+ pulses — cardiogenic shock, an emergency · Basal rales with hypoxemia — pulmonary edema, not consolidation and not bronchospasm · No wheeze — argues strongly against bronchiolitis, whose classic finding it is · Decreased urine output — hypoperfusion; urine output reflects cardiac output · Subcentimetre mobile nodes — reactive to the viral illness and too small for Kawasaki, which requires over 1.5 cm · Fever 4 days with no rash, conjunctivitis or mucosal change — the Kawasaki gate fails on duration and on criteria count
Respiratory distress after a viral prodrome — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Viral myocarditis Can't missCoxsackie B or adenovirus; prodrome then failureGallop plus new apical holosystolic murmur plus poor perfusion after a URI— (the answer)
BronchiolitisRSV; first or second year, coryza then distressWheeze and hyperinflation; heart sounds normalNo wheeze; gallop and murmur unexplained by it
Acute rheumatic feverGAS pharyngitis, then an immune sequelJones criteria 2 to 4 weeks later; migratory arthritis, choreaConcurrent viral URI and no Jones criteria
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young children; can include myocarditisFever 5 or more days plus 4 criteria; node over 1.5 cmFour days of fever, no criteria, subcentimetre nodes
GlomerulonephritisPost-infectious or IgA; may follow a URIHematuria and Nephritic Syndrome, hypertension and edemaHypotensive rather than hypertensive; no hematuria
Management Treatment is supportive: diuresis, afterload reduction and inotropes. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) is an option that may reduce morbidity ⚠︎. Do not treat the shock reflexively. This child's hypotension is cardiogenic, so a rapid large-volume bolus worsens pulmonary edema. Give fluid cautiously and in small aliquots, or not at all, while getting the echocardiogram.
Decision spine Is there a gallop or a new murmur? — Yes means the heart is the failing organ, whatever the lungs are doing · Wheeze or rales? — Rales means edema, not bronchiolitis · What is the blood pressure and what are the pulses? — 60/40 with 1+ means shock · How long has the fever run, and how many Kawasaki criteria? — Four days and none, so the gate is closed · Was the antecedent illness strep pharyngitis 2 to 4 weeks ago? — No, it is concurrent coryza, so not rheumatic fever · So what confirms it? — Echocardiography with troponin, ECG and a chest film
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
ECGFirstSinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST changesSupports myocarditis; watch for arrhythmia, the cause of sudden death
TroponinFirstElevatedMyocyte injury
Chest radiographSupportsCardiomegaly with pulmonary edemaRales are edema, not bronchiolitis or pneumonia
EchocardiographyConfirmsDiffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fractionMyocarditis with heart failure; excludes a structural lesion
Cardiac MRI or endomyocardial biopsyBy branchMyocardial inflammation or lymphocytic infiltrateTissue-level confirmation when the diagnosis remains uncertain
ASO titerSkipNo pharyngitis 2 to 4 weeks earlier, no Jones criteriaConcurrent coryza is the wrong illness at the wrong interval for rheumatic fever
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M, 4 days of rhinorrhea and low-grade fever, now tired with decreased urine output; HR 155, RR 48, BP 60/40, gallop rhythm with a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex, 1+ pulses, basal rales → Viral myocarditis → acute decompensated heart failure
  2. 2 yo with a 4-day viral prodrome who now has a gallop, basal rales and poor peripheral perfusion → Echocardiography with troponin and ECG → diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction
  3. 3 yo with suspected myocarditis, hypotensive with a gallop, rales and hepatomegaly → A rapid 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus → the shock is cardiogenic, not hypovolemic
  4. 8 mo, 3 days of coryza, now wheezing with retractions and hyperinflation; heart sounds normal with no murmur → Bronchiolitis → supportive care and suctioning
  5. 6 yo with migratory polyarthritis and a new murmur 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat → Acute rheumatic fever → Jones criteria with an antistreptolysin O titer
  6. 4 yo with 6 days of fever, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a polymorphous rash and a 2 cm cervical node → Kawasaki disease → IVIG with aspirin
  7. The organisms most commonly responsible for myocarditis in children → Coxsackievirus B and adenovirus → direct viral injury plus immune-mediated myocyte necrosis
  8. 5 yo recovering from biopsy-proven myocarditis who has a syncopal episode and an irregular pulse → Continuous cardiac monitoring → arrhythmia is the mechanism of sudden death
Pearls S3 or new murmur in any child in respiratory distress — heart failure until an echocardiogram says otherwise, however viral the story sounds · A new holosystolic murmur at the apex in a failing ventricle is functional mitral regurgitation — a consequence, not a second disease · Hypotension in myocarditis is cardiogenic: fluid loading fills the lungs and is the commonest management error · Rheumatic fever is defined by its interval, 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis; a murmur appearing during a viral illness is myocarditis · Kawasaki's fever requirement is five days, and it is mandatory
Pairs with Part II Shock in Children covers the perfusion categories and the cardiogenic-versus-distributive fork. Part I Acute Rheumatic Fever covers Jones and the post-streptococcal interval. Kawasaki Disease covers the five-day fever requirement. Ask: is there a gallop or a new murmur, and how long has the fever run?
Transferable rule When respiratory findings are prominent and cardiac findings are subtle, read the cardiac findings first. A gallop, a new murmur or weak pulses point to the heart as the failing organ. The lung signs are then a consequence rather than a cause.
Unchecked attributeAcute rheumatic fever: fever with a new murmur after an infection is its exact shape, but the antecedent is coryza not pharyngitis, the interval is concurrent not 2 to 4 weeks, and no Jones criteria are met.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: genuinely causes myocarditis, but fever is 4 days and no criteria are met; the nodes are subcentimetre against a 1.5 cm requirement.
True-fact-wrong-slotGlomerulonephritis: oliguria after a URI (upper respiratory infection) fits, but it presents with hematuria and hypertension, and this child is hypotensive with unexplained cardiac findings.
Salient decoyBronchiolitis: the whole respiratory picture and the age fit, but it explains nothing cardiac and the classic wheeze is absent while rales are present.

edits.html:
22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome

the syndrome cluster is given; identify the missing component · read the last sentence first

Source vignette Pt — 3 h old F, 38 wk by cesarean for nonreassuring tones, Apgars 8 and 8, moved to the nursery for a dusky appearance; cyanotic and tremulous, with low-set ears, micrognathia and a cleft palate · Labs — pulse oximetry 72% in the right hand and the leg, unchanged after 10 minutes of 100% oxygen by hood · Imaging — chest radiograph shows an absent thymus; echocardiography shows truncus arteriosus · Q — which condition this patient most likely has; options spanned anemia, duodenal atresia, horseshoe kidney, hypocalcemia, hypoglycemia, myelomeningocele and neutropenia
The decision point

The vignette already gives the diagnosis. Conotruncal defect plus absent thymus plus cleft palate plus low-set ears and micrognathia is 22q11.2 deletion. Every answer option is a condition, not a syndrome. CATCH lists the components: Cardiac outflow anomaly, Anomalous face, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia. Four of the five are printed in the vignette; the missing one is hypocalcemia. The clue is in the physical examination: tremulous is neonatal hypocalcemia. This matters because these infants are at real risk of tetany, seizures and arrhythmia.

Defining criteria CATCH-22 — Cardiac outflow tract anomaly such as truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot or interrupted aortic arch; Anomalous face with prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears and micrognathia; Thymic hypoplasia or aplasia reducing T-cell immunity; Cleft palate; and Hypoparathyroidism producing hypocalcemia · DiGeorge versus velocardiofacial syndrome — both are 22q11.2 phenotypes; DiGeorge requires thymic involvement, with a CD3+ T-cell count under 500/mm3, while velocardiofacial requires facial abnormalities · Pathogenesis — loss of genes controlling third and fourth pharyngeal pouch derivation and neural crest migration, which is why the thymus, parathyroids, palate, face and cardiac outflow tract fail together
Pertinent positives & negatives Absent thymus on chest radiograph — third and fourth pouch failure; the most specific finding in the stem and the reason this is DiGeorge rather than isolated truncus · Truncus arteriosus — a conotruncal defect, the cardiac C · Cleft palate, low-set ears, micrognathia — the C and the A; with the thymus, four of five CATCH letters are printed · Tremulous — neonatal hypocalcemia before it becomes tetany · Saturation 72% in right hand and leg — no differential cyanosis, which excludes severe coarctation and interrupted arch physiology, and with them Turner syndrome · Refractory to 100% oxygen for 10 minutes — a fixed right-to-left shunt, confirming cyanotic structural heart disease rather than lung disease · Apgars 8 and 8, uncomplicated pregnancy, primigravida — no asphyxia and no maternal diabetes, closing the usual setups for hypoglycemia · No abdominal or spinal findings — nothing pointing at duodenal atresia or a neural tube defect
The dysmorphic neonate with a heart defect — which syndrome has which finding
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge)Pouch 3 and 4 failure; conotruncal defect, hypoplastic thymus and parathyroidsAbsent thymus plus conotruncal defect plus cleft palate; hypocalcemia is the fourth member— (the answer)
Down syndrome (trisomy 21)Commonest aneuploidy; AV septal defect, hypotoniaDuodenal atresia with a double bubble, single palmar crease, upslanting fissuresThymus present; no gastrointestinal malformation described
Turner syndrome (45,X)Female, short stature, gonadal dysgenesisHorseshoe kidney, coarctation, webbed neck, wide-spaced nipplesEqual pre- and postductal saturations; no renal or neck findings
CHARGE associationColoboma, choanal atresia, ear anomaliesColoboma and choanal atresia alongside the heart defectNo eye or nasal findings; thymic loss is not its signature
Infant of a diabetic motherMacrosomia, transposition, septal hypertrophyHypoglycemia in the first hours with a high birth weightPregnancy uncomplicated in a primigravida, no macrosomia
Management, in one line Once 22q11.2 is suspected, send an ionized calcium and get an echocardiogram. Confirm the deletion with chromosomal microarray or FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization). Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia with intravenous calcium. Until the T-cell count is known, these infants get irradiated, leukoreduced blood products and no live vaccines ⚠︎.
Decision spine Read the last sentence first. — It asks for a condition, not a diagnosis · Name the syndrome from the cluster. — Conotruncal defect plus absent thymus plus cleft palate is 22q11.2 · Recite CATCH and cross off what is printed. — Cardiac, face, thymus and cleft are all given, so H is missing · Look for its bedside tell. — Tremulous means hypocalcemia · Assign each remaining option to its own syndrome. — Horseshoe kidney to Turner, duodenal atresia to Down, hypoglycemia to the infant of a diabetic mother, myelomeningocele to folate · Check the cell line. — DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, not neutrophils or red cells
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygenFirstSaturation unchanged, equal in hand and legFixed intracardiac shunt: cyanotic heart disease
EchocardiographyNextConotruncal defect: truncus, tetralogy or interrupted archRaises suspicion for 22q11.2 deletion
Chest radiographSupportsAbsent thymic shadowThymic hypoplasia or aplasia
Ionized calciumNextLowParathyroid hypoplasia; IV calcium if tremulous or seizing
Chromosomal microarray or FISH for 22q11.2ConfirmsMicrodeletion at 22q11.222q11.2 deletion syndrome
T-cell subsetsStagingCD3 count under 500/mm3DiGeorge immune phenotype: irradiated blood, no live vaccines
Standard karyotypeSkipNormal; the deletion is too small to seeUse microarray or FISH instead
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old F, cyanosis refractory to 100% oxygen, saturation 72% in right hand and leg, low-set ears, micrognathia, cleft palate, absent thymus on chest film, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, tremulous on examination → Hypocalcemia → parathyroid hypoplasia in 22q11.2 deletion
  2. Term neonate with truncus arteriosus, cleft palate and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph → Chromosomal microarray for the 22q11.2 deletion → a standard karyotype does not resolve a microdeletion
  3. Neonate with known 22q11.2 deletion who develops a generalized seizure; ionized calcium is low → Intravenous calcium gluconate → hypocalcemic seizure from parathyroid hypoplasia
  4. 4 mo old with 22q11.2 deletion and a CD3+ T-cell count of 210/mm3, presenting for routine immunizations → The live attenuated rotavirus vaccine → live vaccines are withheld until CD3 and CD4 exceed 500/mm3 and CD8 exceeds 200/mm3 with a normal mitogen response
  5. Newborn with a double-bubble sign on abdominal radiograph, a single transverse palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect → Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
  6. Newborn girl with coarctation of the aorta, a webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples and a horseshoe kidney → Turner syndrome → 45,X
  7. Why the thymus, parathyroids, palate and cardiac outflow tract fail together in this syndrome → Failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development with abnormal neural crest migration → one embryologic field, four organs
  8. 6 yo with 22q11.2 deletion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and poor responses to polysaccharide vaccines → T-cell subsets with quantitative immunoglobulins → humoral failure follows defective T-cell help
Decoy note Tremulous is the bedside sign of both neonatal hypoglycemia and neonatal hypocalcemia. An uncomplicated pregnancy in a primigravida with Apgars of 8 closes off the hypoglycemia route. The equal right-hand and leg saturations read as an incidental vital sign, but they exclude differential cyanosis, and with it coarctation and Turner syndrome.
Pearls Syndrome with a missing component: when a vignette describes most of a syndrome, recite the mnemonic and cross off what is printed. Answer with the remainder; CATCH, JONES and CREST are tested this way · Hypocalcemia and hypoglycemia share a neonatal presentation of jitteriness, tremor and seizure, and the pregnancy history separates them · Differential cyanosis means ductal or arch pathology; equal pre- and postductal saturations mean a fixed intracardiac shunt, which is what truncus produces · DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, so an option of neutropenia or anemia tests which lineage the thymus governs · Until the T-cell count is back, these infants need irradiated leukoreduced blood and no live vaccines ⚠︎ · The same deletion has two names: thymic involvement makes it DiGeorge, and facial abnormality makes it velocardiofacial
Pairs with Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers truncus arteriosus within the cyanosis differential, and the oxygen-refractory shunt logic that leads to it. Antibody Deficiencies covers the downstream question of which immunodeficiency the absent thymus produces. Ask: is the thymic shadow present, and does the face carry a syndrome? Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth places this syndrome beside CHARGE, VACTERL, trisomy 13 and Fanconi anaemia. There, the deciding finding is the one on the fewest lists.
Transferable rule Read the last sentence before the vignette. When a vignette assembles a recognisable syndrome, the diagnosis is given, and the question asks for the component it left out. That component usually has a one-word bedside sign in the physical examination.
True-fact-wrong-slotHorseshoe kidney: a real and memorable syndrome pairing, but it belongs to Turner, and the equal limb saturations already exclude Turner's coarctation.
True-fact-wrong-slotDuodenal atresia: congenital heart disease with low-set ears reads as Down syndrome, but that is where duodenal atresia belongs and Down has no thymic aplasia.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenia: DiGeorge genuinely causes a cytopenia, but the lineage is lymphocytes; red cell and neutrophil counts are unaffected.
Mirror twinHypoglycemia: a tremulous neonate is the classic hypoglycemia cue and also the hypocalcemia cue, but this pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal Apgars.

edits.html:
Rhinitis

Step-up therapy in the right order

The decision point

For moderate-to-severe seasonal rhinitis that has failed antihistamines, step up to an intranasal corticosteroid. It is the single most effective drug class for allergic rhinitis. A visit in "late winter" points to prophylaxis: start it ~2 weeks before pollen season. The steroid suppresses the mucosal inflammatory response and needs lead time.

Option analysis — why each fails
ChoiceWhy it fails
Minimize outdoor activitiesImpractical for pollen (unlike dust mites or pets); inadequate once disease is complicated
Continue OTC antihistaminesAlready failing — and first-generation agents bring sedation and anticholinergic effects
Desensitization (immunotherapy)The real bait — the only disease-modifying option, but reserved for failure of maximal pharmacotherapy. He has never tried a nasal steroid
MontelukastLess effective than intranasal steroids; carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects
Oral prednisoneSystemic steroids for a benign chronic condition — never the answer
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F with moderate seasonal rhinitis failing OTC antihistamines → Intranasal corticosteroid
  2. 28 yo F seeking durable control after several drug classes have failed → Allergen immunotherapy
  3. 28 yo F advised to minimize outdoor activity for her pollen allergy → Impractical for pollen, unlike dust-mite control
  4. 28 yo F with rhinitis and asthma who wants a single oral agent → Montelukast — with neuropsychiatric counseling
  5. 28 yo F using oxymetazoline for 10 days with worsening congestion → Rhinitis medicamentosa → stop the spray
  6. 28 yo F with clear rhinorrhea, no itch or sneezing, triggered by temperature change → Vasomotor rhinitis
The ladder Start with allergen avoidance (when practical), then an intranasal corticosteroid. Next, add a second-generation oral or intranasal antihistamine. Use immunotherapy only after pharmacotherapy fails. Any first-generation antihistamine in a stem is usually there to be replaced, not continued.
Sequencing trap

Flexible laryngoscopy in the officeConfirmsSupraglottic tissue collapses inward on inspiration, mobile vocal cordsLaryngomalacia; normal cord movement excludes vocal cord paralysis
Laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episodeConfirmsCords adduct on inspirationVocal cord dysfunction
Barium swallow or CT angiographyBy branchPosterior indentation of the esophagusVascular ring: biphasic stridor with dysphagia
Lateral neck X-ray in a toxic, drooling childSkipDelays securing the airwayEpiglottitis: go to the operating room first
Mnemonic 4 Ds of epiglottitis: Drooling, Dysphagia, Dysphonia (muffled voice), Distress (tripod position)
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M, barky cough, inspiratory stridor, low-grade fever, steeple sign → Croup → dexamethasone
  2. 4 yo M, unvaccinated, drooling and tripoding with high fever and no cough → Epiglottitis → secure the airway in the operating room
  3. 2 yo M with sudden choking while eating peanuts and a unilateral wheeze → Foreign body aspiration → bronchoscopy
  4. 3 yo M, toxic with high fever and thick purulent tracheal secretions after a viral prodrome → Bacterial tracheitis
  5. 6 mo M in winter with wheeze and crackles following a URI → Bronchiolitis → supportive care
  6. 3 wk M with inspiratory stridor worse supine and better prone, well-appearing → Laryngomalacia → reassurance
  7. 4 mo M with paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting and lymphocytosis → Pertussis → azithromycin
  8. 4 wk F, noisy breathing since birth, inspiratory vibratory sound louder supine and quieter prone, feeding well, no cyanosis → Laryngeal collapse on inspiration → Laryngomalacia — position-dependent, the commonest cause of neonatal stridor
  9. 14 yo F, episodic stridor she calls wheezing, normal voice between episodes, saturation 99% during an attack, no response to albuterol → Vocal cord dysfunction → Paradoxical vocal cord motion — inspiratory and expiratory stridor, not wheeze
  10. Adolescent with recurrent stridor unresponsive to albuterol and a normal saturation → Laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episode → Cords must be seen moving abnormally while symptomatic
  11. 2 yo M, barky cough and inspiratory stridor 3 days after coryza, low-grade fever → Subglottic narrowing from mucosal edema → Croup — the obstruction sits below the cords
  12. 4 yo M, unimmunized, 2 days of fever and rhinorrhea, now severe sore throat and refusing food, temperature 39.4 °C, leaning forward with the chin thrust out, tonsils only mildly erythematous, submandibular space soft → Absent Haemophilus influenzae type b immunization → the risk factor, not the finding
  13. 4 yo M, unimmunized, toxic and tripoding with drooling and a normal-looking pharynx → Intubation in the operating room → visualization happens where the airway can be secured; take him there with anesthesia and ENT present
  14. The organism still isolated most often from pediatric epiglottitis despite universal vaccination → Haemophilus influenzae type b → rates fell sharply but the ranking did not change
  15. Preventing epiglottitis in a healthy infant → Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine → immunization is the whole of prevention here; the conjugate series, from 2 months
  16. Agitated 4 yo with suspected epiglottitis in the emergency department → Depressing the tongue to inspect the pharynx → anything that agitates him can complete the obstruction
  17. 3 mo girl with 2 weeks of squeaky noisy breathing when lying on her back, louder and more persistent over time, quieter when prone; gaining weight and breastfeeding well; no labored breathing or cyanosis; laryngoscopy shows patent nasal passages, small adenoids and tonsils, a normal palate, and arytenoid tissue that intermittently falls into the airway, worse with crying; both vocal cords move normally → Inspiratory stridor → laryngomalacia: inspiration lowers pressure in the collapsible extrathoracic airway
  18. 4 mo boy with noisy breathing since 1 month of age, a low-pitched sound heard mainly on expiration over the central chest, and a brassy cough; worse with crying and during colds; no change with position or with albuterol; feeding well without choking or vomiting; normal growth; afebrile → Tracheomalacia → expiratory stridor from a floppy intrathoracic trachea; bronchoscopy confirms
  19. 7 mo boy born at 26 weeks who was intubated for 6 weeks in the neonatal ICU; now noisy breathing on both inspiration and expiration that is constant and worse with colds; no change with position; afebrile, feeding well → Subglottic stenosis → fixed subglottic narrowing after prolonged intubation gives biphasic stridor
  20. 5 mo girl with inspiratory stridor since 2 weeks of age, worse supine and with feeding; weight has fallen from the 50th to below the 5th percentile, with suprasternal retractions at rest and two episodes of perioral cyanosis during feeds; flexible laryngoscopy shows supraglottic collapse on inspiration with normal vocal cord movement → Referral for airway surgery → laryngomalacia with failure to thrive, distress and cyanosis
Decision spine 1. Stridor (upper) or wheeze (lower)? Then which phase: inspiratory is extrathoracic, expiratory is the intrathoracic trachea, biphasic is fixed and usually subglottic. 2. Sudden + afebrile → foreign body; the absence of fever is a key clue. 3. Toxic + drooling + tripod → epiglottitis, airway first in the OR (operating room). Getting a throat exam or X-ray first is an error. 4. Barky + nontoxic → croup. 5. Croup that is not behaving like croup → bacterial tracheitis. 6. Vaccination status always matters.
Risk factors, and the ones that are not Absent Hib immunisation is the strongest risk factor for epiglottitis in a child · Immune deficiency raises the risk, but far less strongly · Diabetes mellitus raises the rate of epiglottitis in adults, not in children · Obesity raises postoperative and nosocomial infection risk and brings sleep apnoea, but is not associated with epiglottitis · Secondhand smoke causes middle ear disease, dental caries and lower respiratory infection, but not epiglottitis · Poor dental hygiene points instead at Ludwig angina, which needs tender bilateral submandibular induration and an elevated floor of mouth; a soft submandibular space excludes it
Paired pearls Croup improves with racemic epi, tracheitis doesn't · laryngomalacia better prone, croup worse at night · bronchiolitis gets nothing · expiratory film for foreign body because the trapped lung stays inflated.
Pairs with Part II Deep Neck Infections covers Ludwig angina and the retropharyngeal space. These are the two deep-neck mimics of a toxic child with a sore throat. Ask: is the submandibular space soft?
Sequencing trapThroat exam or lateral neck film in a toxic, drooling child: the airway is secured in the operating room first
Unchecked attributeExpiratory stridor: the sound of the floppy intrathoracic trachea (tracheomalacia); laryngomalacia is above the thoracic inlet, so it collapses on inspiration
Unchecked attributeBiphasic stridor: needs a fixed lesion such as subglottic stenosis; the arytenoid tissue in laryngomalacia is mobile and position-dependent
