Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant

neonatal respiratory distress causes · bronchopulmonary dysplasiaHow preterm, did labor occur, when did it start, and what does the film show?

WorkupDistress at birthPreterm clockPractice
Bottom line

Time it first. At birth, four facts decide before any pathophysiology: gestational age, whether labor occurred, when distress began and what the film shows; the oxygen response then separates lung from shunt. In the preterm infant each complication has its own window: check the timing before the findings.

  • Transient tachypnea of the newborn: retained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs; fluid in the fissures; onset within 2 hours, gone within 24 to 72.
  • Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS): preterm surfactant deficiency; distress at birth, ground glass with air bronchograms.
  • Apnea of prematurity: the immature brainstem does not sustain breathing; central pauses, with no obstruction and no lung disease, in an infant well between episodes.
  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD): a preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days of life or more; arrested alveolar development, not fibrotic ventilator injury and not air leak.
Workup
Distress at birth
Gestational age, labor, onset, film
DiagnosisSettingThe tell
Transient tachypneaTerm or late preterm; cesarean without labor, macrosomia, maternal diabetes or asthmaFluid in the fissures, perihilar streaking; resolves in 24 to 72 hours
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency, worsening over 48 to 72 hoursLow lung volumes, diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms
Meconium aspirationTerm or post-term, meconium-stained fluid, fetal distressCoarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation
Group B streptococcal pneumoniaRupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxisFilm mimics RDS exactly; temperature instability, neutropenia
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaViscera crush the developing lungScaphoid abdomen, shifted heart sounds; bowel loops in the chest with a displaced heart
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missFailed transition, often after asphyxia or aspirationPre- to postductal gap above 10%, poorly oxygen-responsive
PolycythemiaIntrauterine hypoxia or placental transfusionPlethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film; venous hematocrit above 65% in a term neonate
Exit ramps Diaphragmatic hernia – never bag-mask (it inflates bowel inside the chest): intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma ⚠︎), decompress with a nasogastric tube; the lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists · Displaced heart sounds – scaphoid abdomen with absent breath sounds on the defect side: hernia; distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant: tension pneumothorax, needle decompression; well, heart on the right, no distress: dextrocardia · Diabetic mother – raises the risk of transient tachypnea and delays surfactant maturation, so RDS can appear at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe
The preterm clock
Apnea of prematurity Definition – a pause over 20 seconds, or a shorter one with bradycardia or desaturation · Diagnosis – clinical, after the mimics are checked: anemia, infection and intraventricular hemorrhage, plus glucose and electrolytes (seizure and reflux are the other usual mimics) · Versus hemorrhage – lethargy, a tense fontanelle, a growing head or seizures; cranial ultrasound · Management – caffeine, a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia Severity – graded by support required at 36 weeks postmenstrual age · Prevention – antenatal steroids plus surfactant turned it from fibrotic injury into developmental arrest; caffeine and vitamin A each reduce it · Management – supportive: oxygen, nutrition, fluid restriction; alveoli keep forming over months · Complications – pulmonary hypertension, systemic hypertension, recurrent respiratory infections, neurodevelopmental delay · Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – first season, under 8 months: nirsevimab or clesrovimab; second season, 8 to 19 months: nirsevimab only, for BPD that needed oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids in the 6 months before the season; palivizumab is no longer available after December 31, 2025 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance)
Practice
  1. 1-hour-old boy born at 40 weeks by cesarean without labor is tachypneic chest x-ray shows fluid in the interlobar fissures Afebrile · birth weight 4200 g · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 88% on room air, 98% on oxygen → Transient tachypnea of the newborn → retained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs: fluid in the fissures appears in no competing diagnosis, and saturation correcting from 88% to 98% on oxygen is alveolar fluid, not a shunt. Cesarean without labor misses the catecholamine surge that switches the epithelium to absorbing fluid; macrosomia adds risk. Respiratory distress syndrome is the right category but a preterm member, and group B streptococcal pneumonia needs risk factors the stem never supplies. Supportive care: onset within 2 hours, and it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so an infant breathing normally by 48 hours fits
  2. 6-week-old boy born at 26 weeks still needs supplemental oxygen on nasal cannula oxygen every day since birth enteral feeds introduced today Weight gain appropriate on total parenteral nutrition Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on 0.5 L/min → Arrested alveolar development → a preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days or more has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and since antenatal steroids and surfactant it is arrested alveolar development: fewer alveoli, less septation, disrupted vasculogenesis. Fibrotic ventilator injury is the old form, and air leak belongs to the first days on high pressures, weeks before this. Feeds introduced today suggest refeeding syndrome, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition
  3. 6-hour-old girl born at term has tachypnea and grunting membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery maternal fever 38.5 °C in labor; no intrapartum prophylaxis Temperature unstable since birth T 35.9 °C · HR 176/min · respiratory rate 74/min → Blood culture and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever and no intrapartum prophylaxis, with temperature instability, is early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis. Its film mimics respiratory distress syndrome exactly, so surfactant misses it, and observing without antibiotics leaves the infection untreated: culture and start ampicillin and gentamicin
  4. 1-day-old girl born at term after delayed cord clamping is plethoric jittery and irritable before feeds Feeding well; no hepatomegaly; normal genitalia Afebrile · venous hematocrit 70% · glucose 35 mg/dL · HR 150/min → Red cells consume glucose → delayed cord clamping adds blood, and the expanded red cell mass takes up glucose, giving hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia; breakdown of the cells adds hyperbilirubinemia. Liver congestion is not the mechanism ⚠︎, and salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia brings ambiguous genitalia in girls, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, days later
  5. Term newborn boy has severe respiratory distress at delivery scaphoid abdomen heart sounds displaced to the right chest x-ray shows bowel gas in the left hemithorax T 36.6 °C · HR 92/min · oxygen saturation 64% → Intubate with limited peak pressures and decompress the stomach → a scaphoid abdomen with displaced heart sounds and bowel in the chest is a diaphragmatic hernia. Bag-mask ventilation inflates bowel inside the chest, so intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma ⚠︎) and decompress with a nasogastric tube. Needle decompression is for a tension pneumothorax: a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant
  6. 4-day-old boy born at 29 weeks in neonatal intensive care several 20-second breathing pauses today, bradycardia and desaturation ends with stimulation; pink, active, feeding well between Cultures negative; antibiotics stopped T 36.9 °C, stable · glucose, electrolytes, hemoglobin, ultrasound normal → Begin caffeine → a central pause from an immature brainstem, starting on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between spells, with the mimics checked (infection, anemia, intraventricular hemorrhage, glucose, electrolytes), is apnea of prematurity. Caffeine is a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue. Antibiotics answer the infant who is ill between spells; dexamethasone and albuterol are used for bronchopulmonary dysplasia, not for apnea
  7. 2-hour-old boy born at 29 weeks is grunting and retracting chest x-ray shows low lung volumes diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms Membranes ruptured at delivery T 36.8 °C · respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 86% on room air → Respiratory distress syndrome → surfactant deficiency in a preterm infant (under 34 weeks) gives distress at birth, worsening over 48 to 72 hours, with low volumes, ground glass and air bronchograms: give surfactant and CPAP. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures in a term infant; group B streptococcal pneumonia mimics this film exactly but needs risk factors (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis) this stem does not supply
  8. 2-day-old boy born at term is plethoric, lethargic and feeding poorly venous hematocrit 72% no better after 12 hours of intravenous fluids Born after delayed cord clamping Afebrile · glucose 48 mg/dL · HR 156/min → Partial exchange transfusion → most polycythemic infants are ruddy and asymptomatic; hyperviscosity brings lethargy, irritability and jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea, respiratory distress, poor feeding and cyanosis. Hydration by feeds or glucose-containing intravenous fluids comes first; symptomatic hyperviscosity despite it needs a partial exchange transfusion, which swaps blood for saline to lower viscosity. A double-volume exchange swaps blood for blood and leaves the hematocrit high, and furosemide removes plasma water and concentrates the blood ⚠︎; true dehydration is rare in the first 2 days, while the neonate still carries excess extracellular fluid
  9. 8-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks is cyanotic preductal saturation 88%, postductal 76% minimal improvement on 100% oxygen chest x-ray nearly clear Delivered through meconium-stained fluid Afebrile · HR 168/min · BP 62/38 mm Hg → Obtain an echocardiogram → a pre- to postductal gap above 10% that barely responds to oxygen is right-to-left ductal shunting: persistent pulmonary hypertension, a failed transition often after asphyxia or aspiration. Echocardiography shows high pulmonary pressure in a structurally normal heart and excludes cyanotic heart disease. Surfactant treats alveolar disease, which corrects on oxygen, and reassurance misses a can't-miss diagnosis
  10. 12-day-old girl born at 26 weeks has abdominal distension bloody stools on day 10 of enteral feeds abdominal x-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis T 35.9 °C · HR 182/min · capillary refill 4 seconds → Necrotizing enterocolitis → a preterm infant on enteral feeds with distension, bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis has bacterial invasion of the bowel wall: keep nil by mouth, give intravenous antibiotics and consult surgery. Allergic proctocolitis is the well infant with bloody stool; pneumatosis intestinalis is the tell that names this can't-miss diagnosis over it and over malrotation with volvulus
  11. 1-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks by cesarean without labor is breathing fast chest x-ray shows fluid in the fissures with perihilar streaking Mother asks to breastfeed now Afebrile · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 93% on oxygen → Keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen → neonatal tachypnea is a respiratory rate above 60 per minute, and feeding at a rate of 80 risks aspiration: keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and oxygen. Intubation and surfactant are for the preterm surfactant-deficient lung, not retained fluid in a term infant
  12. 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, is in preterm labor at 29 weeks cervix dilated 5 cm delivery expected within 48 hours T 37.0 °C · BP 118/72 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 140/min → Antenatal betamethasone → antenatal betamethasone gives the fetal lung the cortisol signal that drives surfactant maturation (the signal fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes); steroids before delivery, with surfactant after birth, converted bronchopulmonary dysplasia from fibrotic injury to developmental arrest; postnatal surfactant gives up the antenatal dose, and tocolysis only buys time for the steroid course; it does not mature the lung ⚠︎
  13. 1-hour-old boy born at 37 weeks has grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled diabetes chest x-ray shows diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms Afebrile · birth weight 4300 g · oxygen saturation 85% on room air → Fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol, delaying surfactant maturation → fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol and suppresses phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol production, delaying surfactant maturation; the pneumocytes are not directly injured, and placental insufficiency is not the mechanism here ⚠︎
  14. 5-day-old girl born at 30 weeks has new apnea and bradycardia since this morning lethargic and mottled between episodes abdominal distension and feeding intolerance No antibiotics so far T 35.8 °C, unstable · HR 188/min · capillary refill 4 seconds → Blood culture and empiric antibiotics → an infant who is ill between spells (temperature instability, feeding intolerance or poor perfusion) has suspected sepsis, not simple apnea of prematurity: culture and treat. Caffeine is for the infant well between spells; anemia of prematurity comes weeks later, pale with a low hemoglobin; this tachycardia is sepsis
  15. 2-day-old girl was diagnosed with a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia at birth intubated; saturations now falling echocardiogram shows suprasystemic pulmonary pressures right hand saturation 92% · foot saturation 78% · HR 170/min → Inhaled nitric oxide → a hand-foot gap above 10% is right-to-left ductal shunting from pulmonary hypertension of the hypoplastic lung. Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) is the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but this cyanosis is not a closing duct; a chest tube treats a pneumothorax, not shunting. The lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists; the gap itself shows the duct is already open, so the target is pulmonary vasodilation
  16. 3-day-old boy born at 27 weeks has abrupt hypoxia on high-pressure mechanical ventilation since birth chest x-ray shows unilateral perivascular cystic lucencies No distended, hyperresonant hemithorax Afebrile · HR 172/min · oxygen saturation 78% → Pulmonary interstitial emphysema → air dissects into the interstitium on high ventilator pressures in the first days: cystic lucencies and abrupt decompensation; reduce ventilator pressures. Tension pneumothorax gives a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax needing needle decompression, and respiratory distress syndrome, though it worsens over 48 to 72 hours, shows ground glass with air bronchograms
  17. 10-hour-old girl born at 29 weeks has needed CPAP since birth rising oxygen requirement, now 60% worsening retractions chest x-ray shows ground glass with air bronchograms T 36.8 °C · oxygen saturation 86% on CPAP → Intubate and give surfactant → worsening surfactant deficiency despite CPAP means CPAP has failed: intubate and give surfactant. Closer observation leaves the failure untreated, and antibiotics alone do not replace surfactant
  18. 6-hour-old boy born at term is ruddy and jittery breathing fast with no retractions chest x-ray is clear; no hepatomegaly; normal heart sounds Mother had preeclampsia Afebrile · glucose 32 mg/dL · respiratory rate 70/min · HR 150/min → Polycythemia → plethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film is polycythemia. Intrauterine hypoxia drives erythropoietin (preeclampsia, maternal diabetes or hypertension, smoking, growth restriction), or placental transfusion adds blood (delayed cord clamping, twin-twin transfusion); hyperviscosity brings jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea, and the expanded red cell mass takes up glucose; check a venous hematocrit (above 65%). Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, glycogen storage disease type I brings hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis, and cyanotic heart disease is excluded by a normal heart and exam
  19. 14-month-old boy born at 30 weeks is seen at a well visit has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, on diuretics until 3 months ago his second RSV season starts next month Afebrile · respiratory rate 36/min · oxygen saturation 96% on room air → Nirsevimab prophylaxis → chronic lung disease of prematurity that needed medical support (supplemental oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids) in the 6 months before the second season qualifies for a second-season dose, and nirsevimab is the product recommended; palivizumab is no longer available from December 31, 2025, and the prophylaxis is an antibody, not an infant vaccine ⚠︎
  20. Term newborn girl has severe cyanosis at 12 hours no improvement on 100% oxygen no retractions; comfortable tachypnea chest radiograph structurally normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 68% on 100% oxygen · HR 160/min → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → cyanosis that does not correct on oxygen in a comfortable infant with a normal film is a shunt (the hyperoxia test, still keyed on exams though largely abandoned clinically): suspect cyanotic congenital heart disease and start prostaglandin E1 pending echocardiography. Surfactant treats alveolar disease that corrects on oxygen; inhaled nitric oxide treats pulmonary hypertension, whose tell is a ductal saturation gap above 10%
  21. 3-week-old boy born at 28 weeks is given caffeine for central apneic spells well between spells His parents ask when the spells should stop Afebrile · HR 150/min · oxygen saturation 97% on room air → By about his expected due date → the brainstem breathing center matures by term corrected age, so spells resolve by about the expected due date; 28 days is the bronchopulmonary dysplasia clock, not the apnea clock
  22. 1-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks has tachypnea and retractions delivered through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress chest x-ray shows coarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation Afebrile · respiratory rate 84/min · oxygen saturation 87% → Meconium aspiration syndrome → term or post-term delivery through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress, with coarse patchy asymmetric infiltrates and hyperinflation; watch for pneumothorax and pulmonary hypertension. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, and for congenital pneumonia nothing in this stem points to infection (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis) ⚠︎
  23. 2-hour-old girl born at 36 weeks has central cyanosis, grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes chest x-ray shows bilateral ground-glass opacities Afebrile · saturation 64% rising to 82% on oxygen · pre- and postductal readings equal → Surfactant → maternal diabetes delays surfactant maturation, so an infant of a diabetic mother can develop respiratory distress syndrome at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe. Ground glass with equal pre- and postductal readings and a partial oxygen response is lung disease, not a ductal shunt, so prostaglandin E1 is not the answer; steroids for the lung are the antenatal betamethasone given before delivery
  24. 4-month-old boy born at 28 weeks has poor weight gain needed supplemental oxygen until 3 months of age loud P2 liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · respiratory rate 56/min · oxygen saturation 93% on room air → Pulmonary artery hypertension → pulmonary hypertension is a complication of bronchopulmonary dysplasia that arrives months later, with a loud P2 and poor growth: obtain an echocardiogram. Systemic hypertension and recurrent respiratory infections are also complications, but a loud P2 is the pulmonic sound, and chronic aspiration does not explain it ⚠︎; the enlarged liver is right heart failure
  25. 4-day-old girl born at term was diagnosed with transient tachypnea on day 1 still breathing fast at 96 hours of life Feeding by nasogastric tube Afebrile · respiratory rate 74/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air → Re-evaluate for another diagnosis → transient is a diagnostic criterion, not a description: it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so tachypnea beyond 72 hours means the diagnosis was wrong; look again. Continued observation and discharge both keep the wrong label
Common wrong answers Refeeding syndrome: feeds introduced today suggest it, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition. Pulmonary interstitial emphysema at 28 days: real ventilator pathology, but it belongs to the first days. RDS in a term infant: the right category, a preterm member. Group B streptococcal pneumonia: needs risk factors the stem must supply. Prostaglandin in a diaphragmatic hernia: the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but the cyanosis comes from hypoplastic lungs and pulmonary hypertension, not a closing duct. Diaphragmatic hernia at an hour with fissural fluid: it presents at delivery with a scaphoid abdomen.
Pairs with Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant: the well infant with bloody stool; here, the ill preterm infant. Ask: is the infant preterm, distended and unwell? Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant: intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia of prematurity, the mimics to exclude before calling a spell apnea of prematurity. Ask: is the infant well between episodes? Part II Posterior Urethral Valves: the same distress in the first hours. Ask: is this fluid in normal lungs, or lungs that never developed? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn: the step before, where work of breathing, the oxygen response and the limb gradient sort lung from heart. Part I Hypoxemia: the physiology under the oxygen response.
Transferable rule

Match the clock before the findings. Birth: RDS or transient tachypnea, sorted by gestational age, labor, onset and the film. Ventilator days: air leak. Day 2 to 3 spells in a well infant: apnea of prematurity. Oxygen at 28 days: BPD. Months: pulmonary hypertension. When the history states a diagnostic criterion exactly, make that diagnosis directly.

edits.html:
Recurrent Vomiting in a Child

Stereotyped episodes, well in between · the pattern is the diagnosis

Source vignette Pt — 9-year-old girl, 8 months of nausea, vomiting and diffuse abdominal pain for several days each month; episodes begin early morning, recur 10–15 times daily for 2 days, nonbloody and nonbilious; more frequent at the start of the school year; two admissions for intravenous hydration · Between episodes — active, eating well, growth at the 25th percentile and unchanged · Exam — well hydrated, erosive maxillary caries, soft nontender abdomen, normal neurologic examination · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned bulimia, chronic pancreatitis, cyclic vomiting, factitious disorder imposed on another, reflux and inflammatory bowel disease
The decision point

Three features together indicate cyclic vomiting syndrome: stereotyped episodes, each self-limited over 1 to 2 days, and complete wellness between them with normal growth. Stress at the start of term is the trigger. Most patients have a personal or family history of migraine. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, supported by wellness between episodes.

The erosive caries are evidence that the vomiting is real and recurrent, not evidence of purging. There is no bingeing, no restriction and no preoccupation with shape.

Defining criteria Stereotyped episodes — the same acute nausea, abdominal pain, headache and vomiting each time · Duration — self-limited over 1 to 2 days · Interval — often regular, around 2 to 4 weeks, and asymptomatic between · Association — personal or family history of migraine · Triggers — infection or stress
Recurrent vomiting in a child — the differentialwhat happens between the episodes
DiagnosisBetween episodesKey discriminatorWhat to do
Cyclic vomiting syndromeEntirely well, growing normallyStereotyped, self-limited, regular intervals; migraine historyRehydration and antiemetics; triptans may abort
Bulimia nervosaPreoccupied with shape and weightBingeing with compensatory behaviourPsychiatric assessment
Chronic pancreatitisPoor growth, diarrhoeaEpigastric tenderness on examinationPancreatic imaging and enzyme studies
Inflammatory bowel diseaseWeight loss, fever, ongoing symptomsDiarrhoea with abdominal tendernessInflammatory markers and endoscopy
Gastroesophageal refluxOngoing low-grade symptomsRegurgitation and substernal pain, not episodic burstsTrial of acid suppression
Factitious disorder imposed on anotherInconsistent history, symptoms unwitnessedNo objective corroboration of the illnessCareful documentation; child protection
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Electrolytes, glucose and BUN during an episodeFirstDehydration changes onlyRehydrate; tests are drawn during the episode to exclude urgent causes
Lipase, liver enzymes and urinalysisBy branchNormalExcludes pancreatitis, hepatobiliary and urinary causes
Upper GI contrast seriesBy branchMalrotation excludedRequired when vomiting is bilious or the pattern is atypical
Brain MRIBy branchMass or hydrocephalusOnly with an abnormal neurologic examination
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsStereotyped episodes, well between, normal growthCyclic vomiting syndrome; the tests only exclude mimics
Upper endoscopySkipAdds nothing with normal growth and no alarm featuresReserve for weight loss, diarrhea or bleeding
Scenario bank
  1. 9 year old with 8 months of stereotyped vomiting episodes lasting 2 days, 10-15 times daily, entirely well between them, normal growth, erosive maxillary caries → Cyclic vomiting syndrome → A diagnosis of exclusion with predictable intervals
  2. The historical association that supports cyclic vomiting syndrome → Personal or family history of migraine → Triggers are often infection or stress
  3. Child with established cyclic vomiting syndrome presenting mid-episode, dehydrated → Intravenous rehydration with an antiemetic → Abortive triptans may shorten the episode
  4. Adolescent with self-induced vomiting after binge eating, preoccupied with body shape, normal weight → Bulimia nervosa → Bingeing and compensatory behavior, not stereotyped episodes
  5. Child with recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, poor growth and epigastric tenderness → Chronic pancreatitis → Growth failure and tenderness, unlike the well-between-episodes pattern
  6. What the erosive dental caries in a child with recurrent vomiting indicates → Evidence that the vomiting is real and recurrent → It supports the history rather than implying purging
Gates Bilious vomiting, weight loss, fever or an abnormal neurologic examination argues against cyclic vomiting and needs urgent evaluation · Growth must be normal — faltering growth needs further evaluation · Laboratory work and imaging are usually done during an acute episode to exclude the urgent causes, not between them · Most children outgrow it during adolescence
Pearls Symptom-free intervals — episodes are regular and predictable, and the child is well between them · Dental erosion shows recurrent acid exposure, not its cause · Migraine history is the most useful historical clue · As a diagnosis of exclusion, the workup targets dangerous mimics
Pairs with Part I Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment covers migraine, which shares this condition's biology. Ask: how is the child between episodes?
Transferable rule For episodic illness, ask how the patient is between episodes. Most of the diagnostic information comes from the interval between episodes.
Salient decoyDental erosion suggests purging, but she has no bingeing, restriction or preoccupation with shape.
Unchecked attributeNormal growth excludes the chronic inflammatory and malabsorptive options.

GI Bleeding in a Child

Occult GI (gastrointestinal) bleeding after a negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy · age decides the next study

Source vignette Pt — 10-year-old boy, 2 months of exertional fatigue and exercise intolerance; no melena, hematochezia or abdominal pain; no medications · Exam — mucosal pallor, no lymphadenopathy, soft nontender abdomen, stool positive for occult blood · Labs — hemoglobin 9.4, MCV 74, platelets 380,000, leukocytes 7,500; ESR and coagulation normal; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies unremarkable · Q — which study most likely reveals the diagnosis; options spanned CT angiography, fecal calprotectin, fecal DNA, technetium 99m pertechnetate scan and tissue transglutaminase antibodies
Source vignette Pt — 2 yo M, dark red formed stool in the diaper; eating and drinking well but more tired than usual; lives on a ranch with cattle and goats; afebrile, pale; abdomen soft, nondistended, nontender, no masses; no anal fissures or hemorrhoids; stool occult blood positive · Labs — WBC 8,000, Hct 27%, platelets 320,000 · Q — the study most likely to confirm the diagnosis; options spanned technetium-99m pertechnetate scan, abdominal CT, abdominal ultrasound, air contrast enema, bacterial stool culture, cow's milk elimination diet and upper endoscopy
The decision point

Iron deficiency anemia with a positive occult blood test and no visible bleeding is occult gastrointestinal bleeding. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are both unremarkable, so the source is in the small bowel, which neither scope reaches. In a child, the most common small-bowel bleeding lesion is a Meckel diverticulum. It is found by a technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, which images ectopic gastric mucosa rather than the bleeding.

An adult with the same negative workup gets capsule endoscopy, because adult small-bowel causes are angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers.

A Meckel diverticulum can also bleed visibly. A toddler with painless dark red or maroon stool, pallor and a soft, nontender abdomen, without diarrhea, vomiting or fever, goes straight to the pertechnetate scan. Endoscopy is not done first. Pain suggests a complication or a different disease and changes the first test.

Defining criteria Occult GI bleeding — positive fecal occult blood and/or iron deficiency anemia without visible bleeding · First step regardless of age — upper endoscopy and colonoscopy · Child, source not found — technetium 99m pertechnetate scan for Meckel · Adult, source not found — capsule endoscopy, then CT or MR enterography · Meckel — failed closure of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, the most common congenital GI anomaly, with ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates adjacent small bowel

  4. Adult with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and a negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Capsule endoscopy → Angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers — the adult small-bowel causes
  5. Child with painless hematochezia and no abdominal pain, age under 2 → Meckel diverticulum → Failed closure of the vitelline duct
  6. Child with slow occult blood loss and stable vital signs; which study is least likely to help → CT angiography → It needs brisk active bleeding to see anything
  7. Child with microcytic anemia, chronic diarrhea and a negative fecal occult blood test → Celiac disease → Malabsorption, not blood loss — the occult blood is negative
  8. 2-year-old boy with dark red, formed stool in his diaper; eating and drinking well but more tired than usual; lives on a ranch with cattle and goats; afebrile and pale; abdomen soft, nondistended and nontender without masses; no anal fissures or hemorrhoids; stool positive for occult blood; hematocrit 27%, leukocytes 8,000/mm3, platelets 320,000/mm3 → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan → Meckel diverticulum: ectopic gastric mucosa takes up the tracer; painless small-bowel bleeding in a toddler, and dark red stool without hematemesis or melena is not an upper GI bleed
  9. 10-week-old boy fed cow's milk-based formula with several days of mucus and streaks of blood in otherwise soft stools; feeding well, gaining weight, afebrile and playful; mild eczema on the cheeks; abdomen soft and nontender; no anal fissure on exam → Switch to an extensively hydrolyzed formula → milk protein proctocolitis: a non-IgE reaction in infants; bleeding clears once cow's milk protein is removed, and it resolves by age 1
  10. 2-year-old boy with 12 hours of sudden episodes of severe crying with his legs drawn up, quiet and sleepy between episodes; vomited twice; one stool of dark red blood and mucus (currant jelly); afebrile; a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant → Abdominal ultrasound → intussusception: pain is the tell; target sign on ultrasound, then air enema to confirm and reduce; a Meckel diverticulum can be the lead point
  11. 3-year-old girl with two episodes of painless maroon stool over the past month; pale, hematocrit 28%, vital signs normal; abdomen soft and nontender; technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower quadrant → Surgical resection → a symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is removed to stop the bleeding and prevent intussusception, diverticulitis and obstruction; iron treats the anemia, not the source
Stool color and bleeding source Stool color follows transit time, not only where the blood started. Dark red or maroon stool in a toddler is a lower source, usually the small bowel, because the blood passes quickly. The upper GI (gastrointestinal) picture is hematemesis with black, sticky melena, and it is more common in adults. This child had neither, so upper endoscopy is not the first test.
Gates Visible bleeding with instability — hematemesis, melena or hematochezia goes to CT (computed tomography) angiography, not a Meckel scan · Scope first for occult bleeding — small-bowel studies are for after a clean upper endoscopy and colonoscopy; a toddler with visible, painless dark red stool goes straight to the pertechnetate scan · Meckel is classically under 2 but presents into adolescence, so age does not exclude it · Balloon-assisted enteroscopy is the fallback when the source stays hidden
Pearls The Meckel scan detects gastric mucosa, not blood, so it works when the lesion is not actively bleeding · Occult bleeding is too slow for angiography · Celiac gives iron deficiency without occult blood; the FOBT (fecal occult blood test) separates them · Here, small bowel means the segment the two scopes cannot reach · Painless hematochezia in a toddler is Meckel until proven otherwise · Rule of 2s: often presents by age 2, usually under 2 inches long, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve · The bleed is painless; pain comes from complications: intussusception with the diverticulum as lead point, diverticulitis that mimics appendicitis, obstruction or perforation · A symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is surgically resected to stop the bleeding and prevent those complications
Pairs with Part I The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers the obstructed and acutely bleeding infant gut. Part I Microcytic Anemia covers the iron-versus-thalassemia fork that precedes this workup. Ask: is the bleeding visible, and have both ends been scoped?
Transferable rule When an algorithm branches on age, the same negative workup can send a child and an adult to different tests.
Class-vs-memberCapsule endoscopy is the adult small-bowel study; a child gets the pertechnetate scan.
Sequencing trapOrdering a small-bowel study before upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are done.
Salient decoyMicrocytic anemia in a child pulls toward celiac serology, which the positive FOBT (fecal occult blood test) excludes.
Unchecked attributeMilk elimination fits painless blood in an infant, but milk protein proctocolitis resolves by age 1; a 2-year-old is past it.

Polyuria

the urine osmolality sorts it before any hormone is named · when the water deprivation test is indicated, and when it has already been answered

Source vignette Pt — 8 yo M, 2 months of excessive urination, drinking large volumes, irritable and restless; normal growth and milestones; no medications · Vitals — normal · Exam — physical and neurologic examination normal · Labs — Na 142, K 4.2, Cl 100, HCO₃ 24, BUN 30, creatinine 1.0, Ca 9.2, glucose 100 · Urine — specific gravity 1.001, no protein, blood, glucose or ketones; osmolality 120 mOsm/kg; 24-hour output 3.7 L · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned chest radiography, fractional excretion of sodium, brain MRI, an oral glucose tolerance test, renal ultrasonography and the water deprivation test
The decision point

Urine osmolality 120 is a water diuresis. The kidney is failing to concentrate, so solute diuresis and every test for it are excluded before any hormone is named. Then serum sodium 142, a normal value, makes the deprivation test necessary rather than redundant. A patient who drinks enough to hold his sodium normal has not yet shown the cause of the dilute urine. It may be a failure to make or to respond to vasopressin, or simply a normal kidney excreting a large water intake. Water deprivation is the manoeuvre that forces that distinction. It drives serum osmolality to the point where vasopressin secretion must be maximal, then shows whether the urine concentrates.

The two imaging studies are right tests in the wrong order. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) localises an established deficiency, and renal ultrasonography localises an established resistance. Both wait on a diagnosis that has not yet been made.

Defining criteria Polyuria — urine output above 3 L/day in an adult, above 2 L/day/m² in a child · Dilute urine — urine osmolality under 300 mOsm/kg, specific gravity under 1.006 · Concentrated urine — 600 mOsm/kg or above, meaning the kidney can concentrate and the diuresis is driven by solute · Deprivation endpoint — water withheld until serum sodium exceeds 145 and serum osmolality exceeds 295, the point at which vasopressin secretion should be maximal · Deprivation result — urine above 600 is primary polydipsia, urine still under 300 is an AVP disorder · Desmopressin result — urine osmolality rises in deficiency and stays low in resistance
FigureWhen water deprivation testing is indicatedshow

Redrawn from the published indications flowchart. Two deliberate changes: the concentrated-urine branch is labelled with what it means — solute diuresis — rather than only with what not to do, and the indicated branch carries its own interpretation, because the exam asks what the deprivation test showed about as often as it asks whether to order it.

Polyuria with dilute urine — the differentialand the two mimics that never need the test
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Primary polydipsiaDrinking drives the urine; psychiatric illness, or a drug that creates thirstSerum sodium low or low-normal; urine concentrates above 600 after deprivationNot excluded — this is one of the two the test is between
AVP deficiency (central DI)Impaired production or release: trauma, neurosurgery, craniopharyngioma or germinoma, hypophysitis, sarcoid or histiocytosis, a familial AVP mutation, pregnancyUrine stays dilute after deprivation, then rises with desmopressinNot excluded — the desmopressin step is what names it
AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)The kidney ignores the hormone: AVPR2 or AQP2 mutation, hypercalcaemia, severe hypokalaemia, lithium, chronic tubulointerstitial diseaseUrine stays dilute after desmopressin too; in a child, usually hereditaryNot excluded — complete resistance leaves the osmolality unchanged, partial raises it slightly
Solute (osmotic) diuresisGlucosuria in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, or an osmotic diuretic such as mannitolPolyuria with a urine osmolality above 600; no deprivation test neededUrine osmolality 120, serum glucose 100, urine glucose negative
SIADHThe mirror image — water retained rather than lost; malignancy, CNS and pulmonary disease, drugsConcentrated urine with hyponatraemia, and no polyuriaDilute urine and a normal sodium — the opposite of the finding
Treatment, and the one child who must not be tested AVP deficiency — desmopressin in nearly all patients, oral, intranasal or parenteral; other agents are rarely needed · AVP resistance — remove the cause first (stop the lithium, correct the calcium and the potassium), then a thiazide with a low-sodium diet as first line; a low-protein diet cuts the solute load further; indomethacin is adjunct; amiloride is the one for lithium, because it blocks lithium entry into the collecting duct · Supervision — the deprivation test is performed in hospital in older children and adults, and is not performed in very young children, because the hypernatraemia it deliberately produces is dangerous in a child who cannot ask for water
Decision spine

1. Is the urine dilute or concentrated? Urine osmolality of 600 or above means the kidney concentrates, so look for solute, not for a hormone. 2. Is there glucose in the urine? Glucosuria explains the whole picture without a hormone. 3. Is the sodium above 145 with osmolality above 295? Then the AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder is already proven; go straight to desmopressin. 4. Is the sodium frankly low? Polyuria with hyponatraemia is primary polydipsia and needs no deprivation test. 5. Is the sodium normal? That is the only value that calls for the test. 6. After deprivation, did desmopressin raise the urine osmolality? If yes, it is deficiency, so image the brain. If no, it is resistance, so look at the kidney and the drug list.

Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo M, 2 months of polyuria and polydipsia, normal growth and neurologic examination, Na 142, glucose 100, urine specific gravity 1.001 and osmolality 120, output 3.7 L/day → Water deprivation test → a normal sodium is what leaves the diagnosis open
  2. 10 yo M with polyuria, serum Na 149 and serum osmolality 302, urine osmolality 110 → Desmopressin challenge → the deprivation endpoint has already been reached spontaneously
  3. 12 yo F whose urine osmolality stayed at 150 through deprivation and then rose to 620 after desmopressin → MRI of the brain → AVP deficiency needs its cause localized
  4. 9 yo M whose urine osmolality is 140 after deprivation and unchanged after desmopressin, with normal calcium, potassium and no medications → A thiazide with a low-sodium diet → first line once resistance is established and reversible causes are excluded
  5. 8 yo M for whom water deprivation testing has been chosen → Admit for supervised inpatient testing → the test works by producing hypernatremia deliberately
  6. 20-month-old with polyuria and a serum sodium of 148 → Water deprivation testing → severe hypernatremia in a child who cannot obtain water
  7. 14 yo M with polyuria and weight loss, urine osmolality 650, serum glucose 420, urine glucose 4+ → Osmotic diuresis → a concentrating kidney moves the problem to solute
  8. 30 yo F on an antipsychotic with polyuria, urine osmolality 90 and serum sodium 128 → Primary polydipsia → polyuria with hyponatremia needs no deprivation test
  9. Child with polyuria whose urine remains dilute when fluids are withheld → Desmopressin after water deprivation → the hormone itself is too unstable in a sample to measure routinely; serial urine osmolality is what is read
  10. 17 yo F with polyuria, constipation and a serum calcium of 12.8 → Hypercalcemia blunts the response to vasopressin → an acquired, reversible AVP resistance; at the collecting duct
Pearls A sodium above 145 makes the test redundant. A sodium below normal already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test. · Serum vasopressin is not measured: its half-life is short and it is unstable in the sample, so the desmopressin response is the assay · AVP deficiency — the current name for central diabetes insipidus · AVP resistance — the current name for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus · Hypothalamic injury kills the magnocellular cell bodies and the deficiency is permanent; injury below the infundibulum is usually transient, because those cell bodies survive · Pregnancy can produce a transient deficiency through placental vasopressinase; it resolves with delivery and returns in the next pregnancy · Lithium causes resistance by inhibiting aquaporin-2, and amiloride is the agent that blocks lithium's entry into the cell
Pairs with Part I Enuresis already links a very low specific gravity to diabetes insipidus and to this test. This brief covers what happens after the test is ordered. Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers the causes of AVP (arginine vasopressin) deficiency and the post-operative case where the diagnosis is not in doubt. Hypercalcemia covers the commonest acquired resistance. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule When the kidney is making dilute urine, the serum sodium shows whether a water deprivation test is still needed. A high sodium already confirms an AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder; a low sodium already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test.
Sequencing trapMRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain: the right study once a deficiency is proven, and nothing has been proven yet.
Sequencing trapRenal ultrasonography: it images the kidney, which is implicated only if desmopressin fails.
Salient decoyA BUN (blood urea nitrogen) of 30 pulls toward renal disease, but the creatinine is 1.0 and the defect is concentration, not filtration.
True-fact-wrong-slotFractional excretion of sodium: it measures perfusion, and perfusion is not in question here.
Salient decoyChest radiography: it looks for SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), which produces concentrated urine and hyponatraemia, both opposite to the findings here.

Inherited Tumor Syndromes

Identify the syndrome from the visible lesion and the organ pattern · What exactly is the retinal lesion, and what color is the skin patch?

Source vignette Pt — 16 yo M, bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, mother had an adrenal tumor resected, one light brown facial patch without freckling · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1 and Sturge-Weber syndrome
The decision point

Bilateral retinal hemangioblastoma points to von Hippel-Lindau, because no other listed syndrome produces one. NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) gives optic gliomas and Lisch nodules. MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) gives conjunctival and corneal neuromas. Sturge-Weber gives a leptomeningeal and choroidal vascular malformation. Li-Fraumeni gives sarcomas with no characteristic eye finding. The mother's resected adrenal tumor reads as a pheochromocytoma transmitted in autosomal dominant fashion. Hemangioblastoma plus adrenal medullary tumor is the von Hippel-Lindau organ pattern, with clear cell renal carcinoma the third member. A single light brown facial macule is a normal café-au-lait spot. It is not the multiple macules of NF1 and not a red-purple port-wine stain.

Consider a teenager found confused after an unwitnessed fall. A fibroma growing from under a toenail and calcified nodules lining the lateral ventricles on CT (computed tomography) indicate tuberous sclerosis complex. The fall was a seizure, and the nodules are subependymal hamartomas. The nail lesion is a periungual fibroma, which appears in adolescence. NF1 puts neurofibromas on the trunk and a glioma on the optic nerve. Ataxia-telangiectasia starts with ataxia in early childhood. The nail-bed sign of endocarditis is a splinter hemorrhage, not a fibroma.

Defining criteria The VHL testing gate — any patient with a retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma undergoes VHL gene testing, family history or not · The café-au-lait gate — an isolated macule is normal; six or more with regular borders plus axillary freckling is NF1 (each macule over 5 mm before puberty or over 15 mm after puberty); a few large macules with irregular borders, often segmental and respecting the midline, without freckling is McCune-Albright ⚠︎. Count, border, distribution and freckling are four separate criteria, and the exam varies whichever one is not being checked · Patch color as a criterion — Sturge-Weber's lesion is a red-purple vascular port-wine stain; a light brown patch is pigmented and belongs to a different family
Pertinent positives & negatives Bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas — essentially syndrome-defining; retinal hemangioblastoma may be the first neoplasm of VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) and by itself triggers gene testing · Mother's adrenal tumor removed — pheochromocytoma in a first-degree relative; autosomal dominant transmission, and the second organ of the VHL pattern · A single light brown 4-cm patch — one café-au-lait macule, a normal finding, lacking the multiplicity of NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and the color of Sturge-Weber · Age 16 with painless progressive blurring — VHL can present at any age but usually presents in early adulthood. Vision falls from retinal edema and distortion · BP 110/72 and an otherwise normal examination — no clinically active pheochromocytoma today, which does not exclude one and is why surveillance is needed
Inherited tumor syndromes — the differential
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Von Hippel-LindauAutosomal dominant loss of the VHL tumor suppressor on chromosome 3; tumors of retina, CNS, adrenal medulla and kidneyRetinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, clear cell renal carcinoma— (the answer)
Neurofibromatosis type 1Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder of skin, nerve and eyeMultiple café-au-lait macules with axillary freckling; cutaneous neurofibromas on the trunk; optic glioma and Lisch nodules; seizures in someOne macule only, which is normal; the retinal lesion is a hemangioblastoma
Sturge-Weber syndromeLeptomeningeal and ocular capillary-venous malformationRed-purple port-wine stain, seizures, glaucoma ⚠︎The patch is light brown and pigmented, not vascular

Management, in one line Confirm with VHL gene testing (VHL: von Hippel-Lindau). Then begin lifelong surveillance: retinal examination, plasma or urine metanephrines, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen. Resect tumors as they appear. For the retinal lesions, laser therapy is the preferred treatment.
Tuberous sclerosis complex Skin — hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas over the cheeks and nose, a shagreen patch (orange-peel plaque on the lower back), and periungual fibromas, which appear in adolescence or adulthood · Brain — subependymal nodules, calcified on CT along the ventricles; cortical tubers, best seen on MRI; a nodule can grow into a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma that obstructs CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) flow and causes hydrocephalus, which needs resection · Seizures — epilepsy in most, often infantile spasms, but the first seizure can come at any age, adolescence included; intellectual disability, autism and behavior disorders · Heart and kidney — cardiac rhabdomyoma; renal angiomyolipoma · Surveillance — skin and eye exams, serial MRI of brain and kidneys, baseline echocardiogram and serial ECGs (electrocardiograms), baseline EEG (electroencephalogram), and neuropsychiatric screening · Not tuberous sclerosis — NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1): café-au-lait macules, trunk neurofibromas, optic glioma; VHL (von Hippel-Lindau): cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas; ataxia-telangiectasia: ataxia from early childhood, poorly coordinated eye movements, conjunctival telangiectasias; endocarditis: fever, murmur and splinter hemorrhages
Neurofibromatosis type 1: tumor risk Optic nerve glioma — the most common brain tumor in neurofibromatosis type 1; usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma of one or both optic nerves or the chiasm · Presentation — insidious vision loss, proptosis and optic atrophy · Eye surveillance — children with neurofibromatosis type 1 need an eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18 · Pheochromocytoma — risk also raised · No established link — medulloblastoma, craniopharyngioma, and arteriovenous malformation, which belongs to Wyburn-Mason syndrome
Decision spine Name the retinal lesion exactly. — Hemangioblastoma → VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) · If it is a different eye lesion: — optic glioma or Lisch nodules point to NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1). Conjunctival neuromas point to MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B). Glaucoma with a choroidal malformation points to Sturge-Weber · Read the skin patch's color. — Light brown pigmented = café-au-lait; red-purple vascular = port-wine · Count the skin lesions. — One café-au-lait macule is normal; multiple plus axillary freckling is NF1 · Read the family's tumor for its organ. — Adrenal medulla with kidney and CNS (central nervous system) points to VHL. Adrenal medulla with thyroid points to MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2)

  6. 28 yo F with von Hippel-Lindau disease, an adrenal mass and elevated metanephrines, scheduled for resection → Alpha blockade started before any beta blockade → Unopposed alpha stimulation otherwise
  7. 4-month-old with a red-purple patch over the V1 distribution and a focal seizure → Brain MRI and ophthalmology referral→ for a leptomeningeal angioma and for glaucoma screening; Sturge-Weber syndrome
  8. 7-year-old with 8 cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules and an optic glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1 → Multiplicity is the criterion, not presence
  9. 24-year-old with medullary thyroid carcinoma, a pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas of the lips and a marfanoid habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B → Neuromas rather than hemangioblastomas
  10. The molecular defect underlying von Hippel-Lindau disease → Loss of a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3 → Autosomal dominant inheritance
  11. 9 year old with painless firm rubbery tongue nodules, marfanoid habitus and long fingers → Medullary thyroid carcinoma → MEN2B — aggressive and early; prophylactic thyroidectomy often in infancy
  12. Child with newly diagnosed MEN2B; what else must be evaluated → Plasma fractionated metanephrines → About half have pheochromocytoma
  13. Adult with primary hyperparathyroidism, a prolactinoma and a gastrinoma → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 → No marfanoid habitus and no mucosal neuromas
  14. Patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid hyperplasia, with a normal habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A → Parathyroid rather than neuromas separates 2A from 2B
  15. Child with perioral pigmented macules and recurrent intussusception → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → Pigmented macules, not neuromas — the risk is polyps and cancer
  16. Adult with recurrent epistaxis and ruby mucosal papules that blanch with pressure → Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia → Telangiectasias blanch; neuromas do not
  17. Newborn with bilateral absence of the iris, hypospadias and an undescended left testis → Wilms tumor → WAGR — serial abdominal ultrasonography from infancy
  18. Newborn with aniridia and genitourinary anomalies; the underlying lesion → An 11p13 deletion → WAGR: Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary, Range of developmental delay
  19. Why Wilms tumor in WAGR differs from isolated Wilms tumor → It is often bilateral and presents earlier → Isolated disease is usually unilateral at age 2 to 5
  20. Macrosomic newborn with macroglossia and hemihyperplasia at risk for embryonal tumors → Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome → Overgrowth rather than aniridia
  21. 17 yo M found confused at the bottom of the stairs after an unwitnessed fall, most likely a seizure; 2-cm forehead contusion; a firm flesh-colored fibroma growing from beneath a toenail; head CT shows calcified nodules along the walls of the lateral ventricles → Tuberous sclerosis complex → Periungual fibroma plus calcified subependymal nodules; surveillance of brain, kidney, heart, eyes and skin
  22. 8 yo F newly diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex after a first seizure, with ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas; normal blood pressure and development so far → Brain and kidney MRI, echocardiogram and ECG, EEG, and skin and eye exams → Surveillance follows the organs the hamartomas occupy, plus neuropsychiatric screening
  23. Asymptomatic 17 yo M at a sports physical with about 10 light brown macules 0.6 to 2 cm across the trunk and limbs and freckling in both axillae → Optic nerve glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1; eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18
  24. 6-year-old with 7 café-au-lait macules over 5 mm, inguinal freckling, normal vision and a normal examination otherwise → Yearly eye examination → Neurofibromatosis type 1; screens for optic nerve glioma
  25. 9-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 and months of painless vision loss in one eye, mild proptosis and a pale optic disc → Optic nerve glioma → Usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma
Decoy note The skin patch drew nearly two in five readers: 20% chose NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and 18% chose Sturge-Weber. A solitary café-au-lait macule is normal, so this most conspicuous physical finding does not discriminate. The mother's adrenal tumor supplies both the inheritance pattern and the second organ. The normal blood pressure does not help the diagnosis, but it indicates that no pheochromocytoma is active yet.
Pearls Retinal hemangioblastoma is von Hippel-Lindau until gene testing says otherwise; the pheochromocytoma and clear cell renal carcinoma follow. · A retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma by itself warrants referral to genetics. VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) testing follows the lesion, with or without a family history. · Eye lesions by syndrome: hemangioblastoma → VHL · optic glioma with Lisch nodules → NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) · conjunctival and corneal neuromas → MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) · choroidal malformation with glaucoma → Sturge-Weber. · Read a patch's color, not merely its presence. Light brown pigmented is café-au-lait, red-purple vascular is port-wine, and they belong to different syndromes. · VHL surveillance covers its organs: retina, brain and spine, adrenal medulla and kidney. The follow-up is therefore an eye exam, metanephrines, and two MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans. · Any pheochromocytoma in a young patient or with a family history is syndromic until proven otherwise. The syndromes are VHL, MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), NF1, or a hereditary paraganglioma gene ⚠︎. · Before resecting a pheochromocytoma, alpha blockade precedes beta blockade; reversing the order leaves alpha stimulation unopposed ⚠︎. · How NBME framed it: a well 17-year-old at a sports physical has about 10 light brown macules and axillary freckling, and the syndrome is never named. After puberty only macules over 15 mm count, so the axillary freckling supplies the second criterion. The lead-in asks which lesion carries a raised risk compared with the general population.
Pairs with Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers pheochromocytoma from the blood-pressure side, reaching the same tumor from a different complaint. Ask: is the pheochromocytoma isolated, or is it one organ of a syndrome? Related conditions without their own brief: the neurocutaneous syndromes as a set, namely NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1), NF2 (neurofibromatosis type 2), tuberous sclerosis and Sturge-Weber. Part I Puberty covers the border and distribution attributes of café-au-lait macules. Part II Abdominal Mass in a Young Child covers the mass itself. Ask: is it within the kidney, and is the child older than 2? Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers ataxia-telangiectasia and its infections. Ask: is the skin lesion vascular, or a fibrous tumor? Part I Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers optic pathway glioma and craniopharyngioma as masses. Ask: does the visual field loss come from the optic nerve or from the sella?
Transferable rule When a visible lesion identifies a syndrome, the lesion's category is shared across syndromes, but its identity is not. Name the tissue and the color before matching. The most conspicuous physical finding may be the one that does not discriminate.
Unchecked attributeNeurofibromatosis type 1, for two café-au-lait macules: Two macules sit between the isolated-is-normal rule and the six of NF1. A count rule alone therefore lands on NF1. The border, the segmental distribution and the absent freckling all argue against it.
Salient decoyNeurofibromatosis type 1: One macule is normal; NF1 requires multiple with axillary freckling, and its eye lesions are optic glioma and Lisch nodules, never a hemangioblastoma
Unchecked attributeSturge-Weber syndrome: The patch is the wrong kind; port-wine stains are red-purple vascular malformations, and this one is light brown and pigmented
True-fact-wrong-slotLi-Fraumeni syndrome: TP53 disease is sarcomas, early breast and adrenocortical carcinoma, with no characteristic eye or skin lesion and no hemangioblastoma
Class-vs-memberMultiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B: Its eye findings are conjunctival and corneal neuromas, and it brings medullary thyroid carcinoma, which nobody in this stem has
Class-vs-memberNeurofibromatosis type 1, for the teenager with the toenail fibroma: Also autosomal dominant with seizures, but its skin tumors are neurofibromas on the trunk and its brain tumor is an optic glioma; calcified subependymal nodules belong to tuberous sclerosis
Unchecked attributeAtaxia-telangiectasia: Autosomal recessive, with ataxia from early childhood and vascular telangiectasias rather than a fibrous nail tumor, and no ventricular nodules
Salient decoyBacterial endocarditis: The nail finding pulls toward it, but endocarditis gives splinter hemorrhages with fever and a murmur, not a firm periungual fibroma
Salient decoyMedulloblastoma, for the teenager with 10 café-au-lait macules: The most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, with raised intracranial pressure and ataxia, but neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotCraniopharyngioma: A Rathke pouch remnant that causes bitemporal field loss; neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotArteriovenous malformation: Retinal and midbrain arteriovenous malformations belong to Wyburn-Mason syndrome, not neurofibromatosis type 1
True-fact-wrong-slotCerebral aneurysm: An adult cause of intracranial hemorrhage; the tumor this skin pattern predicts is an optic nerve glioma

Hemophilia

Hematology · refractory bleeding on replacement = alloantibodies · mixing study proves it

The decision point

A patient with known severe hemophilia A on factor VIII replacement has bleeding that does not respond to increased dosing. The aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) is 112 seconds, massively prolonged despite daily infusions that should be correcting it. The infused factor VIII is being neutralized by alloantibodies. This is inhibitor development, which occurs in ~25% of patients with severe hemophilia A.

An aPTT of 112 on replacement therapy means the intrinsic pathway remains uncorrected even though the missing factor is being given. Platelets of 150K and a normal PT (prothrombin time) exclude every platelet and common-pathway cause.

Defining criteria Inhibitor development — alloantibodies (IgG) against infused factor VIII; ~25% of severe hemophilia A patients · Clinical clue — bleeding refractory to adequate factor replacement therapy · Lab clue — prolonged aPTT that does not correct on a mixing study · Bethesda assay — quantifies inhibitor titer; guides treatment (low <5 BU vs high ≥5 BU)
Refractory bleeding in a hemophiliac — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded by
Inhibitor developmentKnown hemophilia on replacement; increasing bleedsRefractory bleeding + prolonged aPTT on replacement + mixing study does not correct—
Acquired von Willebrand diseaseAutoimmune, lymphoproliferative; mucocutaneous bleedingMucosal bleeding; low vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactorHemarthrosis, not mucocutaneous
Fibrinogen dysfunctionDIC, liver failure; diffuse bleedingBoth PT and aPTT prolonged; low fibrinogenPT is normal
Heparin-induced thrombocytopeniaHeparin exposure; thrombosis + falling plateletsThrombocytopenia + thrombosis; 4T score, PF4 antibodyPlatelets 150K (normal)
Platelet dysfunctionUremia, ASA; mucocutaneous bleedingNormal coagulation studies + prolonged PFA-100aPTT 112; hemarthrosis, not petechiae
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
PT, aPTT and platelet countFirstaPTT prolonged; PT and platelets normalIntrinsic pathway defect, not platelets or the common pathway
Mixing study, incubated at 37 CNextaPTT does not correctAn inhibitor; correction means a simple factor deficiency
Factor VIII and IX activityConfirmsLow factor VIII or IX, when the mix correctsNew diagnosis: hemophilia A or B
Bethesda assayConfirmsInhibitor titer, 5 BU or more is highHigh titer: bypassing agents; low titer: high-dose factor VIII
MRI of the kneeBy branchSynovial thickening and cartilage damageEarly hemophilic arthropathy when radiographs are still normal
Platelet function assay (PFA-100)SkipNormal in hemophiliaJoint bleeding with a long aPTT is a factor problem, not a platelet problem
Bleeding pattern first Factor (clotting) defect — deep bleeding: hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, large ecchymoses, excess bleeding after surgery; the PT or aPTT is prolonged · Platelet defect — mucocutaneous bleeding: nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods, petechiae, small bruises; the count is low or aggregation is abnormal · PT — factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen; factor VII is the only one the PT measures alone · aPTT — factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen · Hemophilia by age — easy bruising in infancy; hemarthroses and deep hematomas once the toddler walks · Factor XI deficiency — the hemophilia lab pattern, but bleeding mainly with surgery or major trauma
Bleeding pattern to lab pattern
DisorderWho bleeds, and howLab pattern (platelets, PT, aPTT)Separating clue
Hemophilia A or B (factor VIII or IX)X-linked, boys; joints, deep muscle, large ecchymosesPlatelets normal, PT normal, aPTT prolonged; aggregation normalA joint or deep bleed in a boy; factor VIII and IX levels confirm
Factor VII deficiencyRare; factor-type bleedingPlatelets normal, PT prolonged, aPTT normalAn isolated long PT
Vitamin K deficiencyNewborn without vitamin K at birth, malabsorption, broad-spectrum antibioticsPlatelets normal, PT prolonged first, then aPTT tooFactor VII has the shortest half-life, so the PT lengthens first; corrects with vitamin K
DICAn ill patient (sepsis, trauma); oozing from lines, petechiae and deep bleedingPlatelets low, PT and aPTT prolonged; fibrinogen low, D-dimer highSick patient; platelets and factors consumed together
Immune thrombocytopeniaWell child; petechiae, small bruises, nose or gum bleedingPlatelets low, PT and aPTT normalIsolated thrombocytopenia
Glanzmann thrombastheniaMucocutaneous bleeding from infancyPlatelets normal, PT and aPTT normal, aggregation abnormalA qualitative platelet defect at a normal count

Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo M with hemophilia A on prophylactic factor VIII, 5 days of right elbow swelling despite daily infusions, aPTT 112, PT normal, platelets normal → Inhibitor development → bypassing agent for acute bleed
  2. 12 yo M with hemophilia A and a known high-titer inhibitor (35 Bethesda units), acute hemarthrosis of the knee → Recombinant activated factor VII → bypasses factor VIII in the coagulation cascade
  3. 8 yo M with hemophilia A and a newly detected low-titer inhibitor (2 Bethesda units), long-term management → Immune tolerance induction with regular high-dose factor VIII → inhibitor eradication
  4. 10 yo M with hemophilia A on replacement therapy, recent increase in bleeding episodes, aPTT prolonged → Mixing study followed by Bethesda assay → confirm and quantify inhibitor
  5. Why a mixing study fails to correct the aPTT in a patient with a factor VIII inhibitor → The inhibitor is a time- and temperature-dependent antibody that neutralizes the normal factor VIII added in the mix
  6. 60 yo F with no bleeding history, new-onset large ecchymoses, aPTT 85, PT normal, mixing study does not correct after 2-hour incubation → Acquired hemophilia A → anti-factor VIII antibody titer
  7. 15 yo M with hemophilia A and inhibitor, life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage not responding to recombinant factor VIIa → Activated prothrombin complex concentrate → second-line bypassing agent
  8. 3 yo M with immediate right knee swelling after a fall, a large hip ecchymosis last week and scattered shin bruises; hemoglobin 13, platelets 187,000, leukocytes 8,500; radiograph shows a large effusion without fracture → Coagulation studies → hemarthrosis after minor trauma suggests a factor deficiency
  9. 4 yo M with recurrent hemarthroses; prothrombin time and platelet count are normal and the activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged → Factor VIII and factor IX activity levels → separates hemophilia A from B
  10. 3 yo M with suspected severe hemophilia presenting with hemarthrosis and easy bruising → Bone marrow biopsy → contraindicated in severe hemophilia because of bleeding risk
  11. 16 yo M with past episodes of sudden knee swelling without injury and prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction, now 6 months of worsening knee pain with a boggy swelling and a knee he cannot fully extend → Hemosiderin deposition and fibrosis → hemophilic arthropathy after recurrent hemarthroses
  12. 3 yo M with severe hemophilia A and a second spontaneous knee hemarthrosis this year → Regular factor VIII prophylaxis → prevents the bleeds that build arthropathy
  13. 14 yo M with hemophilia A, repeated bleeds into the same knee and persistent swelling, with normal radiographs → MRI of the knee → shows synovial and cartilage damage before radiographs
  14. Adult with mild hemophilia A due for a dental extraction → Desmopressin → releases stored factor VIII and von Willebrand factor
  15. 15 mo M, walking since 12 months and bruising after minor bumps since then; now a swollen, tender left ankle with reduced motion after play and no fever; large ecchymoses on both thighs at recent vaccination sites; nares and oropharynx clear, no organomegaly; ankle radiograph shows no fracture → Normal platelet count, normal PT, prolonged PTT, normal platelet aggregation → Hemophilia A or B: deficiency of intrinsic factor VIII or IX
  16. 3-week-old M born at home whose parents declined newborn injections, exclusively breastfed, well-appearing and afebrile, now oozing from the circumcision site with a large scalp bruise → Normal platelet count, prolonged PT, prolonged PTT → Vitamin K deficiency bleeding: factors II, VII, IX and X are low
  17. 6-day-old M who received vitamin K at birth, bleeding from the umbilical stump; platelet count, PT and aPTT all normal → Factor XIII deficiency → XIII cross-links fibrin after the clot forms, so the PT and aPTT stay normal
  18. 5 yo M whose preoperative labs before tonsillectomy show a markedly prolonged aPTT with a normal PT and platelet count; a circumcision and a dental extraction caused no abnormal bleeding, and no relative bleeds → Factor XII deficiency → a long aPTT with no bleeding tendency
Hemophilic arthropathy Hemophilia — X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII (A) or factor IX (B); prolonged aPTT with normal PT and platelets; severity tracks factor activity · Hemarthrosis — spontaneous or trivial-trauma bleeding into a large joint, often a knee, with sudden severe swelling · The link — iron from the extravasated red cells is stored as hemosiderin in the synovium, which inflames it · Then — the synovium thickens and turns boggy, fibroses, and the cartilage and subchondral bone are destroyed · Result — chronic pain, swelling and loss of motion, including a joint that will not fully extend actively or passively · Imaging — radiographs show only late disease; MRI detects damage earlier · Prevention — early prophylaxis with factor concentrate lowers the risk · Treatment — factor replacement; desmopressin for mild hemophilia A · Versus JIA or RA — autoimmune cartilage destruction, no bleeding history · Versus disseminated gonococcal infection — acute onset, not 6 months · Versus avascular necrosis — sickle cell disease, or Legg-Calvé-Perthes at the hip between 4 and 12 · Versus Lyme arthritis — knee effusion, but no bleeding history
Pearls Mixing study — mix patient plasma 1:1 with normal plasma. Correction of the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) means factor deficiency; no correction means an inhibitor. A factor VIII inhibitor is time- and temperature-dependent (incubate at 37°C for 1–2 hours before reading) · Bethesda assay — low-titer (<5 BU) may respond to high-dose factor VIII; high-titer (≥5 BU) requires bypassing agents: rFVIIa (recombinant activated factor VII) or activated PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate) · Immune tolerance induction — repeated high-dose factor VIII to desensitize the immune system; the long-term eradication strategy · Acquired hemophilia A — the adult analogue: autoantibodies in a patient with no prior bleeding history, often autoimmune, malignancy, or postpartum · Hemarthrosis versus petechiae — hemarthrosis indicates a factor problem and petechiae a platelet problem; this division sorts most bleeding disorders before any lab is read
Pairs with Anemia with Thrombocytopenia also uses the coagulation workup. Ask: does the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) correct on mixing? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin K deficiency. Ask: is the PT (prothrombin time) long first, and is factor V normal (vitamin K) or low (liver)?
Transferable rule Bleeding on factor replacement therapy that does not respond to dose escalation, with an aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) still prolonged despite adequate dosing, means the infused factor is being neutralized. The mixing study proves it.
Unchecked attributePlatelet dysfunction: platelets are normal, and the abnormal value is the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time), which is not a platelet test.
True-fact-wrong-slotAcquired vWD (von Willebrand disease): it can lower factor VIII but presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, not hemarthrosis. The patient already has a known factor deficiency.
Unchecked attributeFibrinogen dysfunction: the PT (prothrombin time) is normal, and a fibrinogen (common pathway) defect would prolong both the PT and the aPTT.
