Transfusion Reactions

Timing and associated findings classify transfusion reactions; most need nothing · What are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo F with idiopathic aplastic anaemia, new petechiae and bruising over a week; during a platelet transfusion a chest rash spreads over the body · Labs — absolute neutrophil count 420, platelets 7,000 · Exam — T 37.2, BP 110/82, HR 90, RR 18, saturation 98%; oropharynx normal, lungs clear; diffuse urticarial rash on trunk and limbs plus pinpoint nonblanching macules and bruises at the extremities · Q — the best next step in evaluation of the reaction; options spanned culture of the product, direct Coombs test, no additional evaluation, peripheral smear and coagulation studies
The decision point

Blood pressure is normal, there is no wheeze, the lungs are clear and the oropharynx is normal. This is isolated urticaria in a haemodynamically stable patient. The rash improved after an antihistamine, with an hour of stable observation. It is an urticarial transfusion reaction, caused by preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in the donated plasma, or the reverse. Management is what has already been done: stop the transfusion, give an antihistamine and observe. Improvement with the antihistamine confirms the diagnosis, and the transfusion may be resumed without additional evaluation.

Defining criteria Urticarial reaction — hives and itching only, onset hours into the transfusion, from preformed IgE against a soluble plasma allergen; stop, antihistamine, resume if otherwise asymptomatic, no workup · Anaphylactic reaction — onset seconds to minutes, from anti-IgA antibodies in an IgA-deficient recipient reacting to donor IgA; respiratory distress or wheeze, angioedema, hypotension; epinephrine, and washed products thereafter · Acute haemolytic reaction — ABO incompatibility from clerical error; fever, flank pain, hypotension, haemoglobinuria, direct Coombs positive · Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection — fever, chills, hypotension, most common with platelets; culture both the recipient and the product
Transfusion reactions — timing, company and the movethe vitals sort them faster than the rash does
ReactionOnsetThe company it keepsWhat to do
UrticarialHoursHives and itching, nothing else; vitals normalStop, antihistamine, resume; no workup
Anaphylactic EmergencySeconds to minutesWheeze, angioedema, hypotension; IgA-deficient recipientEpinephrine; future transfusions washed
Acute haemolytic EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, flank pain, hypotension, dark urineStop; direct Coombs, smear, PT and PTT; supportive
Bacterial contamination EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, rigors, hypotension; platelets most oftenCulture recipient and product; empiric antibiotics
Febrile non-haemolytic ⚠︎1–6 hFever and chills without haemolysisStop, antipyretic; leukoreduction prevents
TACO / TRALI ⚠︎Minutes to 6 hRespiratory distress — volume overload vs non-cardiogenic oedemaStop; supportive; the two split on volume status
Pertinent positives & negatives BP 110/82, HR 90, saturation 98% — haemodynamically stable, which excludes anaphylaxis, haemolysis and sepsis · Lungs clear, oropharynx normal — no bronchospasm, no angioedema; the two findings that would make this anaphylaxis · Afebrile at 37.2 — excludes both a febrile reaction and bacterial contamination · Rash improved with diphenhydramine and stayed stable for an hour — confirms the diagnosis · Petechiae and bruises were present before the transfusion — they reflect a platelet count of 7,000 from aplastic anaemia, not a new consumptive process · No flank pain, no dark urine — the findings of a haemolytic reaction are absent · It was a platelet transfusion — platelets are the product most associated with bacterial contamination; without fever, culture is not indicated
Decision spine What is the blood pressure and the saturation? — Normal → the dangerous reactions are out · Is there a fever? — No → not haemolytic, not bacterial, not febrile · Wheeze, angioedema or hypotension? — None → urticaria is isolated, so not anaphylaxis · How fast did it start? — Late, not in the first minutes → urticarial · Did it respond to the antihistamine? — Yes → that is the confirmation · So what is needed? — Nothing further; the transfusion may be resumed
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Vital signs, lung and airway examFirstNormal vitals, clear lungs, hives onlyThe dangerous reactions are excluded
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsHives improve with an antihistamine, vitals stay stableUrticarial reaction; resume the transfusion, no tests
Direct Coombs test, smear, PT and PTTBy branchFever, flank pain, dark urine: Coombs positiveAcute hemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility
Blood cultures of the recipient and the productBy branchFever, rigors, hypotension: growth in bothBacterial contamination, most often a platelet unit
Serum IgA levelBy branchAfter anaphylaxis: IgA absentAnti-IgA anaphylaxis; wash future products
Coombs test or product culture for hives aloneSkipAfebrile and stable: no indicationNothing to find; pre-existing petechiae come from the low platelets
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F with aplastic anemia developing a diffuse urticarial rash late in a platelet transfusion; BP 110/82, saturation 98%, afebrile, lungs clear; rash improves after diphenhydramine and vitals stay stable for an hour → No additional evaluation is indicated → urticarial reaction; the transfusion may be resumed
  2. 30 yo who develops wheezing, facial angioedema and a blood pressure of 70/40 two minutes into a red cell transfusion → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylactic transfusion reaction
  3. Patient with selective IgA deficiency and a history of transfusion anaphylaxis who now requires red blood cells → Transfuse washed red blood cells → washing removes donor plasma IgA
  4. 45 yo who develops fever, flank pain, hypotension and dark urine 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion → Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction → ABO incompatibility from a clerical error
  5. 60 yo who develops fever to 39 C with rigors and hypotension 30 minutes into a platelet transfusion → Culture the recipient and the transfused product and start empiric antibiotics → bacterial contamination, most common with platelets
  6. The mechanism of an isolated urticarial transfusion reaction → Preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in donor plasma → or donor IgE against a recipient allergen
  7. 12 yo with aplastic anemia and platelets of 7,000 who develops hives during transfusion; pinpoint nonblanching macules were documented on her limbs before the transfusion began → Pre-existing thrombocytopenia → the petechiae are not part of the reaction
  8. IgA-deficient patient with prior transfusion anaphylaxis who urgently requires red blood cells → Standard unwashed packed red blood cells → residual donor plasma IgA triggers anaphylaxis
Decoy note The petechiae and ecchymoses look like a new haemorrhagic complication, and they appear in the skin examination beside the urticaria as though they arrived together. They were present before the transfusion: she had bruising a week ago, and her platelet count is 7,000. A finding documented before the intervention cannot be a reaction to it.
Pearls Vital signs: normal blood pressure, no fever and no hypoxia eliminate anaphylaxis, haemolysis, bacterial contamination and TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) · Isolated urticaria is the only reaction in which the transfusion may continue: stop, give an antihistamine, observe, then resume the same unit · Timing separates the two allergic reactions: seconds to minutes with wheeze and hypotension is anaphylaxis; hours with hives alone is urticarial · Anaphylaxis to blood suggests IgA deficiency; the long-term fix is washed products · Platelets carry the bacterial risk because they are stored at room temperature; fever and rigors during a platelet transfusion call for cultures
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers selective IgA deficiency and already keys washed red cells; this brief covers the same topic from the transfusion side. Ask: what are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?
Transferable rule When a treatment has already been given and the response is reported, the response serves as the diagnostic test, and usually nothing further is needed. Check the reported response before ordering anything.
Redundant workupDirect Coombs test: answers "is this haemolysis?", already excluded by normal vitals, no fever, no flank pain and no dark urine.
Salient decoyPT and PTT: indicated only for haemolysis complicated by DIC; her bruising is thrombocytopenic and predates the transfusion.
Redundant workupPeripheral smear: would show schistocytes if microangiopathy were present; there is no haemolysis to look for.
Unchecked attributeCulture of the product: platelets do carry the bacterial risk, but culture requires fever, chills or hypotension; she is afebrile and stable.

Bacterial Meningitis

The CSF 2×2

The decision point

Read the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) as a 2×2: cell type on one axis, glucose on the other.

CSF interpretation — the 2×2
Glucose LOWGlucose NORMAL
NeutrophilsBacterialEarly viral · parameningeal focus
LymphocytesTB · fungal (± partially treated bacterial)Viral
Organism by host
  • Neonate: GBS · E. coli (K1 capsule) · Listeria  |  Unvaccinated toddler: Hib
  • Teen / dorm / military: N. meningitidis  |  Adult (most common): S. pneumoniae
  • >50, pregnant, immunosuppressed: + Listeria → add ampicillin
  • VP shunt: S. epidermidis  |  Basilar skull fracture / CSF rhinorrhea: S. pneumoniae  |  HIV CD4 <100: Cryptococcus
Mechanism pearls Encapsulated organisms need opsonization, so they hit hardest in asplenia/sickle cell (lost filter), cirrhosis (lost complement synthesis) and complement deficiency. Complement deficiency means a lost MAC (membrane attack complex), which causes recurrent Neisseria infection; screen with CH50 (total hemolytic complement) · lipid A of LOS (lipooligosaccharide) triggers TNF (tumor necrosis factor) and IL-1 (interleukin-1) release → shock, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation), Waterhouse-Friderichsen · Listeria escapes the phagosome with listeriolysin O and spreads via ActA-driven host actin polymerization; it has intrinsic cephalosporin resistance · conjugate vaccines convert T-independent polysaccharide into a T-dependent response, which is why they work under age 2.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Blood culturesFirstGrowth of the organismNames the organism if the tap is delayed; never delay antibiotics
Head CTBy branchOnly with a red flag: papilledema, focal deficit, seizure, obtundationGive antibiotics before the scan; an open fontanelle usually removes the need
Lumbar puncture: cell count, glucose, proteinNextNeutrophils with low glucoseBacterial; lymphocytes with normal glucose: viral

Sequencing Get CT before LP (computed tomography before lumbar puncture) only if there is papilledema, focal deficit, seizure, immunocompromise, depressed consciousness or age >60. However, an open fontanelle in an infant generally removes the requirement, since it acts as a pop-off valve. Never delay antibiotics; draw cultures and treat. Empiric therapy is vancomycin + ceftriaxone (+ ampicillin for Listeria). Neonates get cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone (biliary sludging, bilirubin displacement). Dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose: give it to blunt the cytokine burst from bacterial lysis.
Early meningococcal disease Onset — nonspecific fever, headache, vomiting, myalgia or sore throat, easily mistaken for a viral or streptococcal pharyngitis · Red flags — severe myalgia such as leg pain, poor perfusion with pallor, mottling or cold hands and feet, and the worst illness the patient has ever felt · Tempo — petechiae, meningeal signs and altered mental status follow within 12 to 24 hours · Workup — blood cultures and lumbar puncture, with ceftriaxone given without waiting for either · CT first only for — recent seizure, obtundation, focal deficit, papilledema or immunocompromise · Complications — shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, adrenal haemorrhage · Prevention — droplet precautions and chemoprophylaxis for close contacts
Follow-up facts The classic triad is present in only 44% (van de Beek, NEJM 2004; n=696) · the most common sequela is sensorineural hearing loss; check hearing in every survivor · prophylaxis for meningococcus is rifampin, cipro or ceftriaxone; for Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) it is rifampin · eculizumab blocks C5, so meningococcal vaccination is mandatory first.

Vaccines in Special Populations

HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) and the CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count gate for live vaccines · cirrhosis, asplenia, complement deficiency, cochlear implant and pregnancy · hepatitis B serologyIs the vaccine live, and what has the condition taken away?

EligibilitySchedulePractice
Bottom line

Two questions: is the vaccine live, and what has the condition taken away?

  • HIV: check the CD4 count before a live vaccine; HIV alone does not exclude every live vaccine.
  • CD4 200 or higher: varicella, MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) and yellow fever (with caution) are permitted; MMR needs that count, with a CD4 percentage of 15% or higher, for at least 6 months.
  • CD4 under 200: these live vaccines are contraindicated.
  • Never at any CD4: LAIV (live attenuated influenza vaccine; use inactivated influenza), BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin), oral polio.
  • Pregnancy: no live vaccines (MMR, varicella, LAIV).

Cirrhosis loses opsonins and asplenia loses the filter, so their vaccine lists differ.

Antibody Deficiencies

which antibody defect, and what it predicts · Are B cells present, and which isotype is preserved or elevated?

Source vignette Pt — toddler with ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic membrane perforation with otorrhea, weight below the 3rd percentile · Labs — IgM 450, IgG 250, IgA 24; neutropenia (15% of 9,000) · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned CD40 ligand deficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and HIV
The decision point

ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic perforation with otorrhea, and weight below the 3rd percentile establish a primary immunodeficiency rather than ordinary toddler illness. The infection history does not show which one. The panel shows IgM 450 against IgG 250 and IgA 24. XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) requires IgM to be low, and CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) requires it to be low or normal. Selective IgA deficiency and Job syndrome require a normal IgM. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) require a non-immunologic finding this child does not have: microthrombocytopenia and an inverted CD4/CD8, respectively. An isolated elevation of IgM with everything downstream absent is class-switch failure. CD40 ligand on the T cell cannot engage CD40 on the B cell, so the B cell stays locked on its native isotype. The neutropenia (15% of 9,000) is a confirmatory detail: it accompanies CD40 ligand deficiency and does not belong to XLA or CVID.

Defining criteria Class switching (isotype switch recombination) — the CD40L(T cell)–CD40(B cell) interaction that lets an IgM-committed B cell rearrange to IgG, IgA, or IgE; when it fails, IgM is preserved or elevated and every other isotype falls · The CD40L signature — B cells normal, IgM ↑, IgG ↓, IgA ↓, IgE ↓. B and T cell counts are normal; they are dysfunctional, not absent · The B-cell count is the first gate — low or absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia; normal B cells → the block is downstream of B-cell development, and the isotype pattern names it
Pertinent positives & negatives IgM 450 with IgG 250 and IgA 24 — class-switch failure; simultaneously excludes XLA (all isotypes low) and CVID (IgM low or normal, never elevated) and selective IgA deficiency (requires normal IgG and IgM) · Neutropenia (ANC ≈1,350) — common in CD40L deficiency; not a feature of XLA or CVID · Lymphocytes 75%, CD4/CD8 2.2 — normal lymphocyte compartment; excludes HIV, where leukopenia and an inverted ratio are expected · Platelets 260,000 — excludes Wiskott-Aldrich, which requires small, low platelets · Age 14 months with disease since early infancy — argues against CVID, which surfaces in adolescents and young adults · Vaccinations up to date, yet invasive pneumococcal disease — vaccine failure from absent opsonizing IgG, not from missed doses; it also raises a live-vaccine safety question ⚠︎ · Lymphadenopathy — separates HIV from SCID: HIV causes generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly from chronic immune activation, while SCID has absent or tiny lymph nodes because there are no lymphocytes to populate them

SCID: the newborn screen and the cure Defect — gene defects stop T-cell development; B cells fail without T-cell help, so antibody is low too; X-linked or autosomal recessive · Presentation — in the first months: severe viral, fungal (thrush) and opportunistic (Pneumocystis) infection, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive · Labs and exam — lymphopenia with low CD4 and CD8 counts, hypogammaglobulinemia, no palpable nodes or tonsils · Newborn screen — part of US newborn screening: absent T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) on the dried blood spot; lymphocyte flow cytometry confirms · Treatment — hematopoietic stem cell transplant as early as possible; no live vaccines · Not SCID — Bruton agammaglobulinemia has absent B cells but normal T cells and bacterial rather than fungal or opportunistic infection; CVID starts later with normal T- and B-cell counts; CGD has normal lymphocytes and immunoglobulins
Syndromic immunodeficiencies: the tell off the panel Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome — WATER: Wiskott-Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia with small platelets, Eczema, Recurrent infections; X-linked; bleeding at circumcision or from the umbilical stump in early infancy; T-cell dysfunction and low immunoglobulins worsen with age; stem cell transplant · Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome — FATED: coarse Facies (broad nose, prominent forehead), cold staphylococcal Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, high IgE with eosinophilia, Dermatologic eczema; autosomal dominant; impaired Th17 signaling; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis · Ataxia-telangiectasia — autosomal recessive defect in DNA break repair; early childhood progressive cerebellar ataxia and poorly coordinated eye and head movements, then telangiectasias of the conjunctivae and face; recurrent sinopulmonary infection; high malignancy risk; genetic testing confirms · Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with polyendocrinopathy — AIRE deficiency breaks thymic negative selection, giving a T-cell defect against Candida plus autoimmunity; chronic Candida of skin, mouth and nails with hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia, seizure), adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes and thyroiditis
Management, in one line Management is to replace what is missing and cover what the defect exposes. Give immunoglobulin replacement for any low-IgG defect, plus antibiotic prophylaxis with TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) ⚠︎. Give no live vaccines ⚠︎. In selective IgA deficiency, use washed or IgA-depleted products instead of IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) ⚠︎. Allogeneic HSCT (hematopoietic stem cell transplantation) is the only cure for CD40 ligand deficiency ⚠︎.
Long-term treatment: match it to the defect CVID and XLA — lifelong IVIG: the B cells cannot make antibody, so it is supplied; infections fall, but the autoimmune and malignancy risk of CVID remains · SCID — hematopoietic stem cell transplant, as early as possible · Complete DiGeorge syndrome (no thymus) — cultured thymus tissue transplant · CGD — interferon gamma, the immunomodulator, plus TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis · Cellular (T-cell) defects — antiviral and antifungal prophylaxis · Antibody defect with normal T cells — needs antibody replacement, not a transplant or an immunomodulator, although each is right for some other defect
Decision spine Is this beyond normal childhood illness? — ICU pneumonia, perforated TMs, weight <3rd percentile → yes, work it up as primary immunodeficiency · Are B cells / lymphocytes present? — Normal → not XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) · Is IgM high, normal, or low? — High with everything else low → class-switch failure → CD40L deficiency · Is any isotype normal or high? — IgG normal with IgA alone low → selective IgA deficiency; IgE very high → Job · Is every isotype high? — IgG, IgA and IgM all high is polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The primary antibody deficiencies all lower IgG or IgA. With thrush, adenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, test for HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) · Any finding off the panel? — Small low platelets → Wiskott-Aldrich; inverted CD4/CD8 → HIV · Now use the pattern: — which organisms and which treatment does this specific block predict?

  25. 4 mo F with truncus arteriosus repaired as a newborn, hypocalcemic seizures, recurrent oral thrush and no thymic shadow on chest x-ray; flow cytometry shows almost no CD3+ T cells; 22q11.2 deletion confirmed → Cultured thymus tissue transplant → Complete DiGeorge syndrome: without a thymus, T cells cannot mature
  26. 2 yo girl admitted with pneumococcal bacteremia; in the past year three otitis media episodes, two bacterial pneumonias and recurrent thrush; mother has persistent oral candidiasis, chronic diarrhea and a 9-kg weight loss; weight 5th percentile, height 50th percentile; white oral plaques, 2-cm nontender axillary nodes, spleen 2 cm and liver 3 cm below the costal margins; WBC 5,000, platelets 95,000; IgG 2,200, IgA 420 and IgM 400 mg/dL, all above normal → HIV infection → Perinatally acquired; confirm with an HIV viral load, then start antiretroviral therapy
  27. 20 mo boy with recurrent otitis media, two bacterial pneumonias and chronic diarrhea; generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly; IgG, IgA and IgM all high; CD4/CD8 ratio inverted → Perinatal HIV infection → Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio
  28. 14 mo boy with Pneumocystis pneumonia after two pneumococcal pneumonias; IgM high, IgG and IgA low; normal lymphocyte count and CD4/CD8 ratio → CD40 ligand deficiency → Class-switch failure; low IgG and a normal CD4/CD8 ratio separate it from HIV
Decoy note Lymphocytes at 75% look alarming but are expected. Lymphocytosis accompanies active infection. It also confirms that lymphocyte numbers are intact, which excludes XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). The three bronchiolitis episodes read as ordinary infant viral illness but support CD40 ligand deficiency, which impairs viral defense as well as opsonization. Up-to-date vaccination converts the pneumococcal ICU admission into vaccine failure, an immunodeficiency finding rather than a gap in care.
Pearls High IgM with low IgG/IgA is class-switch failure. Absent B cells is XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). Low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and B cells present is CVID (common variable immunodeficiency). · Read the panel in a fixed order: B cells, then IgM, then IgG/IgA/IgE. · The missing isotype predicts the organism. No opsonizing IgG → encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae). A broken CD40 ligand–CD40 axis also breaks T-cell licensing of macrophages → Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium ⚠︎. · Neutropenia alongside hypogammaglobulinemia points at CD40L deficiency rather than XLA. · Selective IgA deficiency is the defect whose management is what you withhold: no IVIG, and washed or IgA-deficient blood products for transfusion ⚠︎. · Any patient on immunoglobulin replacement or with a defective T-cell limb gets no live vaccines ⚠︎; and replacement IgG makes serologic testing uninterpretable afterward. · A mildly low IgG at 6–9 months in a thriving infant with normal IgM, normal B cells, and protective vaccine titers is transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy — recheck, don't treat ⚠︎. · How NBME framed it: the lead-in asks for a mechanism but lists diseases, and the mother's thrush, chronic diarrhea and weight loss hold the deciding clue.
The physiologic IgG nadir The nadir — maternally derived IgG wanes after birth and troughs at 3 to 6 months, when the infant's own synthesis takes over · Transient hypogammaglobulinemia — that synthesis is delayed and the nadir is prolonged beyond 6 months, with recurrent respiratory infection and atopy · Vaccine response is the most discriminating line on the panel — a normal response excludes common variable immunodeficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia at once, whatever the isotype levels say
Pairs with Part I Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease shares the complaint of recurrent otitis media and pneumonia in a child. Ask: does the immunoglobulin panel explain it, or does the anatomy? When the panel is normal, that brief covers the structural and mucociliary axis; when an isotype is out of step, this one does. Part I Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers the phagocyte defects: chronic granulomatous disease, leukocyte adhesion deficiency and Chédiak-Higashi. Ask: are the immunoglobulins normal, and is there pus? Part I 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome covers the thymic T-cell defect with hypocalcemia (CATCH-22); ask: is there a conotruncal heart lesion? Part II Infectious Diarrhea follows a patient with common variable immunodeficiency on immunoglobulin replacement who develops Salmonella gastroenteritis. Ask: does the organism point to the immune defect, or to the food it came from?
Transferable rule With recurrent sinopulmonary infection and an immunoglobulin panel, read the pattern rather than recall a disease. Count the B cells, then ask which isotype is preserved. The preserved isotype names the block, and the missing isotypes name the organisms you must cover.
Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: eczema plus recurrent infection fits its pattern, but it requires small, low platelets. A normal count excludes it, and atopy is itself a feature of transient hypogammaglobulinemia.
Class-vs-memberBruton agammaglobulinemia: That member of the class requires absent B cells and low IgM; IgM is 450 and the lymphocyte compartment is intact
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: CVID leaves IgM low or normal but never high, and presents in adolescence or later, not at 14 months
Salient decoyHIV infection: HIV would show leukopenia and a low CD4/CD8 ratio; here the ratio is 2.2 and WBC 9,000. HIV raises IgG in a polyclonal rise, while this panel has IgG 250.
True-fact-wrong-slotIgA deficiency: Isolated IgA deficiency requires normal IgG and IgM; IgG 250 makes the deficiency global-with-a-block, not selective
Class-vs-memberWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: The syndromic member is defined by microthrombocytopenia; platelets are 260,000 and normal-sized, and there is no eczema
Class-vs-memberSevere combined immunodeficiency: It presents in early infancy with lymphopenia, low immunoglobulins and no palpable nodes. A 2-year-old with every isotype high and 2-cm axillary nodes does not fit.
Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: Platelets of 95,000 are the lure. It classically has eczema and small platelets, and it is X-linked, while this patient with every isotype high is a girl.
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: It lowers IgG along with IgA and/or IgM, and it usually starts after puberty. Here every isotype is high at age 2.
True-fact-wrong-slotChronic granulomatous disease: It causes catalase-positive abscesses and granulomas with an abnormal DHR (dihydrorhodamine) test. Immunoglobulins are normal or high in it, so this panel does not exclude it; the thrush, the adenopathy and the mother's illness point to HIV.
Unchecked attributeChédiak-Higashi syndrome: It needs oculocutaneous albinism and neuropathy, and neither is described in the girl with every isotype high.
True-fact-wrong-slotTerminal complement deficiency: It causes recurrent Neisseria infection, not pneumococcal disease with thrush and every isotype high.
Salient decoyCystic fibrosis: Recurrent pneumonia and low weight fit. It causes lung and pancreatic disease, without thrush, adenopathy or a mother with an AIDS-suggestive illness.

Oral Lesions in a Child

lesion location identifies the virus · front of the mouth or back

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with 2 days of throat pain and poor intake; T 38.3, HR 108 · Exam — scattered 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars with grey shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula; tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared; no rash · Q — the most likely associated pathogen; options spanned adenovirus, coxsackievirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus and Streptococcus pyogenes
The decision point

The lesions are vesicles and ulcers, not exudate. This removes every bacterial and mononucleosis-type pharyngitis. Adenovirus, EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) and S. pyogenes all produce tonsillar exudate, and none produces oral vesicles. The lesions are posterior (soft palate, uvula, anterior palatine pillars), with the tongue, lips and buccal mucosa explicitly spared. Herpangina, from coxsackievirus A, affects the back of the mouth. In herpetic gingivostomatitis, lesions affect the front, with red swollen gums. The spared structures are exactly those HSV (herpes simplex virus) would involve.

Defining criteria Herpangina — coxsackievirus A; ages 3 to 10; late summer and early fall; fever and pharyngitis with grey vesicles progressing to fibrin-coated ulcers on the posterior oropharynx, and no rash; treatment is supportive · Herpetic gingivostomatitis — HSV-1; 6 months to 5 years; no seasonality; clusters of vesicles on the anterior oral mucosa and lips with erythematous, edematous gingiva; treated with oral acyclovir · Hand-foot-and-mouth disease — also coxsackievirus, but anterior oral lesions plus vesicles on palms and soles; herpangina's defining negative is the absent rash
Pertinent positives & negatives Vesicles and ulcers, not exudate — excludes adenovirus, EBV and group A streptococcus in one move · Soft palate, uvula and palatine pillars involved — the posterior distribution, herpangina territory · Tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared — a stated negative that excludes HSV gingivostomatitis, whose distribution is precisely those structures · No rash — separates herpangina from hand-foot-and-mouth disease · No gingival erythema or edema described — a second strike against HSV, whose gingivitis is near-universal · Age 5, starting the fall term in 2 weeks — age 3 to 10 and late summer, both epidemiological features; the school detail is dating the season, not flagging exposure · No adenopathy or splenomegaly — nothing to support mononucleosis
Oral lesions in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Herpangina (coxsackievirus A)3 to 10 yrs, late summer and early fall, abrupt high feverPosterior grey vesicles becoming ulcers: soft palate, uvula, pillars; no rash— (the answer)
Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1)6 months to 5 years, any season; drooling, refuses to drinkAnterior clusters on buccal mucosa, tongue and lips; swollen red gingivaThose exact sites are stated as spared
Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseSame virus family, same seasonAnterior oral lesions plus palms and solesThe skin has no rash
Streptococcal pharyngitisFever, sore throat, no coughTonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, palatal petechiaeVesicles and ulcers rather than exudate
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent with prolonged fatigueExudate plus posterior cervical nodes plus splenomegalyNo exudate, no adenopathy, no splenomegaly
Adenoviral tonsillitisFever, cough, sore throat, sometimes conjunctivitisExudate without vesiclesVesicular lesions are not its picture
Decision spine Vesicles and ulcers, or exudate? — Vesicles means a viral enanthem, and the bacterial and EBV options fall · Front of the mouth or back? — Back means herpangina · Are the gums red and swollen? — Not described, which argues against HSV · Is there a rash on palms and soles? — No, so not hand-foot-and-mouth · Age and season? — Five years in late summer corroborates · So what is the management? — Supportive; it self-resolves within a week
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars and gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash → Coxsackievirus A → herpangina
  2. 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the gingiva, tongue and lips with erythematous edematous gums → Herpetic gingivostomatitis → oral acyclovir
  3. 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease → supportive care
  4. 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs → Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesia → herpangina resolves within a week
  5. 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → rapid antigen testing before treating
  6. 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly → Epstein-Barr virus infection → avoid contact sports
  7. 5 yo with gray vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated → Oral acyclovir → herpangina is an enteroviral illness, not a herpesvirus one
  8. 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours → Intravenous rehydration → dehydration is the principal complication
  9. 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; gray vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and anterior pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash → Herpangina → coxsackievirus A; supportive care
Pearls Anterior is herpes, posterior is coxsackie — both diseases otherwise present with fever, sore throat and a miserable child · Vesicles and ulcers exclude exudate-producing pathogens wholesale: strep, EBV and adenovirus make exudate, not blisters · Herpangina has no rash; hand-foot-and-mouth does — same virus family, separated by the skin · Red swollen gingiva is the HSV signature, and its absence is as informative as any positive finding · Starting the fall term in two weeks is dating the season, not describing an exposure · shedding continues in stool for weeks after recovery ⚠︎, so hand hygiene rather than exclusion is the public-health answer
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule; this brief covers vesicular lesions. Ask: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back? Part II Fever and Rash in a Child sorts hand-foot-and-mouth disease among the other rashes with fever.
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lesion type, the discriminating attribute is usually anatomical, not clinical. Ask where the lesions are before asking what they are. Treat a stated spared structure as an active exclusion, not as background.
Unchecked attributeHerpes simplex virus: oral vesicles in a child retrieves HSV automatically, but HSV is anterior and those sites are explicitly spared, with no gingival swelling.
Class-vs-memberAdenovirus: a common cause of paediatric fever with sore throat, but it produces exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles or ulcers.
Class-vs-memberStreptococcus pyogenes: exudate with tender anterior nodes; vesicles and ulcers argue against it.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus: exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and adolescent age; none present.

Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function

the organism list identifies the diagnosis · Are there granulomas, and is the infection outside the chest?

Source vignette Pt — 2 yo M, 3 days of fever, cough and irritability; perirectal abscess drained at 9 months; T 38.9, bilateral lower-lobe crackles · Imaging — bilateral pneumonia on chest film; after 3 days of antibiotics still febrile, CT shows a small left effusion with paratracheal and hilar lymphadenopathy · Labs — lymph node and lung biopsy shows granuloma formation; culture grows Burkholderia (Pseudomonas) cepacia · Q — the mechanism responsible; options spanned decreased immunoglobulin production, decreased superoxide production, defective opsonization, impaired clearing of airway secretions and impaired neutrophil chemotaxis
Source vignette · NBME Pediatrics CMS Pt — 2 yo M, 2 days of fever and mouth sores, fussy and refusing food, now improving; a year of similar episodes about every 3 weeks, each lasting 3 to 5 days; normal growth and development · Exam — T 38.4 C, HR 120; scattered aphthous ulcers; skin clear; no lymphadenopathy · Labs — Hb 11.5; WBC 4,000 with 4% segmented neutrophils, 84% lymphocytes, 12% monocytes; platelets 250,000 · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, cyclic neutropenia, dyskeratosis congenita, Fanconi syndrome, hypersplenism, leukemia, severe congenital neutropenia, viral illness and vitamin B12 deficiency
The decision point

The pneumonia does not name the defect. Granulomas on biopsy and a Burkholderia cepacia culture together point at one disease: chronic granulomatous disease. It is a disorder of NADPH oxidase, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms. The enzyme drives the neutrophil respiratory burst, so its loss means decreased superoxide production. Phagocytes migrate normally and ingest normally, but have impaired intracellular killing. Neutrophils can borrow hydrogen peroxide made by the pathogen itself. Susceptibility therefore particularly involves characteristic catalase-positive organisms that destroy their own peroxide; this is not an exclusive organism list. The granulomas are the same defect seen histologically: phagocytes arrive but clear pathogens poorly, contributing to granuloma formation.

Defining criteria Chronic granulomatous disease — NADPH oxidase disorder, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms; impaired respiratory burst and reduced reactive oxygen species, so intracellular killing is impaired · The organism pattern — particular susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, because catalase degrades the pathogen's own hydrogen peroxide and denies the neutrophil a borrowed oxidant: S aureus, B cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus · Sites — lungs, skin, liver and lymph nodes; perirectal abscess is characteristic, with diffuse granulomas in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts · Diagnosis — measure neutrophil superoxide production: dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry preferred, nitroblue tetrazolium the older equivalent · Treatment — prophylaxis with TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma; haematopoietic cell transplant is curative
Recurrent infection — reading the mechanismwhich defect, by organism and by histology
MechanismDiseaseThe NBME tellExcluded here by
↓ superoxide productionChronic granulomatous diseaseCatalase-positive organisms + granulomas + abscesses (perirectal, liver)— (the answer)
Impaired airway clearanceCystic fibrosisNasal polyps, clubbing, steatorrhoea; also gets B cepaciaNo granulomas; infections confined to the sinopulmonary tract
↓ immunoglobulin productionX-linked agammaglobulinaemiaEncapsulated organisms; all isotypes low, absent B cellsNo granulomas, no abscesses, wrong organism
Defective opsonisationComplement (C3) deficiencyEncapsulated organisms, recurrent pyogenic infectionSame — and B cepacia is not the pattern
Impaired neutrophil chemotaxisLeukocyte adhesion deficiencyDelayed umbilical cord separation (over 3 weeks), skin and mucosal infections without pus (cellulitis, periodontitis), poor wound healing, marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia; CD18 integrin defectPus was present (abscess drained); no granulomas
Impaired Th17 signalling (JAK-STAT)Hyper-IgE (Job) syndromeCold staphylococcal and Candida abscesses, severe eczema, eosinophilia with a normal white countNo eczema or eosinophilia; granulomas and Burkholderia point to the oxidative burst
Pertinent positives & negatives Granulomas on biopsy — the most specific finding; excludes CF, XLA, complement deficiency and leukocyte adhesion deficiency, none of which form them · Burkholderia cepacia — catalase-positive, and shared with cystic fibrosis, which is exactly why it is not sufficient alone · Perirectal abscess at 9 months — extrapulmonary abscess; CF does not do this, and it is the finding that separates the two · Persistent fever after 3 days of appropriate antibiotics — killing is defective, not coverage · Hilar and paratracheal lymphadenopathy — node involvement, part of the CGD site pattern · Male, age 2 — consistent with the common X-linked form presenting in early childhood; autosomal recessive forms also occur · Normal ear, nose and throat examination — no chronic rhinosinusitis, arguing further against CF
Decision spine Are there granulomas? — Yes → CGD, essentially alone among the immunodeficiencies · What grew? — A catalase-positive organism → confirms · Where are the infections? — Lung and perirectal → extrapulmonary, so not CF · Was there pus? — Yes → chemotaxis and adhesion intact, so not leukocyte adhesion deficiency · What is the mechanism of that defect? — NADPH oxidase → decreased superoxide · How is it confirmed? — Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to

First fork: neutrophil number or function Number — the neutrophil count is low; infections are bacterial, with fever, mouth ulcers, gingivitis and skin, lung or gut infection when the count is lowest · Function — the count is normal or high and the cells fail at a step: adhesion (leukocyte adhesion deficiency), killing (chronic granulomatous disease), granule traffic (Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, which also lowers the count) · Absolute neutrophil count — WBC × (segmented neutrophils + bands); 4,000 × 4% is about 160; under 1,500 is neutropenia and under 500 is severe · Name trap — Fanconi syndrome is proximal renal tubule wasting of glucose, phosphate, bicarbonate and amino acids; Fanconi anemia is inherited marrow failure
Low neutrophil count in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tellExcluded in the periodic-fever child by

Cyclic neutropenia: confirm and treat Confirm — one normal count between episodes proves nothing; check neutrophil counts 2 to 3 times a week for at least 6 weeks to catch the nadirs; genetic testing for the elastase mutation supports it · During an episode — treat any infection, keep up oral and dental hygiene · Long term — G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) keeps the count up and prevents episodes; the same drug treats severe congenital neutropenia
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M with a perirectal abscess drained at 9 months, now with bilateral pneumonia still febrile after 3 days of antibiotics; biopsy shows granulomas and culture grows Burkholderia cepacia → Decreased superoxide production → NADPH oxidase defect in chronic granulomatous disease
  2. 3 yo M with recurrent Serratia marcescens skin abscesses and hepatic granulomas on imaging → Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry → measures the neutrophil respiratory burst
  3. Why are characteristic catalase-positive organisms associated with chronic granulomatous disease? → Catalase degrades the organism's own hydrogen peroxide → the neutrophil cannot borrow the pathogen's oxidant
  4. 2 yo newly diagnosed with chronic granulomatous disease, currently well between infections → TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma prophylaxis → bacterial, fungal and immunomodulatory cover
  5. 5 yo with chronic granulomatous disease and repeated life-threatening infections despite full prophylaxis → Hematopoietic cell transplantation → the only curative therapy
  6. Newborn with delayed umbilical cord separation and a soft tissue infection producing no pus, with a leukocyte count of 38,000 → Leukocyte adhesion deficiency → impaired chemotaxis and adhesion
  7. 4 yo with nasal polyps, digital clubbing, steatorrhea and Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia; biopsy shows no granulomas → Cystic fibrosis → sweat chloride testing
  8. 9 mo M with recurrent Streptococcus pneumoniae infections, all immunoglobulin isotypes low and absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia → immunoglobulin replacement therapy
  9. 3 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess, a perirectal abscess drained in infancy and granulomas on biopsy → Chronic granulomatous disease → confirm with dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry
  10. 3 yo M with eczema since infancy and recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Candida abscesses, now a nontender fluctuant buttock abscess, afebrile; leukocytes 9,000 with 30% neutrophils and 40% eosinophils → Hyper-IgE syndrome → impaired Th17 signaling blunts neutrophil recruitment
  11. 2 yo with recurrent staphylococcal skin infections, silvery hair, pale skin and neutropenia → Chédiak-Higashi syndrome → lysosomal trafficking defect
  12. Why the abscesses of hyper-IgE syndrome are cold, without erythema or tenderness → Th17 defect blunts neutrophil recruitment → few neutrophils arrive, so little inflammation
  13. 2 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus perianal abscess drained at 2 months after failed oral antibiotics, left inguinal lymphadenitis at 7 months, and now a fluctuant right arm abscess that grows Serratia marcescens; leukocyte and platelet counts normal, B and T cells normal; dihydrorhodamine test abnormal → Itraconazole → antifungal prophylaxis in chronic granulomatous disease
  14. 3 yo M with chronic granulomatous disease on TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis, due for vaccines before his family moves to a country where tuberculosis is common → BCG vaccine → live bacterial vaccine; live viral and inactivated vaccines are safe
  15. 2 yo M with 2 days of fever and painful mouth sores, now improving; a year of similar episodes about every 3 weeks, each lasting 3 to 5 days, well and growing normally between them; T 38.4 C, scattered aphthous ulcers, no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly; Hb 11.5, WBC 4,000 with 4% segmented neutrophils, platelets 250,000 → Cyclic neutropenia → neutrophil elastase (ELANE) mutation; confirm with serial counts, treat with G-CSF
  16. 4 yo F with fever, mouth ulcers and sore throat that recur about every 3 weeks and last 4 to 5 days, for 10 months; well between episodes with normal growth; today, on a well day, the examination is normal and a CBC shows WBC 7,200 with 45% neutrophils, normal hemoglobin and platelets → Neutrophil counts twice weekly for 6 weeks → cyclic neutropenia; a single count between episodes can be normal
  17. 5 yo M with cyclic neutropenia confirmed by serial counts and an ELANE mutation; despite good dental care he has painful mouth ulcers every 3 weeks, early periodontal disease and two pneumonias this year, each during a nadir → Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor → keeps the count up and prevents episodes
  18. 2-month-old boy with omphalitis at 3 weeks and now a perianal abscess; the umbilical cord separated at 10 days and the wound drains pus; absolute neutrophil count under 200 on every CBC over 4 weeks, with normal hemoglobin and platelets → Severe congenital neutropenia → G-CSF; lifelong risk of myelodysplasia and AML
Separating chronic granulomatous disease from cystic fibrosis Burkholderia cepacia belongs to two diseases: cystic fibrosis and chronic granulomatous disease. It therefore identifies neither alone. Granulomas and extrapulmonary abscesses are what split them. In the vignette, a perirectal abscess in an infant is the single most specific clue to chronic granulomatous disease. It sits in the past medical history, where it is easy to skim.
Reading the CBC in recurrent abscesses Eosinophilia, normal white count — hyper-IgE syndrome · Marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia — leukocyte adhesion deficiency · Neutropenia with oculocutaneous albinism — Chédiak-Higashi syndrome: giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils on the smear, recurrent bacterial infection, progressive neurodegeneration with peripheral neuropathy; autosomal recessive lysosomal trafficking defect · Small platelets with bruising — Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome · Lymphopenia — DiGeorge syndrome, whose infections are invasive viral, fungal and bacterial rather than cold abscesses · Unremarkable CBC with Candida infections — myeloperoxidase deficiency · Job syndrome, the rest — autosomal dominant; eczema from the first weeks of life, recurrent sinopulmonary infection, broad nose and prominent forehead, retained primary teeth; genetic testing confirms; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis
Pearls Granulomas plus abscesses plus a catalase-positive organism is CGD, and no other immunodeficiency assembles that trio · Catalase-positive is a mechanism, not a list — the neutrophil can use the organism's own peroxide, helping explain susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive organisms; other organisms are not excluded · Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry has replaced nitroblue tetrazolium as the preferred test; both measure the same respiratory burst · Prophylaxis — TMP-SMX for bacteria plus itraconazole for fungi such as Aspergillus, with interferon gamma added for severe disease; transplant is the only cure · Not CGD prophylaxis — G-CSF, because the neutrophil count is normal; IVIG, because immunoglobulins are normal (it treats antibody deficiency such as XLA); valacyclovir, which belongs to T-cell defects · Vaccines — avoid BCG and other live bacterial vaccines; live viral and inactivated vaccines are safe · Phagocytes in CGD migrate and ingest normally; the failure is intracellular killing, which is why pus forms and chemotaxis-defect diseases look different
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers the antibody deficiencies, and this brief covers the phagocyte defects. Together the two cover the common primary immunodeficiencies. Ask: are there granulomas, and is the infection outside the chest?
How NBME framed it No organism or granuloma was named; the clue was a maternal uncle who died of fungal pneumonia, which points to X-linked disease. Four of the five options were steps in leukocyte function, and the key named the killing defect as impaired microbicidal activity.
Transferable rule When an organism belongs to two diseases, it cannot separate them; find the finding that belongs to only one. Here the shared organism is B cepacia, and the findings that belong to only one disease are the granuloma and the perirectal abscess.
Unchecked attributeImpaired clearing of airway secretions: cystic fibrosis makes no granulomas, and its infections stay sinopulmonary; a perirectal abscess is outside its territory.
Class-vs-memberDefective opsonization: complement deficiency gives encapsulated-organism infection without granulomas.
Class-vs-memberImpaired neutrophil chemotaxis: leukocyte adhesion deficiency gives pus-free infections with delayed cord separation; pus was drained here.
True-fact-wrong-slotDecreased immunoglobulin production: XLA gives encapsulated sinopulmonary infection; no granulomas, wrong organism.
Unchecked attributeSevere congenital neutropenia: the right category and often the same gene, but it is persistent from the first months with severe infections; this child is well between regular 3-week episodes.
Salient decoyViral illness: fever and mouth sores look viral, and viruses do lower the count, but once, not every 3 weeks for a year.
True-fact-wrong-slotFanconi syndrome: a proximal tubule disorder, not a marrow one; the marrow disease is Fanconi anemia, which lowers all three lines and brings short stature and thumb anomalies.

The Febrile Infant — Finding the Source

Paradoxical irritability · every stem negative is an eliminated source

Source vignette Pt — 7 mo M, fever 39.5 C, lies quietly when undisturbed and cries violently when picked up · Labs — WBC 16,000 with 83% neutrophils; urine dipstick negative on a concentrated specimen · Q — the most appropriate test; options spanned lumbar puncture, abdominal ultrasonography and stool PCR
The decision point

On examination, he is calm when left alone and screams when picked up. This is paradoxical irritability: handling stretches inflamed meninges, so being comforted makes an infant worse. It is the meningeal sign of infancy because nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski signs are unreliable under roughly 12 to 18 months.

No cough or rhinorrhea closes the respiratory branch. A negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite in urine concentrated to a specific gravity of 1.030 closes the urinary branch. The concentration is what makes the negative trustworthy. When the sources are eliminated one by one and a meningeal sign remains, do a lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Paradoxical irritability — quiet when undisturbed, crying on being picked up or moved · Fever without a source — documented fever with no localising findings after history and examination · Dipstick sensitivity — leukocyte esterase about 83%, nitrite about 53%; both negative in concentrated urine is genuinely reassuring
The toxic febrile infant — where is the source
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Bacterial meningitisAny age; infants show no neck signsParadoxical irritability, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry
Intussusception6 to 36 months, ileocolic, often post-viralParoxysmal crying with pain-free intervals, sausage mass, currant-jelly stool
Urinary tract infectionThe commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infantsPositive leukocyte esterase or nitrite with pyuria
Bacterial gastroenteritisHigh fever with crampingBloody or mucoid stools, many per day, sick contacts
Viral respiratory infectionCough, congestion, coryzaRhinorrhea and cough, both explicitly absent here
Occult bacteremia or pneumoniaFever with leukocytosis, no localising signTachypnea with hypoxia or focal crackles, not fever-driven tachypnea alone
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Catheterized urinalysisFirstLeukocyte esterase and nitrite negative in concentrated urineUrinary source unlikely; positive: urine culture and antibiotics
CBC and blood cultureFirstLeukocytosis with neutrophil predominanceBacterial infection likely; does not locate the source
Head CTBy branchFocal deficit or papilledema: image first, after antibioticsAn open fontanelle usually permits a tap without imaging
Lumbar puncture: cell count, glucose, Gram stain, cultureConfirmsNeutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, positive cultureBacterial meningitis; give antibiotics first if the tap is delayed
Abdominal ultrasoundBy branchParoxysmal crying with a sausage mass: target signIntussusception
Stool PCR for enteric pathogensSkipLoose stools are nonspecific in a septic infantNot a localizing source
Scenario bank
  1. 7 mo M, fever 39.5, lies quietly when undisturbed and cries violently when picked up, WBC 16,000 with 83% neutrophils, urine dipstick negative in concentrated urine → Lumbar puncture for Gram stain and culture → bacterial meningitis
  2. 9 mo M with paroxysmal crying and legs drawn up, calm between episodes, lethargic, sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass → Abdominal ultrasound → intussusception
  3. 8 mo F, fever 39.2, no localizing findings, urine dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase → Urine culture and empiric antibiotics → urinary tract infection
  4. 6 mo M with suspected meningitis in whom lumbar puncture will be delayed an hour → Give empiric antibiotics now and perform the lumbar puncture after → a sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable trade
  5. 3 wk old F with a temperature of 38.4 C, well-appearing, with no identified source → Full evaluation including lumbar puncture, admission and empiric antibiotics → under 28 days, well appearance does not reassure
  6. 10 mo M with fever, irritability, a bulging anterior fontanelle and a high-pitched cry → Bacterial meningitis → neuroimaging only if focal signs are present
  7. 7 mo M with 3 days of fever to 39 C, then defervescence followed by a blanching rose-pink truncal rash → Roseola infantum → human herpesvirus 6, no testing needed
  8. 12 mo F with suspected meningitis, papilledema and a new focal neurologic deficit → Head CT before lumbar puncture → antibiotics first, then CT, then LP
  9. 8 mo M with fever, petechiae and hypotension → Delaying antibiotics to complete the lumbar puncture → treat first, tap after
Sequence and its exceptions Head CT (computed tomography) precedes lumbar puncture only for focal deficits, papilledema, altered consciousness or immunocompromise. In that case, antibiotics precede the CT, not the other way round. In an infant with an open fontanelle the requirement is generally suspended. The fontanelle decompresses rising pressure, so tap without imaging first. Under 28 days, a well appearance does not reassure; full evaluation, admission and empiric antibiotics are needed regardless. Empiric coverage beyond the neonatal period is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin. Neonates get ampicillin plus cefotaxime or gentamicin to cover Listeria.
Pearls Nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski are unreliable in infants; look for paradoxical irritability, a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry · A dipstick is a screen, not a rule-out; nitrite is insensitive because infant bladder transit is too short for nitrate reduction · Loose stools and mild tachypnea are nonspecific systemic responses in a septic infant, not localising findings · Dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid, so this brief stops at the decision to tap. Ask: am I deciding whether to tap, or reading the fluid? Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child covers what a seizure adds to the decision to tap. Part II Neonatal Sepsis and Its Mimics covers the afebrile neonate whose lab result is the only sign. Ask: is the infant febrile, or is the WBC (white blood cell count) the only sign? Aquifer Fever in an Infant covers the workup before a source is found. It covers which tests the age, appearance and vaccines call for, and the febrile UTI (urinary tract infection) that is most often found.
Transferable rule Name the disease first, then choose the test that follows from it. In a febrile infant, reach the diagnosis by elimination: each reliable negative finding closes a source, and the diagnosis is the source that remains.
Mirror twinIntussusception is the other inconsolable-infant diagnosis, but its crying is paroxysmal with calm intervals.
Class-vs-memberUrine culture is the right class of test on the wrong fluid.
Salient decoyThree loose stools cannot produce a fever of 39.5 with 83% neutrophils.

Hearing Loss & Otosclerosis

Start with the Rinne and Weber tests

The decision point

Conductive loss: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, and Rinne shows BC > AC (bone conduction greater than air conduction) in that ear. Sensorineural loss: Weber lateralizes away from the affected ear, and Rinne stays AC > BC bilaterally. A conductive loss with a normal otoscopic exam in a young adult is otosclerosis.

Otosclerosis pathophysiology Otosclerosis is a genetic bone-remodeling disorder of the otic capsule at the fissula ante fenestram. An otospongiotic (hypervascular, resorptive) phase is followed by a sclerotic phase that fixes the stapes footplate. Inheritance: Autosomal dominant with ~40% penetrance, so family history is often absent. Onset is in the 20s–40s, with a 2:1 female predominance. Estrogen and progesterone accelerate it, so it is classically unmasked in pregnancy. Measles virus RNA has been found in otosclerotic foci.
Exam & audiogram Paracusis of Willis — hears better in noisy environments · Carhart notch — dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz, an artifact of ossicular fixation · Schwartze sign — reddish blush from hypervascularity · treatment: amplification or stapedectomy · van der Hoeve syndrome = osteogenesis imperfecta + otosclerosis + blue sclerae (both type I collagen disorders).
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
OtoscopyFirstDrum normal, or effusion, perforation or retraction pocketNormal drum with conductive loss suggests otosclerosis; an abnormal drum names the middle-ear cause
Weber and Rinne tuning forksFirstWeber toward the affected ear, bone conduction over airConductive loss; Weber away with air over bone is sensorineural
Pure-tone audiometryConfirmsAir-bone gap, often with a Carhart notch at 2000 HzConductive loss and its degree; otosclerosis when the drum is normal
MRI with gadolinium, internal auditory canalsBy branchEnhancing mass in the internal auditory canalVestibular schwannoma; ordered for unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus
Temporal bone CTBy branchBone erosion by a middle-ear massCholesteatoma extent before surgery
Head CT for unilateral sensorineural lossSkipCan miss a small schwannomaMRI with gadolinium is the study
Scenario bank
  1. 35 yo F with progressive conductive loss, Weber lateralizing to the affected ear, normal drum → Otosclerosis
  2. 35 yo F with Weber lateralizing away from the affected ear and Rinne AC over BC bilaterally → Sensorineural hearing loss
  3. 35 yo F with conductive loss, foul discharge and a retraction pocket → Cholesteatoma
  4. 68 yo M with symmetric high-frequency sensorineural loss and poor speech discrimination → Presbycusis
  5. 45 yo F with unilateral sensorineural loss, tinnitus and imbalance → Vestibular schwannoma → MRI
  6. 50 yo M with sudden unilateral sensorineural loss over hours → Sudden sensorineural hearing loss → urgent corticosteroids
  7. 5 yo M, progressive hearing difficulty over a year, born small for gestational age at 36 weeks, Weber lateralizes to the unaffected ear with air conduction better than bone conduction bilaterally → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → delayed-onset sensorineural hearing loss
  8. 3 yo F with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, an older brother in hearing aids since infancy, normal development → Connexin 26 mutation → the commonest cause of hereditary sensorineural loss
  9. The most common cause of nonhereditary sensorineural hearing loss in children → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → often asymptomatic at birth, with hearing loss that may be delayed
The sensorineural mimics Aminoglycosides cause sensorineural loss (hair cell damage), never conductive · Ménière = episodic vertigo + fluctuating hearing loss + tinnitus · presbycusis = gradual, high-frequency, elderly · vestibular schwannoma = unilateral SNHL (sensorineural hearing loss) + tinnitus → MRI. All have normal otoscopy. The tuning forks separate them from otosclerosis.
Pairs with Part I Cholesteatoma and Chronic Ear Drainage expands the cholesteatoma line of this brief into its own topic.

The Red Eye

Three questions triage every red eye

The decision point

1. Is visual acuity affected? 2. Is there true deep pain (not gritty or itchy)? 3. Is the pupil, cornea, or globe abnormal? Any "yes" means this is not simple conjunctivitis and points toward urgent ophthalmology.

Conjunctivitis types
TypeDiscriminatorTreatment
Viral (adenovirus)Watery, follicular tarsal conjunctiva, preauricular node, URI prodromeSupportive — cool compresses, artificial tears
BacterialPurulent, lids stuck shut on waking, papillaryErythromycin ointment or polymyxin-trimethoprim
Contact lens wearerAny red eye → think PseudomonasFluoroquinolone; remove lens; urgent ophtho if infiltrate
AllergicITCHING is the hallmark; bilateral, cobblestone papillaeOlopatadine, ketotifen
Gonococcal EmergencyHyperacute (<24 h), copious purulence — can perforate the corneaIM ceftriaxone + irrigation + urgent ophtho
ChlamydialChronic >3 weeks, follicular, sexually active adultOral azithromycin/doxycycline + treat partners
The can't-miss red eyes
DiagnosisThe tellAnswer
Acute angle-closure glaucomaSevere pain, halos, vomiting, mid-dilated fixed pupil, hard globe; triggered by dark rooms or anticholinergicsTimolol + apraclonidine + pilocarpine + IV acetazolamide → laser peripheral iridotomy
HSV keratitisDendritic ulcer on fluorescein, ↓ corneal sensationTopical trifluridine or oral acyclovir — never steroids
Herpes zoster ophthalmicusV1 vesicles + Hutchinson signOral antivirals + ophtho
Anterior uveitisCiliary flush, cell and flare, consensual photophobia; HLA-B27, JIA, sarcoidTopical steroid + cycloplegic — the one place prednisolone is right
ScleritisBoring pain that wakes from sleep, does not blanch with phenylephrine; RA, GPASystemic NSAIDs/steroids
EpiscleritisSectoral, minimal pain, blanches with phenylephrineSupportive
EndophthalmitisPost-op or post-injection, pain + ↓VA + hypopyonIntravitreal antibiotics — emergency
Orbital cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegiaCT orbits + IV antibiotics (preseptal has none of those)
Scenario bank
  1. 24 yo M with bilateral watery red eyes, a preauricular node, recent URI and normal vision → Viral conjunctivitis → supportive care
  2. 24 yo M contact lens wearer with pain, photophobia and a corneal infiltrate → Bacterial keratitis → urgent ophthalmology, never patch
  3. 62 yo F with severe pain, halos, a mid-dilated fixed pupil and vomiting → Acute angle-closure glaucoma → topical agents plus acetazolamide
  4. 24 yo M with a dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining → HSV keratitis → topical antiviral, never steroids
  5. 30 yo M with ankylosing spondylitis, photophobia, ciliary flush and anterior chamber cells → Anterior uveitis → topical steroid plus cycloplegic
  6. 55 yo F with rheumatoid arthritis and severe boring eye pain that wakes her at night → Scleritis
  7. Newborn with purulent conjunctivitis on day 3 of life → Gonococcal conjunctivitis → parenteral ceftriaxone
  8. 9 yo M with bilateral eye itching, watery discharge, cobblestone papillae under the upper eyelids, nasal congestion each spring → Allergic conjunctivitis → olopatadine or ketotifen drops
  9. 5 yo F, 3 days of photophobia with lids crusted shut on waking, diffuse bulbar and palpebral erythema, mucopurulent discharge, acuity unchanged → Bacterial conjunctivitis → Mucopurulent discharge with normal acuity
  10. School-age child with mucopurulent conjunctivitis and no contact lens use; the likeliest organism → Haemophilus influenzae → With S pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis
  11. Child with an undifferentiated red eye and mucopurulent discharge; which is contraindicated before slit-lamp examination → Topical corticosteroid drops → Steroid on an unrecognized HSV keratitis worsens it
Neonatal conjunctivitis by day of onset Day 0–1 chemical · day 2–5 gonococcal → IM/IV ceftriaxone + irrigation · day 5–14 chlamydial → oral erythromycin, or oral azithromycin as the alternative (counsel on pyloric stenosis with either) · day 6–14 HSV (herpes simplex virus) → IV acyclovir. Birth prophylaxis (erythromycin ointment) prevents gonococcal but not chlamydial disease.
How NBME framed it A home birth delivered by the father stood in for missing eye prophylaxis, and Kawasaki disease was listed under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.
Pairs with Part II Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child covers the red eye that comes from a tender lump on the lid margin, and its lid-swelling mimics. Ask: is there a lump on the lid?
The steroid rule Steroids are indicated in anterior uveitis (topical) and scleritis (systemic). Topical steroids are catastrophic in HSV (herpes simplex virus) keratitis, bacterial/fungal keratitis, and undifferentiated red eye. If you cannot name the diagnosis with certainty, do not give steroids.

Sinusitis and Its Complications

A normal neuro exam is a low-sensitivity test

Source vignette Pt — child with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a double-worsening pattern, now with focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness; neurologic examination nonfocal · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned oral antibiotics, lumbar puncture and urgent neuroimaging
The decision point

A double worsening course indicates acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. Focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness are intracranial extension flags. Vomiting is worst in the early morning because ICP (intracranial pressure) rises in recumbency. These flags call for urgent imaging rather than oral antibiotics.

"Neurologic examination is nonfocal" does not exclude a brain abscess; frontal lobe abscesses are neurologically silent until late. When raised ICP is suspected, image before LP (lumbar puncture).

Sinusitis complications — features → next step
ComplicationFeaturesNext step
Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitisEyelid swelling; normal EOM, normal vision, no proptosis; often from a skin break such as an insect bite, eczema or traumaOral antibiotics
Orbital (postseptal) cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegia, ↓ acuity; usual source is ethmoid or maxillary sinusitis (cheek tenderness), less often a maxillary dental infection or orbital traumaCT orbits and sinuses + IV antibiotics; surgical drainage for an abscess
Pott puffy tumorFrontal bone osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess — doughy forehead swellingCT/MRI + IV antibiotics + surgery
Brain abscess EmergencyFocal headache, early-morning vomiting, drowsiness, ± focal deficitCT/MRI → ring-enhancing lesion; IV antibiotics + drainage
MeningitisDiffuse headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobiaImage first if ICP signs, then LP
Cavernous sinus thrombosisCN III, IV, V1–V2, VI palsies, proptosis, spreads bilaterallyMRI/MRV + IV antibiotics
Where orbital cellulitis comes from Sinusitis — the most common source; ethmoid or maxillary, spreading contiguously into the orbit (streptococci, S aureus); cheek tenderness points to the maxillary sinus · Dental infection — only maxillary (upper) teeth sit near the sinus and orbit; a mandibular abscess, especially on the opposite side, does not explain it · Skin break (eczema, insect bite, trauma) — causes preseptal cellulitis, anterior to the orbital septum, without proptosis, vision change or painful eye movements · Otitis media — spreads to the mastoid or meninges, not the orbit
Signs of raised ICP & abscess essentials Early-morning headache and vomiting (recumbent CO₂ retention → cerebral vasodilation) · papilledema · altered mental status · late, the Cushing triad. Contiguous sinus spread means Streptococcus anginosus/milleri group and anaerobes; CT with contrast shows a ring-enhancing lesion, and MRI with restricted diffusion on DWI separates abscess from tumor. Treat with vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole plus drainage. Ring-enhancing differential: abscess, glioblastoma, metastasis, toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, lymphoma.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Clinical course and neurologic historyFirstDouble worsening with no red flagsUncomplicated sinusitis: oral antibiotics, no imaging
Eye exam: movements, acuity, proptosisBy branchPain with eye movement or proptosisOrbital cellulitis: CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast, which shows the source sinus and any abscess to drain
CT or MRI of the head with contrastNextRing-enhancing lesionBrain abscess; order for morning vomiting or drowsiness, even with a nonfocal exam
MRI with diffusion-weighted imagingSupportsRestricted diffusion in the lesionAbscess rather than tumor
MRI with MR venographyBy branchCavernous sinus thrombosisCranial nerve palsies with proptosis, becoming bilateral
Drainage with Gram stain and cultureConfirmsStreptococcus anginosus group or anaerobesNames the organism; drainage is also treatment
Lumbar puncture before imagingSkipRisk of herniation with raised pressureImage first; LP without CT only when no pressure signs
Scenario bank
  1. Eyelid swelling but normal EOM and vision → Preseptal cellulitis → oral antibiotics
  2. Proptosis and painful eye movement → Orbital cellulitis → CT orbits + IV antibiotics
  3. Doughy swelling over the forehead → Pott puffy tumor → imaging + IV antibiotics + drainage
  4. CN VI palsy with proptosis becoming bilateral → Cavernous sinus thrombosis → MRV
  5. Fever + nuchal rigidity with no ICP signs → Lumbar puncture without prior CT
  6. A child has rhinosinusitis with a double-worsening course, focal headache, and 12 days of symptoms. The neurologic examination is nonfocal, and there is no vomiting or drowsiness. → Uncomplicated acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  7. Ring-enhancing lesions in an HIV patient with CD4 <100 → Toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma → multiple basal ganglia lesions favor toxoplasmosis
  8. Child with morning headache and vomiting plus ataxia, no infection → Posterior fossa tumor → same ICP syndrome, non-infectious cause
  9. Adult with a ring-enhancing lesion and recent dental infection → Brain abscess by contiguous spread
  10. 5 yo M, right eye pain since morning with blurred vision for several hours; history of frequent ear infections, recurrent sinusitis, many dental caries, atopic dermatitis and hives after mosquito bites; T 39.4, HR 120; right eye acuity 20/70 with proptosis, conjunctival injection, periorbital swelling and redness, and pain with limited adduction; normal fundus; right cheek tenderness; a large foul-smelling cavity in the left lower second molar → Bacterial sinusitis → Orbital cellulitis from contiguous ethmoid or maxillary spread
  11. 6 yo with a week of purulent rhinorrhea, now fever, proptosis, painful and limited eye movements, and falling visual acuity despite 2 days of IV antibiotics; CT shows ethmoid sinusitis with a large subperiosteal orbital abscess → Surgical drainage with continued IV antibiotics → Orbital abscess
  12. 7 yo with a week of nasal congestion and cough, now fever, a swollen red upper eyelid, proptosis and pain with eye movement; normal mental status and no neck stiffness → CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast → Orbital cellulitis; start IV antibiotics
Pairs with Part II Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child covers the hordeolum and dacryocystitis that can spread into preseptal cellulitis. Ask: is the swelling a focal lump or the whole lid?
Transferable rule A normal neurologic exam is a low-sensitivity test for intracranial pathology. When the symptom pattern is positional and progressive (morning headache, morning vomiting, declining alertness), symptoms of raised ICP (intracranial pressure) outweigh a reassuring exam.
