edits.html:
Night Blindness

Night blindness: the fundus exam identifies the cause · pale disc or cupped disc, and is the front of the eye normal

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo F, 2 months of progressive difficulty seeing at night while driving, with a near-collision; strict vegan eating a variety of plant products · Exam — visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally; lashes, conjunctivae and cornea unremarkable; pupils equal and reactive, extraocular muscles intact, red reflex equal; midperipheral visual field defect both eyes · Fundus — optic disc pallor, attenuation of retinal vessels and focal areas of discoloration, bilateral · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned cataract, open-angle glaucoma, retinal detachment, retinitis pigmentosa and vitamin A deficiency
The decision point

Night blindness has a short differential, and the fundus exam settles it. Optic disc pallor with attenuated retinal vessels and patchy pigmentary change is the triad of retinitis pigmentosa. Rods degenerate first; they are densest in the midperiphery and serve dim-light vision. So the first symptom is night blindness, and the first field defect is midperipheral. Acuity stays 20/20 until cones are lost late. A normal red reflex and 20/20 vision exclude cataract. A pale rather than cupped disc excludes glaucoma. A two-month progressive course with no tear excludes detachment. The normal cornea and conjunctivae exclude vitamin A deficiency, whose ocular disease is xerophthalmia.

Defining criteria Retinitis pigmentosa, funduscopic triad — retinal vessel attenuation from reduced metabolic demand, waxy optic disc pallor from nerve gliosis and atrophy, and abnormal retinal pigmentation in a bone-spicule pattern, which is a late finding · Symptom sequence — night blindness first, then progressive midperipheral field loss, then decreased acuity late when cones are involved; onset from age 10 into adulthood · Xerophthalmia — the mimic's gate: dryness of the cornea and conjunctivae with night blindness, which is what vitamin A deficiency looks like in the eye · Glaucomatous disc — an increased cup-to-disc ratio; the retinitis pigmentosa disc is pale and not cupped
Pertinent positives & negatives Two months, progressive — a degeneration, not an event; excludes retinal detachment · Visual acuity 20/20 — cones intact, so early disease, and inconsistent with cataract · Red reflex equal bilaterally — no lens opacity, closing cataract independently · Cornea and conjunctivae unremarkable — no xerophthalmia, closing vitamin A deficiency on examination rather than on diet · Midperipheral field defect — the rod-dense zone, the signature distribution of early disease · Optic disc pallor, not cupping — the single most efficient discriminator · Vessel attenuation with focal discoloration — the pigmentary retinopathy itself · Age 17 — open-angle glaucoma is a disease of late adulthood
Night blindness — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Retinitis pigmentosaInherited photoreceptor degeneration, rods first; most legally blind by 40Disc pallor plus vessel attenuation plus bone-spicule pigment; night blindness then midperipheral field loss— (the answer)
Vitamin A deficiencyMalabsorption, restrictive diet or povertyXerophthalmia — dry cornea and conjunctivae, Bitot spots, corneal ulcerationCornea and conjunctivae normal; varied plant diet
Open-angle glaucomaPainless gradual peripheral field loss in late adulthoodIncreased cup-to-disc ratio with raised intraocular pressureAge 17, and the disc is pale rather than cupped
Retinal detachment Can't missAcute; myopia, trauma or prior surgeryFloaters, flashes, a curtain; tear or elevation on fundusTwo-month progressive course, no tear or elevation
CataractAge, steroids, diabetes; glare from headlights at nightDecreased acuity plus diminished red reflex plus lens opacity20/20 acuity with an equal red reflex
Management, in one line Refer for formal visual fields and electroretinography, with genetic counselling. Treatment slows rather than reverses the disease, and most patients are legally blind by age 40. Care therefore focuses on prognosis, low-vision support and family screening rather than cure.
Decision spine Is the acuity normal? — Yes, so the problem is not the lens or the macula · Is the red reflex intact? — Yes, so cataract is out · Acute or progressive? — Two months and worsening, so not a detachment · Pale disc or cupped disc? — Pale means retinitis pigmentosa, not glaucoma · Is the front of the eye normal? — Yes, so no xerophthalmia and not vitamin A · Where is the field defect? — Midperipheral, which is the rods
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Visual acuity and red reflexFirst20/20 with a normal red reflexExcludes cataract; cones are spared early
Slit-lamp exam of cornea and conjunctivaeFirstNo xerosis or Bitot spotsExcludes vitamin A deficiency
Dilated fundus examNextDisc pallor, attenuated vessels, bone-spicule pigmentRetinitis pigmentosa; a cupped disc is glaucoma
Formal visual fieldsSupportsMidperipheral field lossRod loss
ElectroretinographyConfirmsReduced or absent rod responsesRetinitis pigmentosa
Genetic testing, exam of relativesCausePathogenic variant identifiedInheritance pattern; screen first-degree relatives
Serum vitamin A for a vegan dietSkipNot needed with a normal cornea and conjunctivaeThe fundus, not the diet, names the cause
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo F, 2 months of progressive night blindness, visual acuity 20/20, midperipheral field defect both eyes, funduscopy shows optic disc pallor with attenuated vessels and focal pigmentary change, cornea and conjunctivae normal → Retinitis pigmentosa → rods degenerate before cones
  2. 4 yo recently resettled refugee with night blindness, dry conjunctivae with Bitot spots and corneal xerosis → Vitamin A deficiency → oral vitamin A supplementation
  3. 17 yo F with night blindness, midperipheral field loss and a fundus showing disc pallor with vessel attenuation → Electroretinography with formal visual fields and genetic counseling → confirming retinitis pigmentosa
  4. 68 yo M with painless gradual peripheral field loss, intraocular pressure 26 and a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.8 → Open-angle glaucoma → topical prostaglandin analog
  5. 55 yo M with sudden floaters and flashes followed by a curtain across the temporal field → Same-day ophthalmology referral → retinal detachment
  6. 72 yo F troubled by glare from oncoming headlights at night, visual acuity 20/60, diminished red reflex → Cataract → lens opacification
  7. Why night blindness is the earliest symptom of retinitis pigmentosa → Rod photoreceptors degenerate before cones → rods serve dim-light vision and the midperiphery
  8. Newly diagnosed 17 yo F with retinitis pigmentosa who has an asymptomatic 12 yo brother → Ophthalmologic examination with genetic counseling for first-degree relatives → most cases are inherited
Decoy note Strict vegan is the decoy. She also eats a variety of plant products, which counters that risk factor. When a risk factor is qualified straight away, the qualifier takes precedence.
Pearls Examination versus history — diet, occupation and travel raise hypotheses, and the examination settles them; when the two disagree, trust the fundus · Pale disc is retinitis pigmentosa; cupped disc is glaucoma — one descriptive word separates a teenager's genetic degeneration from an older adult's pressure disease · vitamin A deficiency and retinitis pigmentosa share night blindness and differ at the front of the eye · Acuity is preserved until late because rods go first, so 20/20 vision argues for the diagnosis in a patient with field loss, not against it · night driving trouble in an older adult is cataract glare; in a teenager with a normal red reflex it is retinal
Pairs with Part I The Red Eye covers everything anterior to the lens, the territory of xerophthalmia. Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers what a plant-only diet actually requires supplementing; that brief's answer is B12, not vitamin A. Ask: is the front of the eye normal, and is the disc pale or cupped? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin A deficiency itself (ask: is fat being malabsorbed, and are there Bitot spots?).
Transferable rule A demographic or lifestyle detail is a prior, not a finding. If a diet, job or country of origin is the only thing still supporting an option, that option is the decoy. Switch only when a stated finding is incompatible with your current answer.
Salient decoyVitamin A deficiency: strict vegan plus night blindness is a taught pairing and it outpolled the key, but ocular vitamin A deficiency is xerophthalmia and the front of the eye is explicitly normal.
Unchecked attributeOpen-angle glaucoma: painless peripheral field loss is genuinely its presentation, but it is a disease of late adulthood and the disc is cupped, not pale.
Unchecked attributeRetinal detachment: a retinal cause of field loss, but acute with floaters, flashes and a visible tear; this is two months of steady progression.
True-fact-wrong-slotCataract: difficulty driving at night from headlight glare is a real cataract complaint, but it requires reduced acuity and a diminished red reflex, both normal here.

Tics and Tic Disorders

Classify the movement first · is the behaviour involuntary, or is it neutralising an obsession

Source vignette Pt — 7 yo M, behavioural concerns at school; repeats exactly what other children say, and last year raised his hand repeatedly then said he was just stretching when called on; plays alone to avoid bullying, prefers books and jigsaw puzzles; says he tries not to be bad but sometimes cannot help it · History — father has obsessive-compulsive disorder; growth tracking at the 60th percentile · Exam — frequent head turning and shoulder shrugging; remorseful and anxious on mental status examination · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned atomoxetine, exposure and response prevention, fluoxetine, methylphenidate, parent management training and risperidone
The decision point

Three of the described behaviours are tics. Head turning and shoulder shrugging are motor tics. Repeating exactly what other children say is echolalia, a vocal tic. The hand-raising, explained away afterward, is a motor tic he covered for; this is how school-age children manage tics. Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic, present over a year with onset before 18, is Tourette syndrome. Among the offered options, the therapy that targets tics is the antidopaminergic risperidone. It is a second-generation antipsychotic, preferred over first-generation agents for its adverse-effect profile.

Defining criteria Tourette syndrome — multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, not necessarily concurrent, present over 1 year, with onset before age 18; more common in boys, typically presenting age 6 to 15 · Motor tics — facial grimacing, blinking, head or neck jerking, shoulder shrugging, tongue protrusion · Vocal tics — grunting, sniffing, snorting, throat clearing, barking, yelling, echolalia, coprolalia · Compulsion — the mimic's gate: a repetitive behaviour performed in response to an obsession to reduce anxiety; absent an obsession, a repetitive movement is a tic · Treatment tiers — habit reversal training is behavioural and first-line; antidopaminergic agents when tics impair function, meaning second-generation antipsychotics, dopamine depleters such as tetrabenazine, or alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine and clonidine
Pertinent positives & negatives Head turning and shoulder shrugging — two motor tics, the examination finding that names the disorder · Echolalia — the required vocal tic; without it this is a chronic motor tic disorder, not Tourette · Symptoms over more than a year — meets the duration criterion, and the waxing and waning course is itself characteristic · Reads books, completes jigsaw puzzles, plays alone quietly — sustained attention, which argues against ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) despite the classroom referral · Remorseful, says he cannot help it — insight and distress consistent with tics, not oppositional defiance · No obsessional thoughts described — closes OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), and with it both exposure therapy and fluoxetine · Bullied and avoiding peers — functional impairment, the gate that licenses pharmacotherapy · Father with OCD — a family-history decoy; OCD and Tourette are comorbid and heritable together, which is why it is plausible and why it is not diagnostic
Repetitive behaviour in a school-age child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Tourette syndromeBoys 6 to 15; waxing and waning; comorbid ADHD and OCDMultiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic over 1 year— (the answer)
Obsessive-compulsive disorderObsessions driving compulsions that relieve anxietyA named obsession; the behaviour neutralises itNo obsessional thought anywhere in the stem
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorderInattention or hyperactivity across settingsFidgetiness, cannot sustain attention, impairment in two or more settingsReads and completes puzzles alone; behaviour is school-confined
Oppositional defiant disorderAngry mood, defiance and vindictiveness toward authorityDeliberate defiance without remorseHe is remorseful and distressed by the behaviour
Provisional tic disorderTics present less than 1 yearSame movements, shorter durationSymptoms span more than a year
Management, and the option list that was not offered Behavioural therapy with habit reversal training is first-line and is the choice whenever it is offered. When tics impair function, add an antidopaminergic or an alpha-2 agonist. Clonidine and guanfacine are both guideline-supported for tics and ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) together. Guanfacine is often preferred first for its milder sedation profile; this is clinical practice, not a guideline ranking. When the guideline first-line treatment is not on the option list, choose the best offered treatment for the diagnosis you made. Do not change the diagnosis to fit an offered drug.
Decision spine Describe the movements. — Head turning, shrugging, hand-raising are motor tics · Is there a sound? — Echolalia is a vocal tic · How long? — Over a year and waxing and waning, so Tourette rather than provisional · Is any behaviour neutralising an obsession? — No, so not OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), and the exposure therapy and fluoxetine options fall · Can he sustain attention? — Books and puzzles, so not ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder), and the stimulants fall · Is function impaired? — Bullied and isolated, so pharmacotherapy is licensed
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo M with head turning, shoulder shrugging and repetition of classmates' words for over a year, now bullied and socially isolated → Risperidone → Tourette syndrome with functional impairment
  2. 8 yo M with mild motor and vocal tics who is performing well academically and has friends → Habit reversal training → behavioral therapy precedes medication when tics are mild
  3. 9 yo M with motor tics who also describes intrusive thoughts of contamination relieved only by repeated handwashing → Comorbid obsessive-compulsive disorder → exposure and response prevention
  4. 7 yo M with head jerking and eye blinking for 8 months and no vocal tic → Provisional tic disorder → duration under 1 year with no vocal tic
  5. How antipsychotic agents suppress tics in Tourette syndrome → Dopamine receptor blockade → tetrabenazine instead depletes presynaptic dopamine
  6. 8 yo with Tourette syndrome and inattention impairing him at home and at school → A stimulant for the comorbid ADHD → stimulants are not contraindicated in Tourette — methylphenidate reduces ADHD symptoms without worsening tics (AAN 2019)
  7. 7 yo with Tourette syndrome whose parents request medication to reduce the tics → Fluoxetine → an SSRI treats comorbid OCD, not tics
  8. 10 yo with moderate impairing tics whose parents decline an antipsychotic because of weight-gain concerns → Guanfacine → alpha-2 agonists are an accepted alternative
Decoy note Family history of obsessive-compulsive disorder in the father is the strongest decoy. It is true in a way that makes it worse: obsessive-compulsive disorder and Tourette syndrome are comorbid and co-heritable. So this history is consistent with Tourette syndrome while pointing toward obsessive-compulsive disorder. The child's own words describe the involuntariness of a tic, not the anxiety relief of a compulsion.
Pearls Describe the movement before you name the disorder — a family history does not change what a movement is · A compulsion requires an obsession; with no obsessional thought, a repetitive behaviour is a tic and exposure therapy is the wrong tool · Echolalia is a vocal tic, and it upgrades a chronic motor tic disorder to Tourette syndrome. It is the criterion most often missed, because repeating words does not seem like a vocal tic · tics wax and wane, so a behaviour that stopped last year and was replaced by a new one is natural history, not improvement · stimulants for comorbid ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) are not contraindicated in Tourette ⚠︎, despite older teaching
Pairs with Part II School Difficulty in a Child is the nearest relative. It shares the same referral route, a school behaviour complaint. The resolution is opposite: there the private interview reveals a learning disorder, and here the examination reveals tics. Ask: what exactly is the child doing, and is it involuntary?
Transferable rule A family history raises the prior probability, but the phenomenology decides. When a relative's diagnosis and a child's behaviour are both given, first describe the behaviour in neutral terms. If the behaviour is involuntary and stereotyped, it is a tic, whatever the family carries.
Salient decoyExposure and response prevention: the father's OCD and the anxious remorseful affect sell it, but exposure therapy treats compulsions driven by obsessions and no obsession is described.
True-fact-wrong-slotFluoxetine: first-line for paediatric OCD and depression, but the same category error, and an SSRI does not suppress tics.
Class-vs-memberParent management training: targets oppositional defiant disorder; he is remorseful rather than defiant, and it does nothing for tics.
Class-vs-memberMethylphenidate and atomoxetine: ADHD is genuinely comorbid with Tourette, but these behaviours are tics and sustained attention on books and puzzles argues against ADHD.

Posterior Fossa Localization

Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral · side first, then structure

Source vignette Pt — 9 yo M, left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, listing to the left, bilateral papilledema, left facial numbness · Q — the most likely localization; options spanned the left cerebellar hemisphere, the right middle cerebellar peduncle and the left frontal lobe
The decision point

Every cerebellar finding is on the left. He has dysmetria reaching with the left hand, slow rapid alternating movements on the left, and a gait that lists to the left. Cerebellar output decussates twice, so the crossings cancel and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral. This rules out the right middle cerebellar peduncle.

Limb dysmetria is hemispheric. A midline vermian lesion gives truncal and gait ataxia with spared limbs. He has both, so the mass is hemispheric and large enough to disturb midline structures. This fits the left facial numbness, because the trigeminal system serves the face ipsilaterally. It also fits the papilledema from fourth-ventricular compression.

Defining criteria Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral — and the patient falls and lists toward the side of the lesion · Hemisphere — limb ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor · Vermis or midline — truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and titubation · Central nystagmus — direction-changing and gaze-evoked, versus peripheral which is unidirectional and suppresses with fixation · Raised-pressure headache — daily or progressive, worse on waking or lying flat, poorly analgesia-responsive, with papilledema
Where is the mass - localizing the pediatric brain tumor
LocationIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Cerebellar hemispherePilocytic astrocytoma most classically, cystic with a mural noduleIpsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, falls toward the lesion
Cerebellar vermisMedulloblastoma, early fourth-ventricular obstructionTruncal and gait ataxia with a wide base, relatively spared limbs
Middle cerebellar peduncleCarries pontocerebellar inputAtaxia is still ipsilateral, so a right peduncle gives right-sided signs
Brainstem, ponsDiffuse intrinsic pontine gliomaCrossed findings — cranial nerve palsy one side, long-tract weakness the other
Pineal regionGerminoma, adolescent boysParinaud syndrome — upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation
Frontal lobeSupratentorial gliomaContralateral weakness, personality change, expressive aphasia
Occipital lobeSupratentorial massContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Neurologic exam and fundoscopyFirstIpsilateral limb ataxia with papilledemaCerebellar hemisphere mass with raised pressure
MRI of the brain with contrastNextPosterior fossa mass with hydrocephalusCystic with a mural nodule: pilocytic astrocytoma; midline: medulloblastoma
Serum and CSF AFP and beta-hCGBy branchElevated markers with Parinaud syndromePineal germinoma
Resection with histologyConfirmsNames the tumor typePilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma or ependymoma
MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytologyStagingDrop metastases or tumor cells in the CSFMedulloblastoma staging
Lumbar puncture with papilledemaSkipRisk of herniationImage first
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M with left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, listing to the left, bilateral papilledema and left facial numbness → A mass in the left cerebellar hemisphere → cerebellar signs are ipsilateral
  2. Why a lesion in one cerebellar hemisphere produces signs on the same side of the body → Cerebellar output decussates twice → the two crossings cancel
  3. 6 yo M with truncal and gait ataxia, a wide-based stance, minimal limb dysmetria and a midline fourth-ventricular mass → Medulloblastoma of the vermis → seeds drop metastases through the CSF
  4. 5 yo F with progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies, right hemiparesis and diffuse expansion of the pons → Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma → crossed findings localize to the pons
  5. 12 yo M with an upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation → MRI of the brain with serum and CSF tumor markers → pineal germinoma
  6. 9 yo M with papilledema and cerebellar signs in whom a lumbar puncture is proposed → Obtain MRI of the brain instead → lumbar puncture risks herniation
  7. 9 yo M whose MRI shows a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus and who has become drowsy → Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation → CSF diversion then resection
  8. 7 yo F with newly confirmed medulloblastoma → MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology → medulloblastoma seeds the cerebrospinal fluid
  9. 4 yo M with 3 weeks of headache waking him from sleep and morning vomiting, with a normal neurologic examination → MRI of the brain → a normal examination does not exclude a posterior fossa tumor
Papilledema forbids the tap With a posterior fossa mass, lumbar puncture risks herniation. Image first. Posterior fossa tumours are 54 to 70% of childhood brain tumours but only 15 to 20% of adult brain tumours. In a child, ataxia with raised pressure is therefore infratentorial until imaged.
Pearls Cerebellum — ipsilateral · Face — ipsilateral · Body long tracts — contralateral, so crossed findings mean brainstem · Medulloblastoma seeds the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid), so staging requires neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology · Red-flag pediatric headache: wakes from sleep, worse on waking, morning vomiting, progressive over weeks, any focal sign, or a child under six · Peripheral vertigo nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation; central nystagmus is direction-changing and unsuppressed
Pairs with Part II Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant carries posterior fossa tumour as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization that identifies it. Part I Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers the anterior compartment. Ask: which region does the endocrine or visual sign point to? Part I Headache in a School-Age Child covers the workup before localization. Ask: is the headache primary or secondary, and do the fundi show raised pressure?
Transferable rule Localize side first and structure second. The cerebellum is the one place where signs stay on the same side as the lesion.
Class-vs-memberThe right middle cerebellar peduncle is the right region on the wrong side.
True-fact-wrong-slotPineal masses are common in children but produce Parinaud syndrome, which he does not have.

Benign Neonatal Rashes

Sort by onset · reassurance vs. removable cause

The decision point

Reassure when a benign, self-limited rash has no modifiable cause. Remove the trigger when a benign rash has an identifiable, removable trigger. Miliaria rubra has its cause in the history: onesies under pajamas under a fleece swaddle. Treat it by unwrapping the baby, not by waiting it out.

Sort by onset age first. At birth: pustular melanosis and milia. Birth to 3 days: erythema toxicum. Any age but never at birth: miliaria rubra. About 3 to 4 weeks: cephalic pustulosis. A rash outside its window, erythema toxicum-like pustules on the palms or soles, vesicles or crusting, or a febrile or irritable infant is not benign until the dangerous mimics below are excluded.

Benign neonatal rashes
RashOnsetAppearance & distributionManagement
Neonatal pustular melanosisAt birthNonerythematous pustules that rupture into hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale; forehead, neck, lower back; may involve palms and soles; more common in darker skin; neutrophilsObserve; pustules clear in days, pigment fades over months
MiliaAt birthFirm white papules on the nose and cheeks, no erythema; retained keratinObserve; resolves within a month; do not extract
Erythema toxicum neonatorumBirth to 3 daysPoorly demarcated erythematous macules and papules that become small firm pustules on an erythematous base; trunk and proximal limbs; spares palms and soles; well infant; eosinophils (smear rarely needed)Reassurance; resolves in about a week
Miliaria rubraAny age, never at birthFine erythematous papules in occluded and intertriginous areas; blocked sweat glandsCool environment, no overbundling, thin cotton; low-potency steroid if severe
Neonatal cephalic pustulosisAbout 3 to 4 weeksErythematous papules and pustules on the face and scalp only; no comedones; linked to MalasseziaObserve (weeks to months); low-potency steroid or ketoconazole if severe; avoid oily emollients
Seborrheic dermatitis2–6 weeksGreasy yellow scale, scalp and foldsEmollient, gentle brushing
Scenario bank
  1. 2 day old M, erythematous macules with central pustules on the trunk and proximal limbs, palms and soles spared, well-appearing → Erythema toxicum neonatorum → reassurance
  2. 2 wk M dressed in a onesie, pyjamas and a fleece swaddle, with tiny clear vesicles → Miliaria rubra → remove the extra layers
  3. Newborn with pustules rupturing to hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale → Transient neonatal pustular melanosis → reassurance
  4. 2 wk M with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base and irritability → Neonatal herpes simplex → PCR and IV acyclovir
  5. 6 wk M with greasy yellow scale on the scalp → Seborrheic dermatitis → reassurance with an emollient
  6. Newborn with 1 mm white papules across the nose → Milia → reassurance
  7. 3 wk F bundled in a fleece swaddle in a warm room, with fine erythematous papules in the neck folds and axillae → Lighter, cooler clothing → miliaria rubra has a removable cause: thin cotton and a cool room
  8. 10 day old, afebrile and feeding well, with clustered vesicles on an erythematous base on the scalp → HSV PCR and IV acyclovir → any vesicular rash in a neonate is HSV until proven otherwise
  9. 4 mo with a beefy red diaper rash involving the inguinal creases, with satellite papules → Topical nystatin → candida involves the creases; irritant dermatitis spares them
  10. 4 mo with blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks noted on a well-child exam → Document the finding and reassure → congenital dermal melanocytosis is benign; documenting it prevents confusion with abuse
  11. 2 day old boy born at 40 weeks by vaginal delivery, breastfeeding every 2 to 3 hours and voiding, with a diffuse rash noticed this morning; mother gets occasional cold sores with stress, last one a year ago; normal vital signs; pustules on erythematous bases over the extremities and scattered erythematous papules on the trunk and back, palms and soles spared → Reassurance only → Erythema toxicum neonatorum; resolves in about a week
  12. 3 week old girl, well and feeding, with erythematous papules and pustules on the cheeks, forehead and scalp; no comedones; trunk, palms and soles clear → Neonatal cephalic pustulosis → Observation; ketoconazole or low-potency steroid only if severe
  13. 6 day old boy, afebrile and feeding well, circumcised on day 2, with a few pustules and flaccid blisters around the circumcision site, some ruptured to honey-colored crusts; no other skin findings → Topical mupirocin → Staphylococcal pustulosis
Not benign: red flags and the dangerous mimics Red flags — palms or soles involved in an otherwise erythema toxicum picture, vesicles or crusting, or fever or irritability; any one means the rash is not benign. Pustular melanosis, present at birth and nonerythematous, is the benign rash that may reach the palms and soles · Neonatal HSV — clustered vesicles on an erythematous base, days 5–14 → PCR (polymerase chain reaction) + IV acyclovir. Any vesicular rash in a neonate is HSV (herpes simplex virus) until proven otherwise · Congenital syphilis — maculopapular rash that includes the palms and soles, snuffles, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, no pustules → IV penicillin · Staphylococcal pustulosis — localized pustules, vesicles or bullae that rupture to honey-colored crusts, in the diaper area or at a wound such as a circumcision → topical mupirocin · Blueberry muffin rash — TORCH (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus) · Langerhans cell histiocytosis — looks seborrheic but is petechial and doesn't resolve · Maternal cold sores — do not diagnose HSV in a well 2-day-old with erythematous pustules and spared palms and soles. Base the diagnosis on the morphology and the infant's well appearance.
Diaper rash rule Candida involves the inguinal creases (beefy red + satellite papules → nystatin). Irritant contact dermatitis spares them (convex surfaces only → barrier cream). · Congenital dermal melanocytosis — blue-grey macules over the sacrum and buttocks, most common in darker-skinned infants, benign and self-resolving by age 3–5 years; document on exam to avoid confusion with non-accidental trauma
Transient color changes Acrocyanosis (symmetric blue-purple hands and feet with crying or cold), cutis marmorata (symmetric lacy violaceous mottling of the limbs that changes with temperature) and harlequin color change (sharply demarcated redness of one side of the body) are clinical diagnoses that need no treatment.
Pairs with Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the non-cutaneous half of the same principle: transplacental hormone, physiologic, self-limited.
How NBME framed it Erythema toxicum appeared as small yellow papules on a red base; each decoy fits another rash: staphylococcal or herpes culture, potassium hydroxide prep, topical steroid.
Transferable rule Before choosing pure reassurance, scan the history for a modifiable exposure: bundling, a soap, a detergent, a medication, a position. When the history describes the environment, removing that exposure is the treatment.

Diaper Dermatitis

Diaper rash that improved on a barrier, then worsened: superinfection · folds spared or folds involved

Source vignette Pt — 18 mo F, one week of diaper rash that improved on petrolatum and zinc oxide and is now worsening; fussy during changes, eating and sleeping normally; diarrheal illness a week ago, resolved; attends day care, no affected classmates · Exam — afebrile with normal vitals; beefy-red confluent plaques involving the inguinal creases with satellite papules; remainder normal · Q — the best next step in management; options spanned oral amoxicillin, topical antifungal, topical permethrin, oral zinc and screening for sexual abuse
The decision point

The diagnosis rests on the rash's trajectory, not its morphology. Barrier therapy is the correct and sufficient treatment for irritant contact dermatitis. A rash that got better on it and then got worse has therefore acquired something the barrier does not treat. Two examination findings identify the cause: the rash involves the skinfolds and has satellite lesions. Irritant dermatitis spares the creases because the convex surfaces contact the wet diaper and the depths of the folds are protected. Candida does the opposite and thrives in the warm, occluded crease. Satellite papules beyond the border of the main plaque are the hallmark of Candida. The recent diarrhea explains the mechanism: fecal bacteria raise local pH and compromise the barrier. Candida albicans from the gastrointestinal tract then colonises the skin. Treat with a topical antifungal applied under the barrier ointment, not instead of it.

Defining criteria Candida dermatitis — beefy-red confluent plaques that involve the skinfolds, with satellite lesions; the second most common diaper rash, a yeast superinfection of irritant dermatitis, treated with a topical antifungal · Irritant contact dermatitis — erythematous papules and plaques on convex surfaces that spare the skinfolds; the most common diaper rash, treated with a topical barrier · Satellite lesion — a discrete erythematous papule beyond the border of the main plaque; the finding that separates the two above when both are red and confluent
Pertinent positives & negatives Improved on barrier, now worsening — the trajectory that defines superinfection; a rash failing first-line therapy from the start would instead question the original diagnosis · Involves the inguinal creases — excludes irritant contact dermatitis, which spares them · Satellite papules — rules in Candida; no other diaper rash produces them · Recent resolved diarrhea — the risk factor, not a diagnosis; it raises stool pH and seeds the skin · Rash confined to the diaper area — excludes scabies, which involves trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles · No perioral dermatitis, no alopecia, diarrhea already resolved — excludes acrodermatitis enteropathica, which needs chronic diarrhea plus the other two · No verrucous papules, no genital ulcers, no adenopathy or fever — no finding that would raise a sexually transmitted infection, and therefore none that licenses an abuse evaluation · Afebrile, eating and sleeping normally — not systemically ill; fussiness confined to changes is local pain
Diaper dermatitis — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Candida dermatitisYeast superinfection of an irritant rash; after diarrhea, antibiotics, or with thrushBeefy-red plaques in the creases with satellite lesions; worse despite barrier— (the answer)
Irritant contact dermatitisStool and urine breakdown of convex skin; the commonest diaper rashSpares the skinfolds; no satellites; responds to barrierCreases involved, and barrier therapy already failed
Perianal group A streptococcal diseaseBacterial; painful defecation and stool withholdingBright red, sharply demarcated perianal rash with or without anal fissuresThe rash is not perianal or sharply demarcated
ScabiesMite; refractory diaper rash in infants with itchy contactsDiffuse — trunk, axillae, neck, palms and solesConfined to the diaper area; no affected contacts
Acrodermatitis enteropathicaZinc deficiency; rare and refractoryChronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis plus alopeciaDiarrhea resolved; no perioral rash, no alopecia
Sexually transmitted infection Can't missThe concern behind any genital rashVerrucous papules in HPV, or ulcers with fever and adenopathy in HSV, or mucopurulent discharge in gonorrhea and chlamydiaNone of those lesions is present
Management, in one line Apply topical nystatin or clotrimazole beneath a barrier ointment. The antifungal treats the yeast, and the barrier keeps stool and urine off skin that is still broken.
Decision spine Did correct first-line therapy work and then stop working? — Yes means look for a superinfection, not a new diagnosis · Folds spared or folds involved? — Involved means Candida · Any satellite lesions? — Yes confirms it · Does the rash leave the diaper area? — No, so scabies is out · Is the diarrhea chronic, with perioral rash and alopecia? — No, so zinc is out · Any lesion that is itself a sexually transmitted infection? — No, so nothing licenses an abuse workup
Scenario bank
  1. 18 mo F, one week of diaper rash worsening despite petrolatum and zinc oxide, diarrheal illness a week ago now resolved, beefy-red confluent plaques involving the inguinal creases with satellite papules → Topical nystatin under a barrier ointment → candidal diaper dermatitis
  2. 8 mo M, erythematous papules and plaques over the convex buttocks and thighs with the inguinal creases spared and no satellite lesions → Barrier ointment with more frequent diaper changes → irritant contact dermatitis
  3. 3 yo F, bright red sharply demarcated perianal plaque with an anal fissure and painful defecation → Oral amoxicillin → perianal group A streptococcal disease
  4. 4 mo M receiving amoxicillin for otitis media, now with beefy-red confluent rash in the inguinal creases and white plaques on the buccal mucosa → Topical nystatin to the diaper area plus oral nystatin → candidal dermatitis with thrush
  5. 5 mo M with a refractory diaper rash plus papules on the trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles; his mother itches at night → Scabies → permethrin for the infant and all household contacts
  6. 7 mo with a refractory perineal rash, perioral dermatitis and diffuse alopecia, and chronic diarrhea → Acrodermatitis enteropathica → oral zinc supplementation
  7. Why a recent diarrheal illness increases the risk of candidal diaper dermatitis → Fecal bacteria raise local pH and compromise the skin barrier → gut Candida albicans then colonizes the broken skin
  8. 10 mo F with beefy-red confluent plaques involving the inguinal creases and satellite lesions → A high-potency topical corticosteroid → occlusion causes atrophy and striae
  9. 5 yo F, 5 days of burning with urination and vulvar redness, afebrile, no medications or serious illness, abuse denied; moderate erythema over the vulva and entire perineum reaching the perianal skin, no vesicles or pustules, scant white discharge at the introitus; vaginal culture pending → Topical nystatin → candidal vulvovaginitis
  10. 4 yo F, toilet-trained, finished amoxicillin for otitis media last week; vulvar itching, erythema over the vulva and perineum extending into the inguinal creases with satellite papules, thick white discharge at the introitus → Candidal vulvovaginitis → topical antifungal such as nystatin
Decoy note The history items "The parents are separated" and "attends day care" raise the abuse and contagion hypotheses, respectively, but neither is an examination finding. No classmate has a rash, which excludes contagion from day care. The initial improvement on barrier therapy is the single most informative detail. It proves the original diagnosis was right and something was added.
Pearls Improvement then deterioration on correct therapy means a second organism, not a wrong diagnosis; the same pattern occurs in otitis with a new fever after day 3, in cellulitis with an abscess forming, and in eczema herpeticum · Folds are the discriminator: irritant dermatitis spares them and Candida involves them · Satellite lesions are near-specific for cutaneous candidiasis · Antifungal under the barrier, not instead of it, because the skin is still broken and still in contact with stool · risk factors that should make you expect Candida before you see it are recent diarrhea, recent antibiotics, and oral thrush · Candidal vulvovaginitis in a toilet-trained girl: dysuria, redness over the vulva and whole perineum reaching the perianal skin, and white discharge at the introitus; treat with topical nystatin, since topical agents are preferred for superficial candidiasis · Risk factors for candidal vulvovaginitis: diabetes mellitus, recent antibiotics and corticosteroids; none is required
How NBME framed it The stem opens on burning with urination and closes on a pending culture, while the diagnosis sits in the white discharge and perineal-to-perianal redness.
Pairs with Part I Benign Neonatal Rashes covers the one-line diaper rule and the newborn rashes that need no treatment at all. Ask: does the rash involve the creases, and are there satellites? Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers vaginal discharge in a newborn girl: is the discharge white with perineal redness, or mucoid in a well newborn?
Transferable rule When a correct treatment works and then stops working, the diagnosis was not wrong; something was added. Ask what the first treatment does not cover, and look for the finding that identifies it.
True-fact-wrong-slotOral amoxicillin: bacterial superinfection is a real cause of refractory diaper rash, but perianal strep is bright red and sharply demarcated around the anus, and this rash is neither.
Unchecked attributeTopical permethrin: scabies genuinely causes refractory diaper rash in infants, but it is diffuse across trunk, axillae, palms and soles, and no contact is affected.
Salient decoyOral zinc: she had a diarrheal illness, but acrodermatitis enteropathica needs chronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis and alopecia, and hers resolved in days.
Sequencing trapScreening for sexual abuse: an abuse evaluation is triggered by findings that are themselves sexually transmitted infections; none is present, and a social detail is not a finding.
Unchecked attributeIntramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin: this treats gonorrhea and chlamydia, which give mucopurulent discharge, not white discharge; in a prepubertal child past the newborn period either infection also prompts a sexual abuse evaluation.
Unchecked attributeOral acyclovir: herpes simplex virus gives painful vesicles on a red base; this perineum has no vesicles or pustules.
Salient decoyOral amoxicillin: burning with urination suggests cystitis, but redness over the vulva and perineum with white discharge points to candidal vulvovaginitis.
True-fact-wrong-slotOral metronidazole: it treats bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis but has no activity against Candida.

edits.html:
Teratogenic Exposures

Identify the teratogen from the malformation pattern · Which single malformation belongs to only one agent?

Source vignette Pt — newborn male, growth restricted at 2.5 kg at 38 weeks, mother 29 with no prenatal care, forceps delivery for fetal heart rate abnormalities, Apgars 6 and 8 · Exam — microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate, and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges · Q — which maternal history would be found; options spanned alcohol use, cocaine use, lisinopril use, phenytoin use and untreated syphilis
The decision point

Cleft palate and distal phalangeal hypoplasia are the two findings that alcohol does not cause. Together they are fetal hydantoin syndrome, from in utero exposure to a folate-antagonising antiepileptic, classically phenytoin. The drug crosses the placenta and produces low fetal folate with high oxidative metabolites. The wide anterior fontanelle and microcephaly complete the pattern. Fetal alcohol syndrome shares the microcephaly and the midface hypoplasia but has no association with clefting. Its signature is a smooth philtrum with a thin vermilion border and short palpebral fissures, none of which is described in this newborn.

Defining criteria Critical periods — 0–2 weeks all-or-none (death or no effect); 3–8 weeks organogenesis, the structural-malformation window; beyond 8 weeks growth restriction, CNS and functional deficits rather than structural defects · Fetal hydantoin syndrome — microcephaly, wide anterior fontanelle, cleft lip and palate, distal digit and nail hypoplasia, cardiac defects, neural tube defects · Fetal alcohol syndrome — smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures, midface hypoplasia, microcephaly, and no clefting · Antiepileptic management — switch to a lower-risk agent such as levetiracetam 6 months before conception, 4 mg folic acid from 3 months before conception, and make no changes after conception; screen with alpha-fetoprotein and anatomy ultrasonography
Teratogenic medications — drug to signaturethe malformation that belongs to only one agent
DrugSignature defect
PhenytoinDistal digit and nail hypoplasia, cleft lip/palate, wide fontanelle, microcephaly, cardiac, neural tube defects
ValproateNeural tube defects — the highest-risk antiepileptic
CarbamazepineNeural tube defects, less than valproate
TopiramateOral clefts, growth restriction, neurodevelopmental effects
PhenobarbitalCardiac, orofacial and urogenital malformations
IsotretinoinMicrotia and small ears, microcephaly, cleft palate, cardiac, thymic hypoplasia, hydrocephalus
MethotrexateLimb and craniofacial defects, cranial ossification defects, neural tube defects, abortion
ACE inhibitors / ARBsRenal dysgenesis → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence, growth restriction
WarfarinNasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia; fetal haemorrhage later
LithiumEbstein anomaly
MethimazoleAplasia cutis, oesophageal atresia, facial anomalies
TetracyclinesTooth discolouration, inhibited long-bone growth
FluoroquinolonesCartilage and bone toxicity
DiethylstilbestrolClear cell adenocarcinoma of vagina and cervix, uterine malformation
ThalidomidePhocomelia
Pertinent positives & negatives Cleft palate — present in hydantoin and absent in fetal alcohol syndrome; the single most discriminating finding in this newborn · Hypoplasia of the distal phalanges — near-specific for antiepileptic exposure · Wide anterior fontanelle — part of the hydantoin pattern, and easily overlooked · Symmetric growth restriction with microcephaly — shared by alcohol, phenytoin, isotretinoin and cocaine, so it discriminates nothing · No smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border or short palpebral fissures — the fetal alcohol facial triad is absent · No prenatal care — explains why a maternal medication history was never taken · No snuffles, hepatomegaly or maculopapular rash — congenital syphilis is excluded on its own features
Decision spine Is there a structural malformation? — Yes → exposure fell in the 3–8 week window · List the findings that only one agent causes. — Cleft palate and distal digit hypoplasia · Which agent causes both? — Phenytoin · Check the nearest mimic. — Alcohol shares the microcephaly but never the cleft · Is there an alternative explanation for the growth restriction? — It is nonspecific and belongs to every option · What would have prevented it? — Pre-conception switch plus 4 mg folate
Scenario bank
  1. Newborn male, growth restricted at 38 weeks to a mother with no prenatal care, with microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges → Maternal phenytoin use → fetal hydantoin syndrome
  2. Child with a smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures and midface hypoplasia with microcephaly, and no cleft lip or palate → Fetal alcohol syndrome → alcohol is not associated with clefting
  3. Newborn with severe oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, flat facies and positional limb deformities; the mother took an antihypertensive throughout pregnancy → Maternal ACE inhibitor use → renal dysgenesis causing Potter sequence
  4. Newborn with Ebstein anomaly on echocardiography whose mother is treated for bipolar disorder → Maternal lithium use → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve
  5. Newborn with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses on radiograph; the mother has a mechanical mitral valve → Maternal warfarin use in the first trimester → low molecular weight heparin should have been substituted
  6. 26 yo on valproate for epilepsy who hopes to conceive in about a year → Switch to levetiracetam now and begin 4 mg folic acid → change the regimen before conception, not after
  7. 28 yo on carbamazepine who presents newly pregnant at 9 weeks gestation → Switching to a different antiepileptic now → organogenesis is largely complete and overlapping agents doubles exposure
  8. 22 yo about to start isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne → Two negative pregnancy tests 19 or more days apart with two forms of contraception → iPLEDGE risk-management requirements
  9. 2-week-old boy born at 38 weeks to a 27-year-old first-time mother after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with no maternal alcohol or drug history recorded; birth weight about 2.3 kg; length, weight and head circumference at the 5th percentile; short palpebral fissures, flat midface, small jaw and thin upper lip; soft systolic murmur with normal femoral pulses; mild hypotonia → Fetal alcohol syndrome → the face and growth decide without an exposure history; the palpebral fissures are short, not upslanting
Anticoagulation in pregnancy Low molecular weight heparin and unfractionated heparin have no fetal effects; warfarin is teratogenic to bone and cartilage. Heparins do not cross the placenta, and warfarin does. Patients with mechanical valves therefore take LMWH in the first trimester, warfarin in the second and third, and unfractionated heparin near delivery.
Pearls Cleft plus distal digit hypoplasia is phenytoin; alcohol affects the philtrum and the palpebral fissures, not the palate or the fingertips · Timing predicts the kind of damage — before 2 weeks all-or-none, 3–8 weeks structure, after 8 weeks growth and brain · Change antiepileptics before conception, never after; once pregnancy is recognised organogenesis is mostly done, and switching adds seizure risk plus a second teratogen · Valproate is the worst antiepileptic and levetiracetam the usual substitute · Oligohydramnios with Potter sequence should suggest ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors as well as renal agenesis, two different first causes of the same cascade · Lithium → Ebstein anomaly is the one psychiatric-drug-to-cardiac-lesion pairing worth memorising outright
Fetal alcohol syndrome without an exposure history FAS (fetal alcohol syndrome) can be diagnosed from the examination when no exposure history is given. The 2016 revised Institute of Medicine criteria require all four of these. First, 2 of 3 facial features: short palpebral fissures (at or below the 10th percentile), a thin upper lip vermilion and a smooth philtrum. Second, height or weight at or below the 10th percentile. Third, a head circumference at or below the 10th percentile, a structural brain anomaly, or recurrent nonfebrile seizures. Fourth, neurobehavioral impairment, which under age 3 means developmental delay. Confirmed alcohol exposure is not required; a confirmed absence of exposure excludes the diagnosis. Short fissures point to FAS. Upslanting fissures with epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease point to Down syndrome.
How NBME framed it No maternal alcohol history was given; the face, with length, weight and head size at the 5th percentile, made the diagnosis in a hypotonic 2-week-old. Short palpebral fissures separated it from Down syndrome, whose fissures slant upward; trisomy 13, fragile X, Klinefelter syndrome and congenital toxoplasmosis were the other decoys.
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves covers the oligohydramnios cascade that this brief reaches from the drug side. Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers Ebstein anomaly. Ask: which single malformation does only one drug on the roster cause?
Transferable rule To identify a teratogen, find the one malformation that belongs to only one agent. Ignore the shared features that every candidate agent can produce.
Unchecked attributeAlcohol use: shares microcephaly and growth restriction, but has no association with cleft lip or palate, and none of the facial triad is described.
True-fact-wrong-slotCocaine use: causes preterm delivery, abruption and growth restriction, but no congenital defects.
Class-vs-memberLisinopril: a named teratogen, but it produces renal failure and Potter sequence, not clefting or digit hypoplasia.
True-fact-wrong-slotUntreated syphilis: symptomatic cases show snuffles, hepatomegaly and a maculopapular rash, none present here.
Unchecked attributeDown syndrome: hypotonia and a soft murmur fit, but Down syndrome gives upslanting palpebral fissures with epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease. These fissures are short.
True-fact-wrong-slotTrisomy 13 syndrome: it causes cleft lip and palate, holoprosencephaly, small eyes, scalp defects and extra digits, none of which this newborn has.
Unchecked attributeFragile X syndrome: the long face, large ears, prominent jaw and large testes appear later in childhood and after puberty; this newborn has a small jaw.
Unchecked attributeKlinefelter syndrome (seminiferous tubule dysgenesis): boys with 47,XXY look normal at birth; small testes, tall stature and gynecomastia appear at puberty.
Salient decoyCongenital toxoplasmosis: growth restriction fits, but it brings chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, scattered intracranial calcifications and an enlarged liver and spleen, not a facial pattern.

Primary Amenorrhea

uterus present or absent, then read the FSH · Is there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low?

Source vignette Pt — 15 yo, no menses, distressed at looking younger than peers; no headache or visual change; mother and grandmother menarche at 13; height below the 3rd percentile, weight 20th · Exam — no breast development, normal external genitalia, Tanner 2 pubic hair; urine beta-hCG negative · Imaging — pelvic ultrasonography shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries · Labs — FSH 60 (normal under 40), LH 52 (normal 5–25) · Q — the next step in management, then the underlying cause; options spanned hormone measurements, imaging, karyotype and reassurance
The decision point

Primary amenorrhea is no menarche by 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 without them. The first step is pelvic ultrasonography. The obstruction can sit anywhere from the hypothalamus and pituitary to the ovary, uterus and vagina. Imaging is the only test that answers the anatomical half of that chain in one move. Every hormonal test is interpretable only once you know whether there is a uterus. Uterus present → read the FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone). High FSH with high LH (luteinizing hormone) is primary ovarian insufficiency. With short stature, that is Turner syndrome: gonadal dysgenesis from loss of an X. Turner syndrome gives streak ovaries and absent oestrogen, while intact adrenals still produce pubic hair. Uterus absent → read the pubic hair. Pubic hair present means the androgen receptor works, so the diagnosis is 46,XX Müllerian agenesis. Absent pubic hair means it does not, so the diagnosis is 46,XY complete androgen insensitivity.

Defining criteria Primary amenorrhea — no menarche by age 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 without them · First step — pelvic ultrasonography, to establish whether a uterus is present before any hormone is measured · Uterus present, FSH high — primary ovarian insufficiency; with short stature, Turner syndrome (45,X on karyotype, FISH if mosaicism is suspected) · Uterus present, FSH low or inappropriately normal — central: MRI for a hypothalamic or pituitary lesion, or GnRH deficiency, Cushing syndrome, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea · Uterus absent — serum testosterone: female-range with normal pubic hair is Müllerian agenesis (46,XX); male-range with absent pubic and axillary hair is complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)
Primary amenorrhea — the two-step algorithmanatomy first, then the gonadotropins
StepFindingConclusionConfirms, then
Before step 1: urine hCGNegativePregnancy excludedThen the ultrasound
1. Pelvic ultrasoundUterus presentGo to the FSHAnatomy only; the FSH picks the branch
1. Pelvic ultrasoundUterus absentGo to the testosterone and the pubic hairAnatomy only; the karyotype settles the branch
2a. FSH high± short staturePrimary ovarian insufficiency → karyotype → Turner if 45,X45,X karyotype, FISH if mosaicism is suspected; then echocardiogram and renal ultrasound
2a. FSH low or normal± anosmia, weight loss, athlete, cushingoidCentral: MRI, or functional, Kallmann or CushingMRI shows a sellar lesion, or is normal with anosmia in Kallmann; check TSH and prolactin
2b. Testosterone female-rangePubic hair presentMüllerian agenesis (46,XX) → evaluate the renal tract46,XX karyotype; then renal ultrasound
2b. Testosterone male-rangePubic hair absentComplete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)46,XY karyotype; then gonadectomy, usually after puberty, for tumor risk
Pertinent positives & negatives Height below the 3rd percentile — the key Turner clue; almost all patients develop short stature, often the only feature besides amenorrhea · No breast development with Tanner 2 pubic hair — oestrogen absent, adrenal androgens intact; the dissociation that points at the ovary rather than the axis · FSH 60 and LH 52 — loss of oestrogen negative feedback; hypergonadotropic hypogonadism · Prepubertal uterus with small ovaries — streak gonads; the uterus is present but was never stimulated · No headache or visual change — argues against a sellar mass, which is the central branch · Normal external genitalia — the genital tubercle is unaffected in every diagnosis on this list · Negative beta-hCG — pregnancy must be excluded before anything else
Decision spine Is the definition met? — No menarche by 13 without secondary characteristics → yes · What is the first test? — Pelvic ultrasound; anatomy before hormones · Is there a uterus? — Yes → read the FSH · Is the FSH high or low? — High → ovarian failure, not a central cause · Is she short? — Below the 3rd percentile → Turner · What confirms it? — Karyotype showing 45,X, with FISH for mosaicism if normal
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo with no menarche, no breast development, Tanner 2 pubic hair, height below the 3rd percentile, normal external genitalia and a negative urine beta-hCG → Pelvic ultrasonography → establish the anatomy before measuring hormones
  2. 14 yo with primary amenorrhea and no secondary sexual characteristics in whom ultrasonography has confirmed a uterus → FSH level measurement → it separates central (low or normal) from peripheral (high) causes
  3. 15 yo with primary amenorrhea, no breast development and short stature; ultrasound shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries and FSH is 60 with LH 52 → Turner syndrome → 45,X on karyotype
  4. 16 yo distance runner with primary amenorrhea, Tanner 4 breast and pubic hair, normal external genitalia; ultrasound shows normal ovaries and no uterus → Müllerian agenesis → failure of paramesonephric duct development
  5. 16 yo with primary amenorrhea, Tanner 4 breast development, absent pubic and axillary hair, tall stature and no uterus on ultrasound → Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome → 46,XY with male-range testosterone
  6. 15 yo with primary amenorrhea, a uterus on ultrasound, FSH 3 and LH 2, normal weight and normal sense of smell → MRI of the brain → a low FSH points centrally
  7. 16 yo newly diagnosed with Müllerian agenesis → Renal ultrasonography → renal tract anomalies are commonly associated
  8. 17 yo gymnast training twice daily with a BMI of 16, primary amenorrhea, a uterus present, and low FSH and LH → Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea → energy deficit suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
  9. Why girls with Turner syndrome develop pubic hair but no breast development → Adrenarche is intact while ovarian estrogen production fails → the adrenal glands are unaffected by loss of an X chromosome
Test order A 17-hydroxyprogesterone, a testosterone, a karyotype and an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) are each the right move in some branch of this algorithm. Each is uninterpretable until the ultrasound has shown whether there is a uterus, so ordering it first is one step too early. Reassurance is right for a girl under 15 who has secondary sexual characteristics. It is wrong here because the definition is already met and her height is below the 3rd percentile.
Pearls Ultrasound first, always — every hormone in this workup is uninterpretable until you know whether there is a uterus · Uterus present → FSH. Uterus absent → pubic hair. These two questions, in that order, resolve almost every case of primary amenorrhea · High FSH means ovarian failure; low FSH means a central cause — the gonadotropins tell you which end of the axis to investigate · Turner patients have pubic hair, because adrenarche is adrenal and the adrenals are normal; pubic hair without breast development points to ovarian failure · Müllerian agenesis and androgen insensitivity both present with an absent uterus and differ in pubic hair · Müllerian agenesis obliges a renal ultrasound — the ducts develop alongside the urinary tract, so anomalies travel together · An athlete with amenorrhea can still have a structural cause; functional hypothalamic amenorrhea never explains missing anatomy
Pairs with Part I Adolescent Abnormal Uterine Bleeding covers the opposite complaint on the same axis, too much bleeding rather than none, and shares the immature-axis physiology. Part II Puberty covers the staging vocabulary this brief uses throughout. Ask: is there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low?
Transferable rule When a workup has an anatomical branch and a hormonal branch, image first. A hormone measured before you know the anatomy produces a number you cannot interpret.
Sequencing trap17-hydroxyprogesterone: real in the amenorrhea workup for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, but indicated only once a uterus is confirmed and with suggestive features.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance and observation: the definition is already met, and height below the 3rd percentile is itself a finding.
Unchecked attributeAndrogen insensitivity: requires an absent uterus; she has one.
Mirror twinDevelopmental failure of the urogenital sinus: produces a vaginal dimple with a uterus present, the mirror image of Müllerian agenesis.
Salient decoyAbnormal GnRH pulsatility: twice-daily training is a real risk factor, but central causes give low gonadotropins and cannot remove a uterus.

Preventive Care: Ranking Interventions

Most beneficial intervention: rank by magnitude of benefit

Source vignette Pt — 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia · Q — the intervention that most reduces mortality; options spanned smoking cessation, a statin and lisinopril
The decision point

When every option is guideline-supported, rank them by magnitude of benefit. Smoking cessation reduces all-cause mortality more than any drug on the list. It cuts CV (cardiovascular) risk substantially within 1–2 years and approaches never-smoker risk over ~15 years.

Ranking preventive interventions — why each loses
ChoiceLegitimate claimWhy it loses
Smoking cessation—Largest mortality benefit of any intervention
LisinoprilDiabetic + HTN → ACE-I preferred, especially with albuminuriaBP only mildly elevated, no proteinuria — real but smaller
StatinDiabetic 40–75 → indicated regardless of LDLTrue indication, but ~25% relative risk reduction — cessation dwarfs it
↑ HCTZBP above goalMarginal, and worsens glucose and lipids in a diabetic
↑ MetforminA1c above targetGlycemic control reduces microvascular complications; weak macrovascular effect (UKPDS)
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia; which most reduces mortality → Smoking cessation
  2. 58 yo M who has already quit; which intervention is next → A statin
  3. 58 yo M asking how soon quitting helps → Cardiovascular risk falls within 1 to 2 years
  4. 58 yo M ready to quit within the month → Varenicline plus behavioral support
  5. 58 yo M who is not ready to quit → Motivational interviewing
  6. 58 yo M with 30 pack-years who quit 5 years ago → Annual low-dose CT screening
The hierarchy to bank For macrovascular outcomes, the order of benefit is smoking cessation > BP (blood pressure) control > statin > glycemic control. If the patient smokes and smoking cessation is an option, choose it. The exception is an outcome limited to a specific organ. For risk of nephropathy progression, choose an ACE-I (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor) and BP control. For microvascular complications, choose glycemic (A1c) control. Lifestyle advice ranks low when vague ("recommend exercise") and high when specific and high-magnitude (smoking or alcohol cessation).
